A file is named after the table it changes, matched exactly, capital letters included: VehicleData.csv, never vehicledata.csv. A file naming a table that does not exist is skipped, and the log says so.

You may use either format, or both. Within one mod the .csv files are applied first and the .json files after, so a command can refine a row a CSV file added.

docs.title: Single cells - <Table>.json
docs.text:
A list of commands, run top to bottom. This is the format to reach for: it touches only the values you name and leaves everything else alone.

{
  "Commands": [
    { "Command": "Replace", "Id": "gladiator", "Cells": { "Fuel Capacity": 350, "Movement Speed": 7 } },
    { "Command": "Add",     "Id": "storage_box", "Cells": { "Planks": 3, "Metal": 1 } },
    { "Command": "Remove",  "Id": "Chair", "Columns": [ "Tarp" ] },
    { "Command": "Remove",  "Id": "Drawer" }
  ]
}
Command Fields What it does Replace Id, Cells Changes only the listed cells of an existing row. Everything else keeps its value. Add Id, Cells Adds a new row. Only possible in ResourceCost and PropsInfluence (see Adding and removing rows). Remove with Columns Id, Columns Clears the listed cells of a row. Remove without Columns Id Removes the whole row. Only in ResourceCost and PropsInfluence.

Rules of the format:

  • Plain JSON - no comments, no trailing commas.
  • Command and Id ignore capitalisation. The keys inside Cells and the entries in Columns are column headers and must match exactly, including spaces.
  • Values may be written as JSON strings, numbers or booleans - 300, 1.5, true and "300" all work.
  • An empty string, a string of only spaces, or null in Cells clears that cell, the same as listing it under Columns in a Remove.
  • Remove does not take Cells; list the cells to clear in Columns.
  • At most 200 commands per file. A file that does not parse, or has no Commands, is skipped whole.
  • Each command is judged on its own - a bad one is skipped with a warning and the rest still apply.

docs.title: Whole rows - <Table>.csv
docs.text:
A spreadsheet file carrying complete rows. Use this when you would rather edit a table in a spreadsheet program and ship the finished rows.

Name,Value
TurboTimeScaleMultiplier,20
RandomActionChatProbability,0.6
  • The header row must list exactly the table's columns: the id column first, then every value column, in any order, none missing and none extra. The id column's own header is ignored, so only the value columns have to match.
  • Include only the rows you want to change - a file does not have to cover the whole table.
  • A row whose id matches a built-in row replaces that row completely. Ids ignore capitalisation.
  • Give every row the same number of cells as the header row. A short row makes the file unreadable and the whole file is skipped; extra cells beyond the header are silently ignored.
  • A cell that contains a comma must be quoted, as a spreadsheet program does: "Sleep,Chill". A line break inside a quoted cell is not supported - it ends the row.
  • At most 200 rows per file. Fully blank lines and lines starting with # are ignored, so you can leave notes. A line that starts with an empty id cell but has other cells is read as a continuation of the row above, and that row is then refused as spanning several lines.
  • The same id on two separate lines makes the file unreadable; on two neighbouring lines it is treated as one row and refused.
  • Each row is judged on its own - a bad row is skipped and the built-in row stays.

docs.title: Columns only take the kind of value they already hold
docs.text: A column that holds numbers in every built-in row takes only numbers; one that holds TRUE/FALSE takes only those. Movement Speed = fast is refused. Columns that hold text are freer, but most of them still have a rule of their own - the tables further down say which values each one accepts.

docs.title: Empty cells
docs.text:
A cell may only be left empty in a column where the game already leaves some row empty. Everywhere else, blanking a cell is refused, because the game has no "no value" case for it.

Two columns are special and are filled in for you instead of being left blank:

  • Any ResourceCost cell you leave out, clear, or set to "" becomes 0. An Add therefore only needs the resources that actually cost something.
  • Associated Task in BuildingComponents becomes None, meaning "this object gives no task".

docs.title: Adding and removing rows
docs.text:
You are normally changing cells of rows that already exist. Whole rows can only be added or removed in two tables, because everywhere else the game and your save files expect a fixed set of ids:

Table Rows can be added or removed ResourceCost yes, for any built-in object or aircraft id PropsInfluence yes, for any built-in object or aircraft id every other table no

An added row must use an id that already exists as a building object or an aircraft - you are giving an existing thing a build cost or a mood effect it did not have, not inventing a new thing.

docs.title: Rows that take up several lines
docs.text:
A few tables spread one row over several lines, because that row holds a list - a task with several settings, a mood effect with one variant per bed type. A single mod row cannot express a list, so those rows are refused. The table sections below name them.

In ResourceCost only, some rows carry a leftover heading in their Money cell and so count as several lines. There a whole-row CSV is the fix: it rewrites every cell and tidies the row up at the same time. The affected ids are KickstarterCustomMonument, RadioTower, window_wood, window_tent, window_brick, window_hangar, window_concrete, Distillery, ParkingLarge and gravel.

docs.title: Checking what happened
docs.text:
Every accepted change and every refusal is one line in the game's log, Player.log (where to find it: How mods work). On Windows there is also an HTML version in the same folder that is easier to read. The label at the start of each line is the mod's id.

[Mod my_balance_mod] CSV/ResourceCost.json command 1 replaced cells Planks of row 'wall_wood'.
[Mod my_balance_mod] CSV/VehicleData.csv overrides built-in row 'gladiator'.
[Mod my_balance_mod] CSV/PropsInfluence.json command 4 removed row 'Drawer'.

A refusal names the file, the row or command number, and the reason:

[Mod my_balance_mod] CSV/VehicleData.json command 3 rejected: 'Fight Power' exceeds 2x the highest built-in value (60).
[Mod my_balance_mod] CSV/AirBaseData.json command 1 rejected: 'Missions Per Week' holds numbers in every built-in row; 'seven' is not one.

Note

These lines are written as information and warnings. The released game writes mainly errors to its log, so you may not see them there. In that case check the effect in the game instead - load a level and look at the value you changed.

A misspelled table name or a header row that does not match still produces a skipped: line naming the file. If you see no [Mod ...] lines at all and the change does not show, the game did not pick the mod up: the CSV/ folder was still empty when the game started (press Refresh in the Mods window), the mod is switched off in the Mods window, or the mod folder is a symbolic link or junction, which is never followed.

docs.title: Finding a table's column headers
docs.text: The game ships header templates for four tables (BuildingComponents, PropsInfluence, ResourceCost and VehicleData) in GroundOfAces_Data/StreamingAssets/Modding/Templates/ inside the installation folder (on macOS: GroundOfAces.app/Contents/Resources/Data/StreamingAssets/Modding/Templates/). For the rest, the column list is on this page, and every table section links the built-in file. Or ask the game: write a deliberately wrong header, load once, and the log prints the columns it expected.

docs.title: Load order
docs.text: Mods are applied in the order described on Which mod wins - Workshop first, then your own, lower LoadOrder first. When two mods change the same row, the later one wins for the cells it touches: a whole-row CSV replaces everything an earlier mod did to that row, a Replace only the cells it names. A mod switched off in the Mods window contributes nothing.

docs.title: When changes take effect
docs.text:
CSV tables are rebuilt every time a level is loaded - return to the main menu and load again. The same happens when the main menu or the map editor opens. Edit a file while a level is running and the change appears on the next load, so you can try out values without restarting. A file you keep open in a spreadsheet program is still read.

A brand-new mod folder, a CSV/ folder that was still empty when the game started, or a changed config.json needs the game to look at the mod list again: press Refresh in the Mods window (main menu → Mods) and then load a level, or restart the game.

docs.title: The tables
docs.text:
Thirty tables can be modded. Three files that exist in the game but are not loaded - ResourceDegradation, StartTimeValues and StateInfluence - cannot.

Each section lists the columns, what values they take, and what the built-in rows use. Where a column has no special rule, only the generic ones above apply.

docs.title: VehicleData - aircraft
docs.text:
Built-in file: VehicleData.csv

One row per aircraft. Rows cannot be added or removed.

Column Value Built-in range Notes Name localization key airplane/spitfire must not be empty Type Fighter, Bomber, MultiRole, Special Crew comma list of seats; repeat a role for two seats Pilot, "Pilot,Gunner,Navigator" roles: Pilot, Gunner, Navigator, BombAimer, FlightEngineer, RadioOperator Runway Tier whole number 1–5 above 5 and no airstrip can serve it Parking Size whole number 0–2 above 2 and it can never park Victory Points Cost whole number 0–12 0 makes it free Movement Speed whole number 5 taxi speed; 0 and it never reaches the runway Landing Length whole number 60–170 longer than any buildable strip and it can never land Health whole number 100 Initial Integrity whole number 1000 hours of wear the aircraft can take before it is worn out (1000 h ≈ 41 days) Fuel Capacity whole number 200–1260 Voxel Size AxBxC 10x0x10 Fight Power min-max 0-0 … 43-60 0 ≤ min ≤ max, and max at most twice the highest built-in value Bomb Power min-max 0-0 … 50-80 same Recon Power min-max 5-10 … 42-60 same Manoeuvrability min-max 2-10 … 28-50 same Transport Capacity min-max 1-5 … 60-90 same Stealthiness min-max 10-48 … 88-98 same Wreck Resource Type /-list of resources Metal/RepairParts both wreck columns set, or both empty Wreck Resource Amount /-list of whole numbers 10/5 same length as the type list Low Caliber Ammo Capacity whole number 0–3300 GunAmmo carried; 0 = none High Caliber Ammo Capacity whole number 0–300 AntiAirAmmo; 0 = none Plane Bombs Capacity whole number 0–32 PlaneBombs; 0 = none

Warning

An aircraft already parked at your base keeps the health, integrity and fuel capacity it was built with. Only newly delivered aircraft pick up changed values - so a save made while a mod was active keeps that mod's numbers even after you remove it.

docs.title: AirBaseData - the HQ rank ladder
docs.text:
Built-in file: AirBaseData.csv

Rows 1–6, one per base category. All six must exist and their ids cannot change.

Column Value Built-in Notes Airstrip Tier whole number 1,2,3,4,5,5 required to reach the rank Minimum Airstrip Count whole number 1–5 Minimum Parking Count whole number 1–20 Missions Per Week whole number 6–18 slots the week offers; 0 and no missions are scheduled Minimum Missions Per Week whole number 2–10 above Missions Per Week makes the quota impossible Minimum Success Rate fraction, not percent 0.4–0.8 above 1 is unachievable Available Shipment Slots whole number 4–8 0 disables supply

docs.title: AirstripTiers
docs.text:
Built-in file: AirstripTiers.csv

Rows 1–5.

Column Value Built-in Notes Length whole number 80,120,140,160,200 tiers match on "length or more", so keep them ascending Width whole number 12,14,18,22,26 same Material text dirt, sand, gravel, concrete, tarmac must not repeat another tier's material; it also names the ResourceCost row that prices the surface Biome Id whole number 6,20,22,15,13 ground painted under the finished strip Build Time whole number 5,2,2,2,2 in-game minutes of work per tile for one crew member; two workers halve it

docs.title: Biomes
docs.text:
Built-in file: Biomes.csv

Rows 0–23, the ground types. All columns are numbers, so this table is easy to tune safely.

Column Built-in Notes Airstrip Tier 0–5 tier a runway laid on this ground counts as Character Speed Modifier 1 … 1.2 0 freezes anyone standing on it Airplane Speed Modifier 0.5 … 1.2 Degradation Penalty 0 … 0.2 extra wear on goods stored here Fire Spread Modifier 0.5 or 1

docs.title: ScrambleData - enemy aircraft in a scramble
docs.text:
Built-in file: ScrambleData.csv

Rows Fighter, Diver, Bomber. The names cannot change. All columns are whole numbers.

Column Built-in PlaneHealth 18, 26, 34 PlanePower 23, 17, 14 PlaneWinDealDamageMin / Max 15–120 - damage to your aircraft when the enemy wins PlaneLooseDealDamageMin / Max 5–25 - damage when the enemy loses

docs.title: AttacksComposition - what an air raid is made of
docs.text:
Built-in file: AttacksComposition.csv

The row id is the raid severity. Normal play reaches 1–25; rows 99, 101, 200 and 300 are not reached by the normal severity ladder and are kept for special raids. The ranges below describe rows 1–25; the four special rows go beyond them (9-9 bombers, 10-10 divers, 0-0 fighters) and point at themselves in the last two columns.

Column Value Built-in (rows 1–25) Notes Bombers min-max 0-0 … 4-6 whole numbers, 0 ≤ min ≤ max Divers min-max 0-0 … 6-6 same Fighters min-max 1-2 … 8-8 same LowAttacks whole number 1–14 severity used instead when the map is set to easier raids - must name a row this table has HighAttacks whole number 2–25 severity used when the map is set to harder raids - same

docs.title: EquipmentData - AA guns, searchlights, towers
docs.text:
Built-in file: EquipmentData.csv

Rows are equipment ids: Bofors40mm, Searchlight, RadioTower, VickersGunAA, OerlikonGun, Lookout, ControlTowerMetal, ControlTowerBrick, ControlTowerConcrete.

Column Value Built-in Notes Range number 10–70 0 makes the piece useless Damage number 0–6 0 switches the whole weapon off - fire rate, ammo and aiming are then ignored Fire Rate whole number 0–720 rounds per minute Ammo Type resource name or None GunAmmo, AntiAirAmmo, None, 0 anything that is not a resource name (None, 0) means the piece stores no ammo Ammo Capacity whole number 0–80 rounds loaded at once Ammo Load Time number 0–6.5 seconds to reload Ammo Storage whole number 0–500 0 means it never draws ammo Damage Bonus number 0 or 0.25 granted to others in range (searchlight) Firing Angle number 0, 140, 360 0 is read as a full circle Aiming Speed number 0–170 degrees per second Range Bonus number 0 or 16 granted to others in range (lookout) Attacker Priority Bombers, Divers, Fighters, Nearest, None anything else falls back to None

docs.title: BuildingComponents - objects and building parts
docs.text:
Built-in file: BuildingComponents.csv

One row per object, wall piece, floor, roof, workbench and piece of equipment. Rows cannot be added or removed.

Column Value Built-in Notes Dimensions WxHxD, or dynamic/1x0x1 for roofs 1x3x1, 1x0x1, 2x2x2 Build Time whole number 0–420 in-game minutes of work for one crew member; two workers halve it Health whole number 0–10000 the huge value marks the indestructible pieces Associated Task task name or None Sleep, Chill, UseEquipment, PlayPiano, UseTrainingObject, MonitorAirspace, UseRadio, SaluteTheFlag, Grieve, ListenToMusic, PlayDartboard, PlayGuitar, PlayBilliardTable, UsePlanningBoard pointing an object at a task its art does not fit is allowed, and looks wrong Users Limit whole number 0–5 0 on a usable object means nobody can use it Is Wall Deco TRUE/FALSE Is Floor Deco TRUE/FALSE Is Fireproof TRUE/FALSE Placement Requirement None, Indoors, Outdoors

Note

A Replace is checked against the finished row, so a row that leaves Dimensions or Users Limit empty cannot be patched unless you also set that cell in the same command - or ship the row as CSV. Empty Dimensions: PropagandaPoster, MusicPoster, AirplanePoster, CompanyMascotPoster, CurtainsClosed, CurtainsOpen, EntranceSign, tombstone, storage_box. Empty Users Limit: the workbenches and the three parking sizes.

docs.title: ResourceCost - what something costs to build
docs.text:
Built-in file: ResourceCost.csv

One row per object or aircraft id, one column per resource. Rows can be added and removed. A removed row means "no build cost". A cost of 0 means "not required", so zeroing every column has the same effect. An added row's id must be an existing BuildingComponents or VehicleData id; anything else is refused as "neither a built-in prop nor a built-in plane".

Every cell is a whole number, zero or more. The columns are:

Money  VictoryPoints  Trash  Wood  Clay  Sandbags  Stone  Food  RawWater  Herbs  Metal  Bricks
Planks  Tarp  Cement  Fuel  PurifiedWater  Meals  SimpleMedicine  Intel  Machinery  Electronics
LuxuryGoods  MilitaryConstruction  Camouflage  FoodRations  StrongMedicine  RepairParts  GunAmmo
AntiAirAmmo  PlaneBombs

Runway surfaces are rows here too - dirt, sand, gravel, concrete, tarmac - so changing gravel changes what a tier-3 runway costs per tile.

docs.title: PropsInfluence - the mood effect an object radiates
docs.text:
Built-in file: PropsInfluence.csv

One row per object that lifts or lowers the mood of crew nearby. Rows can be added and removed; an object without a row simply has no effect.

Column Value Built-in Notes Buff Name localization key prop_effects/organised_sleep must not be empty Radius number 0.5–50 in tiles; the control towers reach 20, 30 and 50 Associated Tasks Or Action comma list of task names Sleep, "Sleep,Chill", UseEquipment must not be empty. A name that matches no task is accepted and the effect simply never fires Effect 1 <signed number> <name> +0.5 Mood … +10 Mood, -1 Mood, -1.5 Energy, +2 Energy, +1 Confidence names: Mood, Confidence, Energy; the built-in rows go from -1.5 to +10 Effect 2 same, or empty Effect 3 same, or empty no built-in row uses it

The sign is part of the number, so 1 Mood means +1. Names are matched loosely, so +1 mood works. A name other than the three above is stored as a special effect (the game uses -1 Accident on the three control towers); an invented name is accepted and does nothing.

docs.title: MapObjects - trees, rocks, ponds and other harvestables
docs.text:
Built-in file: MapObjects.csv

One row per world object. Ids are used by map files and cannot change.

Column Value Built-in Notes LocKey_Name localization key map.obj.tree.name LocKey_Description localization key Dimensions WxHxD 1x4x1, 2x2x2, 3x1x3 Resource Harvested resource name, or empty Wood, Stone, Herbs, Food, RawWater, Clay, Sandbags, Metal, Planks, Fuel, seeds empty means nothing to harvest Farming Time whole number 0–400 in-game minutes of work per harvest for one crew member; two workers halve it Resource Amount whole number 0–50 yield per harvest Resource Total whole number 0–500 total before it is used up Limited Harvest Amount whole number 0, 20, 30, 100 cap for endless sources; 0 = uncapped Destroyed On Depletion TRUE/FALSE FALSE with Refresh Time 0 leaves something that can never be harvested again Refresh Time whole number 0–21600 minutes until it regrows Health whole number 1–2147483647 the huge value marks the indestructible ones Is Fireproof TRUE/FALSE making trees fireproof removes fire spread from the map

docs.title: GrowingData - saplings becoming trees
docs.text:
Built-in file: GrowingData.csv

Two rows, young_tree and young_tree_big.

Column Value Built-in To a MapObjects id tree, tree_big Min Hours whole number 672 Max Hours whole number 840

A sapling that is already on the map when a save is loaded draws its remaining time between half of Min Hours and Max Hours; only newly planted ones use the full minimum.

docs.title: GardeningData - the four crops
docs.text:
Built-in file: GardeningData.csv

Rows grain, beans, potato, tomato.

Column Built-in Notes Growth 3, 6, 15, 10 watered days until harvest - the plant gains one at midnight for every day its tile was watered; 0 is harvestable instantly Food 3, 4, 20, 7 food per harvest Seeds 2, 5, 3, 1 seeds per harvest; 0 makes the crop unsustainable Regrowth only tomato is TRUE regrows instead of being consumed

docs.title: ResourceData - what a resource is
docs.text:
Built-in file: ResourceData.csv

One row per resource, named exactly as the game names it.

Column Value Built-in Notes Initial Integrity whole number 0–50000 hours before a pile spoils; 0 rots instantly Carry Limit whole number 0–250 how much one person carries; 0 means it can never be moved Stack Limit whole number 0–2000 pile cap outdoors Double Stack Limit whole number 0–3000 pile cap in proper storage; below Stack Limit shrinks storage Resource Tier Meta, Basic, Advanced, Military, Trash Category Food, Seeds, or empty removing Food from everything edible means the crew can never eat Always Degrades TRUE/FALSE spoils even under a roof Explosiveness whole number 0, 2, 3 0 is inert Flammable TRUE/FALSE VariantAmountMapping /-list of whole numbers 1/2, 1 picks the pile's look

docs.title: WorkbenchProjectData - crafting recipes
docs.text:
Built-in file: WorkbenchProjectData.csv

The row id is <Workbench>.<Output>. Rows cannot be added, so this changes existing recipes rather than introducing new ones.

Column Value Built-in Notes Workbench Type workbench name FieldKitchen, IndoorKitchen, SawStation, Brickstation, CementMixer, MetalworksWorkbench, CanningStation, ElectronicsWorkbench, TailorStation, EspionageRadio, WaterCooker, HerbDryer, Distillery Output Resource Type resource name Output Resource Amount whole number 1–200 Input Resource Type /-list of resources, or None Food/RawWater, Metal, None None means made from nothing Input Resource Amount /-list of whole numbers 2/2, 0 must have as many entries as the type list Time To Craft whole number 10–180 in-game minutes of work for one crew member; two workers halve it Valid Entry TRUE/FALSE TRUE left over; the game does not read it

docs.title: ShipmentData - the supply catalogue
docs.text:
Built-in file: ShipmentData.csv

One row per orderable item.

Column Value Notes Shipment Type Resource or Prop Category Military, Miscellaneous or Large capitalisation matters - military is refused Amount whole number, 1–5000 units delivered per slot Slots whole number, 1–4 more slots than any rank offers makes the item unorderable

docs.title: CharactersInitialStats - starting skills per job
docs.text:
Built-in file: CharactersInitialStats.csv

Rows are job and crew role names: Pilot, Gunner, BombAimer, FlightEngineer, Navigator, RadioOperator, RAFAirCrew, AAFCook, FieldMechanic, FieldEngineer, RAFMedic, AAFLabour, None, Custom.

Columns are the six skills - Flying, Shooting, Bombing, Endurance, Engineering, Navigating - and the value is a rank, 0 to 6, not a point total. 0 is Untrained and 6 is Ace. Keep it inside that range. Endurance also sets maximum health, which is why every row has at least 1 there.

docs.title: CharactersStatsRankProgression - points per rank
docs.text:
Built-in file: CharactersStatsRankProgression.csv

Rows must stay Untrained, Rank1 … Rank5, Ace. LevelUpPoints (0, 10, 14, 22, 36, 58, 90) is the points total at which that rank is reached, and the rank is picked as the highest one a character has passed - so the values must ascend. Out of order, crew get stuck low or jump straight to Ace.

docs.title: CharacterStatsCheck - what a rank is worth
docs.text:
Built-in file: CharacterStatsCheck.csv

Rows are the same seven ranks. For each of the six skills there are two columns: <Skill>Value is a flat bonus added to a mission roll, <Skill>Percentage is a fraction - 0.25 means 25%. Writing 25 gives a 2500% bonus. Column names cannot be renamed.

docs.title: CharacterJobPriority - what each job is willing to do
docs.text:
Built-in file: CharacterJobPriority.csv

Rows are the job names: None, Custom, AAFCook, FieldMechanic, FieldEngineer, RAFMedic, AAFLabour, RAFAircrew.

There is one column per kind of work - Building, Gardening, CraftingAndRepairs, Labor, Cooking, Medicine, PlaneWork, Harvest, BaseSafety, Leisure, UseRecreationalItem, Socialize, ConsumeLuxuryGood, Train, Sleep, PilotPlane, FunctionalGroup, Emergency - holding a priority: 0 means the job never does this kind of work, 1 is the highest priority and 3 the lowest. (A medic has Building 0 and Medicine 1.) No column may be dropped or renamed.

These numbers also identify a job: a crew member whose priorities match a row exactly is that job, and one matching none is Custom. Give two jobs identical priorities and the game can no longer tell them apart.

docs.title: CharactersData - names, nicknames and ranks
docs.text:
Built-in file: CharactersData.csv

Six of the eight rows are long lists - first names, surnames, nicknames, base crew ranks, pilot ranks - and cannot be changed.

The two you can change are the pilot ranks themselves, where Goal is how many successful missions earn the promotion:

Row Value Goal OfficerCadet 2 3 PilotOfficer 3 10

docs.title: MoraleValues
docs.text:
Built-in file: MoraleValues.csv

Name and value, all numbers: BaseMoraleBufferDays, MoraleLevelMin (-100), MoraleLevelMax (100), LeisureThreshold, MoraleTrendTreshold, MoraleBreakingThreshold, MoraleEffectPositiveThreshold, MoraleEffectNegativeThreshold, AirBaseMoraleGameOverThreshold.

Setting AirBaseMoraleGameOverThreshold above MoraleLevelMax loses the run immediately; putting MoraleLevelMin above MoraleLevelMax leaves every limit inverted.

docs.title: MoraleInfluenceValues - what changes a crew member's mood
docs.text:
Built-in file: MoraleInfluenceValues.csv

Column Value Built-in Notes Itentifier row id (note the spelling) Sleep, Chill, Panic, BaseAttacked IdentifierType Task, TaskGroup, TaskCategory, WarPhase, GameEvent, - a type that does not suit the id means the row is ignored Parameter the variant key; comma-separates aliases default, Prop.Bed, ResourceType.Meals no alias may be listed twice Raw Parameter a note not read by the game Confidence / Mood / Energy numbers -30 … 50 Influence Type Timed or OnEventTrigger

Timed values apply every tick and are therefore much smaller than OnEventTrigger ones. Copying a +20 event value into a Timed row pins a crew member's mood to the ceiling within a minute.

Six rows hold one variant per line and cannot be changed at all: Sleep, Eat, WorkOnWorkbench, UseRecreationalItem, MissionCompleted, Death.

docs.title: FlightMissionData - the mission modifiers
docs.text:
Built-in file: FlightMissionData.csv

The row id names what is being measured: AirplaneIntegrity, AirplaneHealth, AirplaneFuel, Mood, Energy, Confidence, SeatsConfiguration, CrewHealth, CrewOnFire.

Column Value Built-in Notes ModifierCategory a label low, high, zero, critical, mismatch ModifierType SkillRollModifier or NoFlightModifier ModifierRange min/max whole numbers 0/-5, 2/0 bonus applied to the roll Parameter space-separated crew roles, or Default Default, CrewRole.Pilot every role must carry the CrewRole. prefix - a bare Pilot never matches, and neither does an unknown role ThresholdRange min/max whole numbers 1/40, -100/-90, 50/100 the range of measured values this row covers

NoFlightModifier is the hard block that grounds an aircraft - out of fuel, or a crew member at rock-bottom mood. Widening its ThresholdRange grounds your whole squadron; setting it to something unreachable such as -1000/-999 effectively switches it off.

Rows spanning several lines and therefore unchangeable: AirplaneIntegrity, AirplaneHealth, Mood, Energy, Confidence.

docs.title: TaskValues - durations and thresholds per task
docs.text:
Built-in file: TaskValues.csv

Three columns: the task id, a Variable Name and a Value.

Variable Name is the key the game looks the setting up by, so only Value can be changed. The names in use are Duration (minutes), Distance, Chance, ExperienceGain, HealthAmount, IntegrityAmount, IntegrityPenalty, ScheduleThreshold, ScheduleThresholdPercentage, ResourceToFuelRatio, Targets, Initiation and Active.

Tasks with several settings take up several lines and cannot be changed. These are: Chat, Chill, Panic, AirAttackPanic, CelebrateSuccessfulMission, BreakThings, RepairAirplane, MaintainAirplane, Refuel, RepairEquipment, RefillAirplaneAmmo, UseTrainingObject, the six …Simple… and six …Advanced… training tasks, and BeOnFire. Everything else - UseRadio, Eat, Salute, Bury, Recover, MonitorAirspace and the rest - has a single setting, almost always Duration (RefillEquipmentAmmo has only ScheduleThresholdPercentage), and can be changed normally.

Value also accepts text (one built-in row names a chair), so a non-number in a numeric setting is accepted and then fails when the task runs. This is the one place in this table where you can still write nonsense.

docs.title: DaySchedule - the phases of a day
docs.text:
Built-in file: DaySchedule.csv

Four rows, 0–3.

Column Value Built-in Phase Work, Leisure, Sleep StartHour whole number, inclusive 0, 5, 7, 22 EndHour whole number, exclusive 5, 7, 22, 24

The four spans are expanded hour by hour, so gaps and overlaps both matter: an hour no row covers has no phase at all and the crew idle through it. Keep the spans continuous from 0 to 24.

docs.title: DayNightSystemData - sun and shadows
docs.text:
Built-in file: DayNightSystemData.csv

Name and value, all numbers, purely visual.

Row Meaning Built-in Morning Time, Dawn Time, Day Time, Evening Time, Dusk Time, Night Time hour each lighting stage begins 4, 7, 10, 17, 22, 23 Sun Min Rotation / Sun Max Rotation sun elevation sweep, degrees 15 / 165 Sun Yaw Offset compass rotation -90 Sun Tilt degrees 10 Shadow Day Intens / Shadow Night Intens shadow strength 0.85 / 0

Keep the six time rows ascending and within 0–23, or the lighting stages flip back and forth.

docs.title: GameGoalAlerts - when the game warns the player
docs.text:
Built-in file: GameGoalAlerts.csv

Name and value, all numbers, alerts only: LowMoraleThreshold (-50), CriticalMoraleThreshold (-65), LowFoodThreshold (20), FewLeisureItemsThreshold (5), MissionTimerMinutesThreshold (150), LowWaterThreshold (20).

docs.title: Variables - the global number bag
docs.text:
Built-in file: Variables.csv

Name and value, 86 entries, each read by whichever part of the game needs it.

This column accepts anything, because a few entries hold text or a min-max range rather than a number. Write abc where a number belongs and it is accepted, then read as 0 - the feature quietly stops working and the log carries an error. This is the table to be most careful with.

Entries worth knowing before you change them:

  • TimeTickInterval (0.6666) - real seconds per in-game minute. Halving it doubles the speed of the entire game, including every timer balanced against it.
  • AirplanesLimit (24) - how many aircraft a base may own.
  • CharacterBaseHealth (7) - plus the Endurance rank, this is a crew member's maximum health. Below CharacterHeavyInjuryThreshold (3) everyone starts badly injured.
  • MaxVictoryPoints (12) - the aircraft-ordering budget.
  • ScrambleFuelNeeded (80) - flat fuel per scramble, whatever the aircraft.
  • AttackHourMin / AttackHourMax (12/23) - pulled back into 1–23 if you go outside it.
  • DiverBombFiresCount, BomberBombFiresCount, CharredTerrainRevertTimeDays - these three are min-max ranges, not single numbers.

Eight entries are left over and nothing reads them, so changing them does nothing at all: AttackedCharacterId, BikeMovementSpeedMultiplier, LichfieldIntroCrewMembersCount, AirplaneIntegrityModifierTreshold, AirplaneHealthModifierTreshold, AirAttackFighterHealth, AirAttackDiverHealth, AirAttackBomberHealth.

docs.title: FeedbackVariables
docs.text: The in-game feedback form: API Endpoint, Feedback Character Limit, Screenshot Height, Survey Link, Survey Link Demo, Survey Opened Player Prefs. There is no reason for a gameplay mod to touch this, and pointing API Endpoint elsewhere sends players' feedback to that address.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Mods/my_balance_mod/CSV/ResourceCost.json - give the storage box a build cost, make wooden walls cheaper, and drop the chair's tarp cost:

{
  "Commands": [
    { "Command": "Add", "Id": "storage_box", "Cells": { "Planks": 3, "Metal": 1 } },
    { "Command": "Replace", "Id": "wall_wood", "Cells": { "Planks": 1 } },
    { "Command": "Remove", "Id": "Chair", "Columns": [ "Tarp" ] }
  ]
}

Mods/my_balance_mod/CSV/Variables.json - speed up turbo mode and make crew chatter more common. Value in this table takes any text, so a typo such as 0,6 is accepted silently and then read as 0 - check the number twice:

{
  "Commands": [
    { "Command": "Replace", "Id": "TurboTimeScaleMultiplier", "Cells": { "Value": 20 } },
    { "Command": "Replace", "Id": "RandomActionChatProbability", "Cells": { "Value": 0.6 } }
  ]
}

The same two changes as Mods/my_balance_mod/CSV/Variables.csv:

Name,Value
TurboTimeScaleMultiplier,20
RandomActionChatProbability,0.6

docs.title: Table command files
docs.text:
There is no spreadsheet window inside Ground of Aces. Table changes are made with files: you write a short list of commands, Add, Replace or Remove, into a <Table>.json file in your mod's CSV/ folder, and every time a level loads, the game carries them out on its data tables, one by one, checking each change before it writes it.

This page explains how those commands behave in detail. The format itself, the list of tables and the rules for each column are on CSV tables; read that first.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
Make the Gladiator carry more fuel and the wooden wall cheaper. Two files in one mod:

Mods/
  my_balance_mod/
    CSV/
      VehicleData.json
      ResourceCost.json

VehicleData.json:

{
  "Commands": [
    { "Command": "Replace", "Id": "gladiator", "Cells": { "Fuel Capacity": 350 } }
  ]
}

ResourceCost.json:

{
  "Commands": [
    { "Command": "Replace", "Id": "wall_wood", "Cells": { "Planks": 1 } }
  ]
}

Return to the main menu and load a save: the changes are in. No restart needed.

docs.title: How a command is carried out
docs.text:
For every command, in the order they appear in the file, the game:

  1. Finds the row by Id. Capitalisation of the id does not matter; the table's own spelling is kept.
  2. Builds the complete row as it would look after the change, on the side, without touching the real table yet.
  3. Fills cells the table must never leave empty with the game's default, if your change left them empty.
  4. Checks the whole row against the table's rules (value types, allowed ranges, references to other tables, see CSV tables).
  5. Only if everything passes, writes the row into the table. Otherwise it writes nothing, logs the reason, and moves on to the next command.

So a rejected command never leaves a half-changed row behind, and one bad command does not stop the others.

docs.title: Replace: change cells of an existing row
docs.text:
{ "Command": "Replace", "Id": "gladiator", "Cells": { "Fuel Capacity": 350, "Movement Speed": 7 } }
  • Changes only the columns named in Cells. Every other cell keeps its current value.
  • A cell given as "", only spaces, or null is cleared (or reset to the table's default where a cell cannot be empty).
  • The row must already exist. Otherwise: '...' is not a built-in row; use Add to create one.
  • Every key in Cells must be a column of the table, spelled exactly. Otherwise the message lists the table's columns.
  • The whole resulting row is checked, not just the cells you named. A row that was fine before stays fine unless your values break a rule.
  • A few built-in rows span several lines in the game's own table. They cannot be patched cell by cell; the log tells you to ship the whole row as a <Table>.csv instead.

docs.title: Add: create a new row
docs.text:
{ "Command": "Add", "Id": "storage_box", "Cells": { "Planks": 3, "Metal": 1 } }
  • Only in the tables that allow new rows (see CSV tables). Elsewhere: new rows are not supported in '...'; only built-in rows can be changed.
  • The id must not exist yet. Otherwise: '...' already exists; use Replace to change it.
  • Columns you leave out get the table's default or stay empty; the row check then decides whether that is acceptable.

docs.title: Remove: clear cells, or delete a row
docs.text:
{ "Command": "Remove", "Id": "Chair", "Columns": [ "Tarp" ] }
{ "Command": "Remove", "Id": "Drawer" }
  • With Columns: clears the listed cells, exactly like a Replace with empty values.
  • Without Columns: deletes the whole row. Only in the tables that allow it; elsewhere the log says the rows cannot be removed because saves and other content use their ids.
  • Remove never takes Cells.

docs.title: Order
docs.text:
• Inside one file, commands run top to bottom. An Add can be followed by a Replace of the same row.
  • Inside one mod, all .csv files are applied before any .json file, so commands can refine rows your CSV files brought in.
  • Between mods, the mod applied later works on the result of the earlier ones and wins where both touch the same cell. The order is described in How mods work.

docs.title: When changes take effect
docs.text:
Tables are rebuilt from the game's own data and all enabled mods every time a level loads. After editing a command file, save your game, choose Options → Quit to main menu, and load the save again. No restart is needed; if in doubt, restart anyway. See Testing and reloading. A brand-new CSV/ folder, or a new mod, is only noticed after you open Mods in the main menu (press Refresh) or restart.

Because the tables are rebuilt from scratch, removing a command, or switching the mod off, restores the original value at the next load.

docs.title: File
docs.text: Rule Value Location Mods/<mod>/CSV/<Table>.json, directly in CSV/ File name The table's name, exactly: VehicleData.json, not vehicledata.json Root An object with one key, Commands, holding a list Commands per file At most 200. A longer file is skipped whole. Syntax Plain JSON: no comments, no trailing commas

docs.title: Command fields
docs.text: Field Type Used by Notes Command text all Add, Replace or Remove, any capitalisation. Id text all The row id, any capitalisation. Required. Cells object: column name to value Add, Replace Required for those two. Values may be strings, numbers or true/false; they are read as text. Columns list of column names Remove Optional. Without it, the whole row is removed.

docs.title: Log messages
docs.text:
Every message starts with [Mod <mod id>] CSV/<Table>.json. Applied commands:

[Mod my_balance_mod] CSV/VehicleData.json command 1 replaced cells Fuel Capacity of row 'gladiator'.
[Mod my_balance_mod] CSV/ResourceCost.json command 2 added row 'storage_box'.
[Mod my_balance_mod] CSV/PropsInfluence.json command 3 cleared cells Tarp of row 'Chair'.
[Mod my_balance_mod] CSV/PropsInfluence.json command 4 removed row 'Drawer'.

Problems with the whole file (nothing in it is applied):

Message ends with Meaning skipped: could not be parsed (...) Not valid JSON. The part in brackets points to the spot. skipped: it holds no "Commands". The root key is missing, misspelled, or the list is empty. skipped: 250 commands exceed the limit of 200. Split the commands over several mods, or use a <Table>.csv. skipped: ... (other reasons) The file name is not a table that mods may change.

Problems with one command (only that command is skipped):

Message ends with Meaning rejected: it is empty. A null in the Commands list. rejected: '...' is not a command; use Add, Replace or Remove. Misspelled Command. rejected: it has no "Id". Id missing or blank. rejected: Replace needs "Cells". / Add needs "Cells". Cells missing or empty. rejected: Remove lists the cells to clear in "Columns", not in "Cells". Use Columns with Remove. rejected: '...' is not a column of ...; available: ... Column name misspelled. Copy it from the list in the message. rejected: '...' is not a built-in row ... No row with that id. rejected: '...' already exists; use Replace to change it. Add of an id that exists. rejected: followed by a rule The value breaks one of the table's rules, see CSV tables.

The released game may write only errors to Player.log; the full list of lines appears in development builds.

docs.title: Missions
docs.text:
A mission is a flight the player sends aircraft on: it appears on the war map, costs time and fuel, and comes back with an outcome. There are two ways to make one:

What it is Best for The Mission Editor A window inside the game. Fill in fields, press Validate, press Save. A first mission, and anything whose numbers you want to try out quickly. JSON and Python files A .json file with the numbers and an optional .py file with the text and logic. Everything else - chains, campaigns, missions that react to what the player did.

They are the same thing underneath. The editor writes exactly the JSON you would have written by hand, so you can start in the editor and keep going in a text editor.

Page Contents Write your first mission a guided walkthrough from empty folder to a flown mission Chains and campaigns missions that follow each other, and campaign maps Locations every place a mission can happen, with coordinates Reference every JSON field and every handler in detail How mods work where a mod folder lives, and how the game finds it CSV tables changing the game's numbers rather than adding missions

docs.title: Where missions come from
docs.text:
The game reads missions from several places, and later ones win when two carry the same id:

  1. Shipped missions - inside the game (and the Supporter Pack, if you own it), read-only. You can override one by re-using its id, but you cannot edit it in place.
  2. Mods - Mods/<your mod>/Missions/, holding .json and .py files. This is how you hand a mission to somebody else. See How mods work.
  3. Your own saved missions - the folder the in-game Mission Editor writes to:
Platform Folder Windows %USERPROFILE%\AppData\LocalLow\Blindflug Studios\Ground Of Aces\Missions\ macOS ~/Library/Application Support/Blindflug Studios/Ground Of Aces/Missions/ Linux ~/.config/unity3d/Blindflug Studios/Ground Of Aces/Missions/

That third folder always wins, which makes it a good place to try changes out - and a place to remember to clear when a mission of yours seems to ignore the copy in your mod folder.

docs.title: The Mission Editor
docs.text:
Open the game and choose Mission Editor in the main menu.

Note

The editor always opens on a single working mission called new_mission. It loads yours if you have saved one under that id, and otherwise starts a fresh one. Rename it in the Mission Id field before saving, and the next visit starts a new new_mission, so you can write one mission after another.

There is no mission browser yet, so the editor cannot open a shipped mission or reopen one you renamed and saved. To come back to a saved mission, edit its .json in the Missions folder above, or start again from a copy.

docs.title: What you fill in
docs.text:
Identity. The mission id, and the tags that decide which maps the mission can appear on. An id must be lower-case letters, digits and underscores only.

Tags. Tags are free-form labels, not map names. A map lists the tags it supports in its Metadata.json (the _tags field inside the .goamap file), a mission lists the tags it is written for (the _tags field of the mission JSON), and the mission can only turn up on that map when the two lists share at least one tag. Several tags on a mission mean "any of these" - one match is enough.

Type them into the mission tags field as one comma-separated list without spaces: naval,atlantic. A tag follows the same rules as an id - lower-case letters, digits and underscores - and the field enforces that as you type, turning capitals into lower case and dropping anything else. The match against a map ignores capitalisation anyway, so a map that spells its tag Campaign_Debden still counts.

Leaving the list empty is the normal case. An empty list on either side counts as the single tag default, and every shipped map lists default, so an untagged mission is available on all of them. Tag a mission campaign_debden and it appears only on maps that also list campaign_debden - and nowhere else, not even on the shipped maps, unless you add default alongside it. A map made for a campaign usually lists only its own tag, precisely to keep the regular missions out.

Quests have no tags

Tags are for missions only. A quest has no tags field. A map picks its quests through the StartingQuestIds list in its Metadata.json; with none listed it starts the game's default quest line (quest0). See Quests and maps.

Validate warns you when a mission carries a tag that no known map declares. That mission can never appear anywhere, which is only what you want if a script hands it out directly.

Timing and size. How many aircraft the player may send, how long the mission waits on the map before it expires, and how long the flight itself takes. Both times are ranges - the game rolls a value between the two numbers.

Difficulty. The chance the mission goes as planned, a difficulty rating from 1 to 3, and the enemy strength the intel report shows the player.

Text. The mission name and description, the intel threat report, and the radio transmissions for each ending. Type them straight in. A mission written in the editor does not need a script, because every mission without one runs on the game's shared default mission script.

Locations. Where on the war map the mission can appear. Pick from the list and add as many as you like; the game chooses one when the mission is created. The full list, with coordinates, is on Locations.

Requirements. Conditions that must hold before the mission shows up at all - a runway tier, a date window, or another mission having been completed.

Stats. The skills the mission rolls against. You need exactly two: the first is used when the flight goes to plan, the second when it does not.

Outcomes. Exactly four endings, and what each one gives or costs - morale, victory points, damage.

Historic day. Tick this to make the mission part of the storyline: it appears on or after a date you choose, takes a scheduled slot when it is due, and is gone for good once it has succeeded.

docs.title: Validate before you save
docs.text:
Validate lists everything it can find. Save runs the same check and refuses if anything is an error.

Errors block saving:

Error Meaning Mission id empty, or has characters other than a-z, 0-9 and _ Mission id is reserved a shipped mission already uses it Mission with given ID already exists saving would silently replace another mission you saved A tag has invalid characters tags follow the same rules as ids Not exactly four outcomes the game picks one of four and never checks the count Not exactly two stats the skill roll reads both Time to start: minimum above maximum Time to complete: minimum above maximum, or under 5 minutes A runway tier or date requirement that is not a whole number A completed-mission requirement the game cannot read

Warnings let you save, and are worth reading anyway:

Warning Meaning No locations the mission can never be placed on the map Duplicate location names Unknown map tag no known map carries this tag, so the mission is unavailable everywhere - intended only if a script hands it out Difficulty rating outside 1–3 Fewer than one aircraft slot nobody can fly it Time to start never expires the mission sits on the map forever A historic day that cannot be used the date is malformed, empty or implausibly early, so the mission has no earliest date at all A stat whose minimum is above its maximum An outcome effect the game cannot read that one effect silently never applies An outcome uses Max Victory Points the game works that value out itself and ignores it when you write it Missing narrative text that text slot shows nothing in game

The missing-text warning does not appear for shipped missions, which carry translated text rather than text typed into the editor.

docs.title: What the editor cannot do
docs.text:
• Open or copy a shipped mission.
  • Write the Python side. Anything that has to decide something - react to the crew that flew, hand out a follow-up mission, change the text depending on what happened - needs a script.
  • Build a chain beyond a single "this mission must have been completed" requirement. Longer chains are easier to see and manage in the files. See Chains and campaigns.

For any of those, open the mission file in a text editor, straight from the file browser.

docs.title: JSON and Python
docs.text:
A mission is a .json file holding the numbers, and optionally a .py file of the same name holding the text and any logic. The file name is the mission id. Both go into your mod's Missions/ folder (or, while you try things out, into your own Missions folder above).

Mods/
  my_mod/
    Missions/
      mymod_coastal_patrol.json
      mymod_coastal_patrol.py

Three things catch people out, and all three are limits of the game rather than of your files:

  • Exactly four outcomes, in order. The game picks one by position and never checks how many there are. Three entries crash the mission when it finishes - long after you have stopped suspecting the JSON.
  • At least two mission stats. The first is used when the mission goes to plan, the second when it does not. One entry crashes the skill roll.
  • Prefix your ids with your mod name. A duplicate id silently replaces the mission it duplicates, and which one wins depends on load order.

The Mission Editor's Validate button catches all three before you ever launch. Every field of the JSON is described on Reference, and complete, working missions are collected on Examples.

docs.title: The two modes
docs.text:
How much of the script the game uses depends on whether the mission has a .json beside it.

  • With JSON - the numbers come from the file. The script supplies text and reactions only, and the handlers that report numbers are never called.
  • Without JSON - the script supplies everything, including the numbers. Every handler below is called. What the JSON would otherwise carry - stats, location, slots, tags - is set from initialize_mission through missions_api (for example missions_api.SetMissionLocation and missions_api.SetTags).

This is the single most common source of confusion: a handler that works perfectly in a script-only mission is simply ignored once you add a .json.

docs.title: Mission event handlers
docs.text:
A handler is a Python function the game calls at a certain moment of the mission's life. Each name below links to its full description on Reference.

Handler What it does When it runs get_mission_id the identifier of the mission always - required initialize_mission set the mission up as it is created always send_mission_event report progress while the flight is in the air always set_mission_impact apply consequences once the outcome is known always send_mission_result_text the text shown when the mission ends always send_mission_cancelled_text the text shown when the player aborts always get_mission_result_text the text in the result window always get_mission_name the name in the mission info window script-only missions get_mission_description_text the description in the info window script-only missions get_time_to_start how long the player has to start it script-only missions get_completion_time how long the flight lasts script-only missions get_threat_level the threat level in the info window script-only missions get_enemy_count how many enemies are present script-only missions get_mission_events_count how many progress reports to send script-only missions get_fuel_level the fuel the mission needs script-only missions get_mission_result whether the mission succeeded script-only missions

In a script-only mission, the getters from get_mission_name to get_fuel_level are optional: leave one out and the game uses a default value instead. For a mission with JSON, the number of progress reports is fixed at 3, so get_mission_events_count is ignored there.

Handlers that are never called

Do not implement get_mission_icon, calculate_mission_modifiers, calculate_airplane_modifiers or calculate_pilot_modifiers. Their names still exist, but nothing calls them - the game works out mission modifiers by itself now. Older example scripts implement them at length; that code never runs.

get_mission_fatalities no longer exists either. Losses are handled through the Damage outcome effect.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Write your first mission - build and fly one, step by step.
  • Reference - every field, handler and outcome effect.
  • Examples - complete missions to copy, from a single patrol to a five-part campaign. Start with the coastal patrol.
  • Scripting - how Python scripts are loaded, and event scripts that are not missions.

docs.title: Chains and campaigns
docs.text:
One mission is a sortie. Several missions that follow from each other are a story. This page covers three levels of that, from pure JSON to a campaign with a memory:

  1. Chains: a mission appears only after another one has ended a certain way. JSON only.
  2. Historic missions: story beats that are guaranteed to appear, optionally on a real date. JSON only.
  3. Campaigns: follow-ups that depend on counting, remembering people or player choices. Needs a script.

Working examples: chain_convoy (a fork), chain_airfield (a straight line four deep) and campaign_kanalkampf (a campaign). See Examples.

docs.title: Chaining on an outcome
docs.text:
A requirement of type 3, CompletedMission, makes a mission wait for another one:

{ "Name": "CompletedMission", "_requirementType": 3, "_value": "mymod_convoy_spotted,success" }

The value is a mission id, optionally followed by a comma and the outcome it must have ended with:

Value Meaning "mymod_convoy_spotted" finished, with any outcome (including cancelled) "mymod_convoy_spotted,success" finished successfully "mymod_convoy_spotted,failure" flown and failed "mymod_convoy_spotted,cancelled" called off by the player

cancelled is its own outcome: a mission the player called off does not count as a failure.

"Success" means the outcome the dice picked has "_missionSuccess": true in the JSON. It is not the same as the skill roll: outcome index 1 (gone wrong, skill passed) can be a success if you mark it so. That is what makes a salvaged mission feel different from a clean one.

The game remembers every finish for the whole campaign. A player who failed a mission and later won it satisfies both ,failure and ,success.

docs.title: Branching
docs.text:
Two follow-ups gated on opposite outcomes give you a fork:

mymod_convoy_spotted
   |
   +-- success --> mymod_convoy_strike
   |
   +-- failure --> mymod_convoy_search

Nothing stops you from gating several missions on the same outcome, or from chaining more steps onto the follow-ups. Requirements combine with AND, so a mission can require both a finished predecessor and a runway tier:

"_missionRequirements": [
    { "Name": "RunwayTier",       "_requirementType": 0, "_value": "2" },
    { "Name": "CompletedMission", "_requirementType": 3, "_value": "mymod_convoy_spotted,success" }
]

There is no OR. To accept either of two predecessors, write two versions of the follow-up mission.

docs.title: Historic missions
docs.text:
A normal mission sits in a pool and is drawn at random across the week. For a follow-up that is usually wrong: the player finishes step one and then waits, possibly for weeks, possibly forever if the pool is large.

"_isHistoric": true changes that. A historic mission:

  • never enters the random draw. The moment its gates pass, it is guaranteed to appear.
  • appears on its date when it has a _historicDay: at the first day change on or after that date where its other gates also pass. This does not use the weekly slots.
  • keeps the normal lead time when it has no _historicDay: it takes the next weekly mission slot instead of a random mission, so a follow-up arrives with the same delay as any other mission rather than dropping onto the map instantly.
  • never expires. _timeToStartRange is ignored, so the player has unlimited time to fly it.
  • is one-shot on success. Once won, it never appears again. A failed or cancelled attempt brings it back, so a chain gated on success can be retried.
  • is never on the map twice. While one copy is waiting or in flight, no second copy appears.

Its gates combine with AND:

Has a CompletedMission gate Has a _historicDay Appears no no at the next weekly slot yes no at the next weekly slot after the predecessor ended right no yes at the first day change on or after the date yes yes on the date if the predecessor already ended right; otherwise at the first day change after it does

That combination is exactly what a story beat needs. Use it for every step of a chain except, usually, the first.

docs.title: Controlling when a chain can start
docs.text:
"_isHistoric": true,
"_historicDay": { "Year": 1940, "Month": 8, "Day": 13, "Hour": 0, "Minute": 0 }

The date is a floor: the mission is not available before it, and stays available after it until it is won. A year below 1900 counts as "no date", which is why example files carry "Year": 1 when they mean none.

To close a mission off after a certain point, use a LatestAppearanceDay requirement (type 2), counted in days from the start of the campaign. It works on any mission, historic or not.

Put together, each operation becomes available on its real date, and one that was missed can be closed off.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
Duplicate ids. Two missions with the same id means one silently replaces the other, decided by load order. Prefix every id with your mod name, and remember to update the ids inside every CompletedMission value when you rename.

Forgetting _isHistoric on follow-ups. The chain works, but steps may take a very long time to surface, and a finished step can be drawn again.

Several historic missions due at once. They all appear together: dated ones on their day, undated ones in the same slot. If you want them one after another, chain them on each other's outcome or give them different days.

Chaining on a mission that never appears. A gate on a mission whose own requirements never pass, or which is tagged for a different map, silently blocks the rest of the chain. Test each step on its own before linking them.

Testing with the cheat. create_mission ignores every gate. It proves a mission loads, not that the chain unlocks. See Testing and reloading.

docs.title: When JSON is not enough
docs.text:
A requirement can only ask about a previous mission's outcome. When the condition is something else (who flew it, what the base looks like, how many times this has already happened), a script can create the follow-up itself:

@event_handler(MissionEvent.SET_MISSION_IMPACT)
def set_mission_impact(mission_entity_id):
    if missions_api.IsMissionSuccessful(mission_entity_id):
        missions_api.CreateMission("mymod_pursuit")

CreateMission puts the mission on the war map at once, skipping the weekly draw. It still checks the target mission's own requirements and map tags: if they do not pass, nothing is created and a warning is written to Player.log. Call it from set_mission_impact, where the outcome is known; from initialize_mission it is refused.

What it does not protect you from: nothing stops a script handing out the same mission twice, and a historic mission created this way is not blocked the way the automatic spawn blocks it.

Use the JSON route wherever it fits. It survives saving and loading, the validator can check it, and it cannot hand out a mission the base cannot fly. Reach for CreateMission when the decision genuinely depends on something only a script can see.

docs.title: From a chain to a campaign
docs.text:
A chain has no memory. Fly chain_airfield twice and it plays identically both times, because every condition in it is a single yes or no about the mission before.

A campaign remembers. game_api.GetScriptDataPath(id) gives your script a folder of its own inside the game data folder; a JSON file in it survives the flight, the day and the session.

import json
import os

CAMPAIGN_ID = "mymod_campaign"

DEFAULTS = {
    "raids_survived": 0,
    "raids_lost": 0,
    "first_blood": None,
}


def _path():
    # The folder belongs to the id, NOT to the save game. Without the save's
    # guid in the file name, a second save would continue - and overwrite -
    # the first one's campaign.
    return os.path.join(
        game_api.GetScriptDataPath(CAMPAIGN_ID),
        "campaign_{}.json".format(game_api.GetAirBaseGuid())
    )


def load():
    state = dict(DEFAULTS)

    try:
        with open(_path(), "r") as handle:
            state.update(json.load(handle))
    except (IOError, OSError, ValueError):
        pass          # no file yet, or a half-written one: start clean

    return state


def save(state):
    try:
        with open(_path(), "w") as handle:
            json.dump(state, handle)
    except (IOError, OSError):
        pass          # the mission must still fly

The id you pass to GetScriptDataPath may contain only letters, digits, _, - and ., up to 64 characters.

Three things are easy to get wrong, and all three bite later rather than at once:

  1. Give every key a default. A save written before you added a key will otherwise fail with a KeyError on load, inside a handler, mid-flight.
  2. Put the save's guid in the file name. GetScriptDataPath gives one folder per id, shared by every save game.
  3. Wrap every read and write. A campaign that cannot write its state still has to let the mission fly.

Mod scripts can import one another, so put the state in one module (say mymod_campaign_state.py in the same Missions/ folder) that every mission imports. Then they cannot disagree about what has happened.

docs.title: What the memory buys you
docs.text:
Conditions no requirement can express:

state = campaign_state.load()

if state["raids_lost"] >= 3:
    missions_api.CreateMission("mymod_regroup")     # counting
elif state["first_blood"] is not None:
    pass                                            # remembering a person

It also lets a mission tune itself against the campaign's history, in initialize_mission:

@event_handler(MissionEvent.INITIALIZE_MISSION)
def initialize_mission(mission_entity_id):
    state = campaign_state.load()

    if state["raids_survived"] >= 2:
        # The enemy has seen this squadron before.
        missions_api.SetMissionStat(mission_entity_id, "Fight", 76, 115)
        missions_api.SetAsPlannedChance(mission_entity_id, 35)

Same mission, same JSON, measurably harder the fifth time than the first.

The campaign_kanalkampf example is the worked version: five missions, two of whose conditions are counts. The Examples page compares it with the chains.

docs.title: Write your first mission
docs.text:
A mission is a flight the player sends planes on. By the end of this page you will have written one from scratch, installed it, and seen it on the war map.

You need two files, both named after your mission:

  • a .json file with the numbers: when the mission appears, how hard it is, what it costs and what it pays
  • a .py file with the text: what the crew radios in, and how it reads afterwards

The .py file is optional (you can put the text in the JSON instead, see Localization), but writing one teaches you how missions work, so this page uses it.

The finished result is the coastal_patrol example: examples/coastal_patrol. Copying it and changing things is the fastest way in.

docs.title: 1. Pick an id
docs.text:
The id is the mission's name inside the game. It is the file name without the extension, and it appears in every text key the mission uses.

It must be unique across every mission the game knows, including the built-in ones and other people's mods. A duplicate does not cause an error: it silently replaces the other mission. So prefix your ids with your mod name:

mymod_coastal_patrol

Use only letters, digits and underscores.

docs.title: 2. Write the JSON
docs.text: Create mymod_coastal_patrol.json. The easiest start is a copy of coastal_patrol.json from the example. These are the parts that need thought.

docs.title: When it can appear
docs.text:
"_missionRequirements": [
    { "Name": "RunwayTier",            "_requirementType": 0, "_value": "1" },
    { "Name": "EarliestAppearanceDay", "_requirementType": 1, "_value": "3" }
]

Each entry is a gate, and all of them must pass. Type 0 is the runway tier the base must have; type 1 is the earliest day, counted from the start of the campaign. Type 3 makes the mission follow another one, see Chains and campaigns. The full list is in the Reference.

docs.title: How the dice fall
docs.text:
Two rolls decide every mission:

  1. _asPlannedChance (0–100) is the chance that the mission goes as planned.
  2. Then a skill roll decides whether the crew pulls it off.

Two rolls with two answers each give four possible endings.

docs.title: The four outcomes: order is mandatory
docs.text:
index 0   gone wrong,  skill failed
index 1   gone wrong,  skill passed
index 2   as planned,  skill failed
index 3   as planned,  skill passed

_missionOutcomes must have exactly four entries, in exactly this order. The game does not check: with fewer than four, the mission crashes when it ends.

Each outcome says whether it counts as a success (_missionSuccess) and carries effects: crew or base morale, damage to the planes, victory points.

{
    "Name": "3 - as planned, skill passed",
    "_missionSuccess": true,
    "_outcomeEffect": [
        { "_outcomeEffectType": 7, "_effectValue": "1",  "_effectIcon": "ui_resource_victoryPoints" },
        { "_outcomeEffectType": 5, "_effectValue": "15", "_effectIcon": "ui_confidence" }
    ]
}

_effectValue is always written in quotes. For Damage (type 3) it is a range like "20-60", rolled for each plane. For everything else it is a whole number like "-40". All effect types are in the Reference.

docs.title: The stats: at least two
docs.text:
"_missionStats": [
    { "Name": "Recon",           "_missionSkillType": 2, "_statRange": { "x": 10.0, "y": 45.0 } },
    { "Name": "Maneuverability", "_missionSkillType": 4, "_statRange": { "x": 20.0, "y": 60.0 } }
]

The first entry is used when the mission goes as planned, the second when it goes wrong. The range is the difficulty: the game rolls a target inside it, and the squadron's combined skill has to reach that target. With fewer than two entries the skill roll crashes.

docs.title: Where it happens
docs.text: _potentialLocations lists candidate places on the war map. One is drawn each time the mission appears. Copy entries from the Locations page, including the coordinates: the game works out distance and fuel from the coordinates in your file.

docs.title: How a mission script actually runs
docs.text:
Before any code, one idea that makes everything else simple: a mission script is not a program that runs from top to bottom. It is a set of functions the game calls at fixed moments. You never call them yourself, and you never write a loop that waits for something.

The @event_handler(...) line above a function says when the game should call it:

@event_handler(MissionEvent.SEND_MISSION_EVENT)
def send_mission_event(mission_entity_id):
    ...

This registers send_mission_event for "a progress step happened in flight". The game calls it, hands it the number of the mission in question, and does something with what it returns. Between calls your script does nothing at all. Such a function is called a handler.

Everything outside a handler (text definitions, constants, helper functions) runs once, when the game loads the file. That is why text is registered at the top level of the file and not inside a handler.

docs.title: The order the game calls handlers in
docs.text:
For one flight of one mission:

When Handler Typical job the mission is created initialize_mission set up state in flight, once per progress step send_mission_event roll, and radio in what is happening the flight ends set_mission_impact react to the outcome the planes are back send_mission_result_text a closing line in the event log the player opens the result window get_mission_result_text which text that window shows

send_mission_event is the one that fires several times: three times for a mission with a JSON file, at one third, two thirds and the end of the flight. It is not told which step it is, so the script asks:

events_sent = missions_api.GetNumberOfEventsSent(mission_entity_id)

if events_sent == 1:      # first step: roll whether it goes to plan
    ...
elif events_sent == 2:    # second step: roll whether the crew pulls it off
    ...

That is all the events_sent checks in mission scripts mean: "which of my three moments in this flight is this?"

docs.title: Roll once, read afterwards
docs.text:
Each of the two rolls is made exactly once:

  • MakeAsPlannedRoll performs the as-planned roll and stores it.
  • MakeSkillRoll performs the skill roll and stores it.

GetAsPlannedRoll and GetSkillRoll read the stored result back. Every handler after the roll uses Get.... Rolling a second time would tell the player one story and hand them the outcome of another.

docs.title: Which mission am I?
docs.text: Every handler receives mission_entity_id: the number of the one mission this call is about. The same script can be running for two flights of the same mission at once, so never keep per-flight information in a variable at the top of the file. Ask missions_api about the number you were given.

docs.title: 3. Write the Python
docs.text: Create mymod_coastal_patrol.py next to the JSON. The script does two jobs: define the text, and decide which text appears when.

docs.title: Define the nine texts
docs.text:
A mission uses nine text slots, all named missions/<id>/<slot>. Register them at the top level of the file with localization.SetTerm, so they exist as soon as the script loads:

from Blindflug.FlightMission import MissionEvent

MISSION_ID = "mymod_coastal_patrol"


def _term(slot, text):
    localization.SetTerm("en", "missions/{}/{}".format(MISSION_ID, slot), text)


_term("mission_name", "Coastal Patrol")
_term("mission_description", "Fly the shoreline. Report anything that moves.")
_term("intel_threat_report", "Low. No enemy activity reported.")
_term("ap_transmission", "Patrol is airborne. Clear skies along the coast.")
_term("gw_transmission", "Cloud came in thicker than forecast.")
_term("ap_success_transmission", "Patrol complete. Nothing to report.")
_term("ap_failure_transmission", "The patrol flew its route but came back with nothing usable.")
_term("gw_success_transmission", "Despite the weather the flight brought back a full report.")
_term("gw_failure_transmission", "The flight lost the coastline in the murk and turned back early.")

ap means "as planned", gw means "gone wrong". The first three names are read by the game itself and cannot be changed; if one is missing, the mission window shows the raw key. The other six are used by the script, and every shipped mission uses these names, so stick with them. More in Localization.

docs.title: Three handlers are enough
docs.text:
The id. Return exactly the file name:

@event_handler(MissionEvent.GET_MISSION_ID)
def get_mission_id(mission_entity_id):
    return MISSION_ID

The flight. Roll in the first two steps and radio in what happened:

@event_handler(MissionEvent.SEND_MISSION_EVENT)
def send_mission_event(mission_entity_id):
    events_sent = missions_api.GetNumberOfEventsSent(mission_entity_id)

    if events_sent == 1:
        going_as_planned = missions_api.MakeAsPlannedRoll(mission_entity_id)
        slot = "ap_transmission" if going_as_planned else "gw_transmission"
        event_log.Create("missions/{}/{}".format(MISSION_ID, slot))

    elif events_sent == 2:
        going_as_planned = missions_api.GetAsPlannedRoll(mission_entity_id)
        skill_passed = missions_api.MakeSkillRoll(mission_entity_id)
        event_log.Create("missions/{}/{}".format(MISSION_ID, _result_slot(going_as_planned, skill_passed)))

The result window. Only read the rolls, never roll here:

@event_handler(MissionEvent.GET_MISSION_RESULT_TEXT)
def get_mission_result_text(mission_entity_id):
    going_as_planned = missions_api.GetAsPlannedRoll(mission_entity_id)
    skill_passed = missions_api.GetSkillRoll(mission_entity_id)
    return "missions/{}/{}".format(MISSION_ID, _result_slot(going_as_planned, skill_passed))


def _result_slot(going_as_planned, skill_passed):
    prefix = "ap" if going_as_planned else "gw"
    suffix = "success" if skill_passed else "failure"
    return "{}_{}_transmission".format(prefix, suffix)

Any handler you do not write falls back to the game's shared default mission script. That is also why a mission with a JSON file and no script at all still flies: the default script does exactly what the code above does.

docs.title: 4. Install and run
docs.text:
Put both files into the Missions folder of a mod:

Mods/my_first_mod/Missions/mymod_coastal_patrol.json
Mods/my_first_mod/Missions/mymod_coastal_patrol.py

Where Mods/ lives on your computer is explained in How mods work; in the game, Main menu → Mods → Open folder takes you there.

Then start the game and load a save. The game reads mission files and scripts every time a save is loaded, so if the game was already running, go back to the main menu and load the save again.

To see the mission without waiting for the weekly draw, open the cheat console (see Cheat console) and type:

create_mission mymod_coastal_patrol

The mission appears on the war map straight away. Testing and reloading explains the edit loop and what to check when nothing shows up.

docs.title: What not to write
docs.text: Four handler names exist in the game but are never called: get_mission_icon, calculate_mission_modifiers, calculate_airplane_modifiers and calculate_pilot_modifiers. Old scripts implement them at length. That code does nothing. The icon comes from _missionIcon in the JSON.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• Missions that unlock other missions: Chains and campaigns
  • Scripts that react to the base instead of owning a mission: Events
  • Every handler, field and number: Reference

docs.title: Locations
docs.text: Every mission happens somewhere. A mission lists the places it can appear, and the game picks one of them each time the mission is created. This page explains how that choice works, what the location flags mean, and lists every place that ships with the game, with its coordinates.

docs.title: How a location is chosen
docs.text:
When a mission is created, the game draws one entry from the mission's list of locations (_potentialLocations in the mission JSON). If that spot is already used by another mission on the map, it draws again, up to five more times. If every draw comes up taken, it keeps the last one, so two missions can end up sharing a location.

If a mission lists no locations at all, the game falls back to a random place from the list below.

Distance is not decoration: the fuel a flight costs is worked out from the great-circle distance (the shortest distance over the globe) between the location and the loaded map's own coordinates, multiplied by FuelConsumptionPerKilometer from the Variables table (see CSV tables). A mission over Berlin is far more expensive to fly than one over the Channel.

docs.title: Using a location
docs.text:
In the Mission Editor, open the Locations section, pick a place from the dropdown and add it. Add as many as you like; the same place cannot be added twice.

In a mission .json, each entry of _potentialLocations looks like this:

{
    "_locationId": "dover",
    "_locationName": "dover",
    "_coordinates": { "x": 51.13512, "y": 1.312756 },
    "_flags": 4
}
Field Meaning _locationName The name of the place. This is the field the game actually uses: to tell whether a spot is already taken, and to look up the place's flags. _locationId Informational only. Keep it identical to the name. _coordinates x is latitude, y is longitude, in degrees. Used for the marker on the war map and for the distance (and so the fuel cost). _flags A number describing the place (see below). Must be a number - "Sea" is not accepted.

A list with several places lets the same mission turn up in different spots:

"_potentialLocations": [
    { "_locationId": "dover_strait", "_locationName": "dover_strait", "_coordinates": { "x": 51.0598, "y": 1.5825 }, "_flags": 2 },
    { "_locationId": "english_channel", "_locationName": "english_channel", "_coordinates": { "x": 50.166, "y": -1.7013 }, "_flags": 2 },
    { "_locationId": "seine_bay", "_locationName": "seine_bay", "_coordinates": { "x": 49.7154, "y": -0.672 }, "_flags": 2 }
]

From a script, a script-only mission (one without a .json) is placed with missions_api.SetMissionLocation(mission_entity_id, location_name), usually from initialize_mission. It accepts only a name from the list below, never coordinates of your own, and returns False for an unknown name. Without a location, a script-only mission sits at the map origin. See Reference.

docs.title: Location flags
docs.text:
Value Name Meaning 0 None none 1 Land over land 2 Sea over the sea 4 OwnTerritory over friendly territory 8 EnemyTerritory over enemy territory

They add up, so 10 is Sea + Enemy territory (2 + 8) - the most common value for a coastal target on the far side of the Channel.

The flags in your mission file are not read

The _flags value in a mission file is kept for completeness, but the game does not read it. Every shipped mission leaves it at 0. Quest steps such as "fly a mission over the sea" look the mission's location name up in the list below and use the flags recorded there. The quest step writes the flag name, not the number: location,sea, location,ownterritory, location,enemyterritory (see Quests).

Two consequences: a location name that is not on the list passes every location condition automatically, and because no shipped location carries Land, a location,land condition can never be met.
