docs.title: Using your own coordinates
docs.text:
Nothing stops a mission from naming a place that is not on the list. The coordinates live in the mission's own file, not in a shared table, so you can put a mission anywhere. The name and coordinates are yours; the flags a quest step sees are not - they come from the shipped list by name (see above), so a place of your own matches every location condition. A script cannot use your own place: missions_api.SetMissionLocation only accepts names from the list.

The war map shows latitude 40.75 to 61.25 and longitude -11.75 to 21.64 (a Mercator projection, the usual flat world map). The range of the shipped places above is simply where they happen to be, not the map's limit. A location outside the map's box still works - distance and fuel are just maths - but its marker is pushed to the nearest edge of the map, so the player sees it at the border rather than where it really is. It stays clickable.

Tip

Give your own places a name with your mod's prefix (mymod_scapa_flow). A name the game already uses would share that place's "already taken" check with every mission that uses it.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
Everything a mission can contain, in one place: how the game finds your files, the order in which it calls your script, every handler, every JSON field and every number the JSON expects.

New to missions? Start with Write your first mission and come back here when you need a detail.

docs.title: Two ways to build a mission
docs.text:
A mission is identified by its id, which is simply its file name without the extension. coastal_patrol.json is the mission coastal_patrol.

With a JSON file (the normal way) Script only (no JSON) Files <id>.json, optionally <id>.py <id>.py Base values (time window, flight time, enemies) from the JSON from the getter handlers, each optional Skill stats _missionStats missions_api.SetMissionStat in initialize_mission Map location _potentialLocations missions_api.SetMissionLocation As-planned chance _asPlannedChance missions_api.SetAsPlannedChance Outcomes four _missionOutcomes missions_api.SetOutcome and AddOutcomeEffect, or get_mission_result In-flight events per flight always 3 get_mission_events_count (default 3) Appears on its own (weekly draw, historic spawn) yes no, see Script-only missions

Use the JSON way unless you have a reason not to. It survives saving and loading, it can be checked by the validator, and it appears in the game without any other script handing it out.

docs.title: Which script runs
docs.text:
Every mission runs on a script, but you rarely have to write one:

  • If a .py file named exactly like the mission exists, the game uses its handlers.
  • For every handler that file does not define, and for every mission without its own file, the game uses the shared default mission script that ships with the game. It reads the mission's id and emits the standard transmissions from the nine text slots (see Localization).

So a JSON file plus its text is a complete mission. Write <id>.py only to change what happens in flight or which text appears. The match is on the exact file name: a script called recon.py never attaches itself to a mission called dangerous_recon.

docs.title: Where the game looks
docs.text:
Mission files are read from several places, in this order. When two places hold the same id, the last one wins, and replaces the earlier mission completely:

  1. the game's own missions
  2. DLC missions
  3. the Missions/ folder of every enabled mod (Workshop mods first, then mods you installed by hand)
  4. the Missions/ folder in the game data folder (see How mods work)

This is why an id that matches a built-in mission replaces that mission, and why a local copy of a mod beats the Workshop version you are subscribed to. Prefix your ids with your mod name (mymod_coastal_patrol) unless you really mean to replace something.

A mod's Missions/ folder is also its only script folder. Event scripts, helper modules and quest text scripts all go there. See Scripting.

docs.title: Script-only missions
docs.text:
A mission with a .py and no .json never turns up by itself. The weekly draw and the historic spawn only consider missions whose data the game already knows, and a script-only mission has no data until it has been created once.

It can be created two ways:

  • missions_api.CreateMission("<id>") from another script. This is how a campaign hands out a follow-up.
  • the create_mission <id> cheat, for testing.

Three consequences to plan for:

  • After the first creation the draw can pick it. The data your script authored now exists, so the weekly draw treats the mission like any other. If your script added no gates, the mission can appear on any map and any date. Always call AddMissionRequirement (and SetTags if it belongs to one campaign) from initialize_mission.
  • From the second creation on, the getters are no longer asked. The game now builds the mission from the data authored the first time, like a JSON mission: the name, description and threat line come from the text slots missions/<id>/mission_name, missions/<id>/mission_description and missions/<id>/intel_threat_report, and the flight has 3 events. Register those three terms even in a script-only mission.
  • The authored data is not saved. It lives in memory for the current session only. If the player loads a save with such a mission in flight, the authored outcomes are gone and the game asks get_mission_result instead. If that handler is missing, the mission fails with an error when it ends. Any script-only mission should define it.

See the script_only_scramble example on the Examples page.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
What happens to one mission, from the week it is planned to the result window:

# Step What happens 1 Weekly schedule At the start of each week the game spreads a number of mission slots across the week. The number depends on the base's rank. 2 Historic missions with a date At every day change, each historic mission with a _historicDay whose gates pass is created, outside the weekly slots. 3 A slot comes due Every historic mission without a date whose gates pass takes this slot. Only when none is due does a random draw run. 4 Random draw All non-historic missions whose gates pass form a pool. One is drawn and removed from the pool. When the pool is empty it refills. 5 Gates A mission is eligible when all _missionRequirements pass, the current map shares one of its _tags, and (for historic missions) it has not been won yet and is not already on the map. 6 Creation The game picks a location (up to 5 tries to avoid two missions on the same spot), works out distance and fuel from it, and sets up the mission from JSON or script. Then it calls initialize_mission. 7 Waiting The mission sits on the war map until the player sends planes or its start window runs out. Historic missions never run out. 8 Flight The clock starts once all assigned planes are airborne. send_mission_event fires each time the flight passes another step (by default at one third, two thirds and the end). 9 Outcome With data: the rolls pick one of the four outcomes, its effects are applied, then set_mission_impact runs. Without data: get_mission_result decides, then set_mission_impact runs. 10 Return Planes land, crew records update, events fire. Then send_mission_result_text, or send_mission_cancelled_text if the player called the mission off. 11 Result window When the player opens it, get_mission_result_text supplies the text.

docs.title: The two rolls and the outcome index
docs.text:
Two dice rolls decide every mission:

  1. As planned? A roll against _asPlannedChance (0–100). Did the situation develop as briefed?
  2. Skill passed? The game rolls a target inside the range of one mission stat, then adds up the skill of the squadron. If the squadron reaches the target, the roll passes. The first stat is used when the mission went as planned, the second when it did not.

The two answers pick the outcome:

Index As planned Skill roll Meaning 0 no failed Gone wrong and failed 1 no passed Gone wrong but salvaged 2 yes failed Went to plan, still failed 3 yes passed Full success

For programmers: index = (skillPassed ? 1 : 0) | (asPlanned ? 2 : 0).

Exactly four outcomes, in this order

The game does not check how many outcomes you wrote. With fewer than four, the mission crashes the moment it ends, long after you stopped suspecting the JSON. With more than four, the extras are never used.

At least two mission stats

The skill roll reads the first and the second entry of _missionStats directly. With only one, the mission crashes on the skill roll.

"Success" in a chain or a quest does not mean index 3. It means the chosen outcome has "_missionSuccess": true. Index 1 (gone wrong, but salvaged) can count as a success if you say so.

docs.title: Handlers
docs.text:
A handler is a Python function the game calls at a fixed moment. You mark it with the @event_handler(...) decorator and the name of the moment:

from Blindflug.FlightMission import MissionEvent

@event_handler(MissionEvent.SEND_MISSION_EVENT)
def send_mission_event(mission_entity_id):
    ...

The function name is up to you; the decorator is what counts. Every handler receives exactly one argument, mission_entity_id: the number of the mission this call is about. Pass it on to every missions_api call. The same script can run for two flights of the same mission at once, so never store per-flight state in a module-level variable.

Handler MissionEvent constant Returns Called in get_mission_id GET_MISSION_ID str both modes initialize_mission INITIALIZE_MISSION nothing both modes send_mission_event SEND_MISSION_EVENT nothing both modes set_mission_impact SET_MISSION_IMPACT nothing both modes send_mission_result_text SEND_MISSION_RESULT_EVENT nothing both modes send_mission_cancelled_text SEND_MISSION_CANCELLED_EVENT nothing both modes get_mission_result_text GET_MISSION_RESULT_TEXT str both modes get_mission_name GET_MISSION_NAME str script only get_mission_description_text GET_MISSION_DESCRIPTION_TEXT str script only get_time_to_start GET_TIME_TO_START int script only get_completion_time GET_COMPLETION_TIME int script only get_threat_level GET_THREAT_LEVEL str script only get_enemy_count GET_ENEMY_COUNT int script only get_mission_events_count GET_MISSION_EVENTS_COUNT int script only get_fuel_level GET_FUEL_LEVEL int script only get_mission_result GET_MISSION_RESULT bool only without data get_mission_icon GET_MISSION_ICON - never called calculate_mission_modifiers CALCULATE_MISSION_MODIFIERS - never called calculate_airplane_modifiers CALCULATE_AIRPLANE_MODIFIERS - never called calculate_pilot_modifiers CALCULATE_PILOT_MODIFIERS - never called

"Script only" handlers are asked once, when a mission without a JSON file is created for the first time (see Script-only missions). A mission with a JSON file ignores them.

docs.title: get_mission_id
docs.text:
Returns the mission's id as a string.

MISSION_ID = "mymod_coastal_patrol"

@event_handler(MissionEvent.GET_MISSION_ID)
def get_mission_id(mission_entity_id):
    return MISSION_ID

A script-only mission must define it: that is how the game recognises the file as a mission of its own. Return exactly the file name. In a script next to a JSON file the game does not read the value, but your own code usually builds text keys from it, so keep it identical to the file name there too. The shared default script returns missions_api.GetMissionId(mission_entity_id), which works for any mission.

docs.title: initialize_mission
docs.text:
Called once, right after the mission has been created and before it appears on the war map.

This is where a script-only mission writes everything a JSON file would carry: gates, stats, location, slots, difficulty, outcomes. A mission with a JSON file can use it too, for example to adjust difficulty to the campaign so far:

@event_handler(MissionEvent.INITIALIZE_MISSION)
def initialize_mission(mission_entity_id):
    if campaign_state.get("raids_survived") >= 2:
        missions_api.SetMissionStat(mission_entity_id, "Fight", 76, 115)
        missions_api.SetAsPlannedChance(mission_entity_id, 35)

Calling missions_api.CreateMission from here is refused and logged, because this handler runs in the middle of creating a mission.

Note

On a mission with a JSON file, SetMissionStat, SetOutcome, AddOutcomeEffect, AddMissionRequirement and SetTags change the data the game loaded from that file, for the rest of the session. Every later copy of the mission sees the change, and effects you add pile up. Adjust stats and chances freely; add effects and gates only in script-only missions.

docs.title: send_mission_event
docs.text:
Called while the mission is in flight, once per progress step. A mission with a JSON file always has three steps; a script-only mission has as many as get_mission_events_count returns. The steps fall evenly across the flight time, the last one at the end.

The handler is not told which step this is. Ask:

@event_handler(MissionEvent.SEND_MISSION_EVENT)
def send_mission_event(mission_entity_id):
    events_sent = missions_api.GetNumberOfEventsSent(mission_entity_id)

    if events_sent == 1:
        going_as_planned = missions_api.MakeAsPlannedRoll(mission_entity_id)
        ...
    elif events_sent == 2:
        skill_passed = missions_api.MakeSkillRoll(mission_entity_id)
        ...

GetNumberOfEventsSent returns 1 on the first call, 2 on the second, and so on.

Roll once, read afterwards. MakeAsPlannedRoll and MakeSkillRoll perform a roll and store it; GetAsPlannedRoll and GetSkillRoll read the stored result. Make the as-planned roll first, because the skill roll uses it to pick which stat to roll against. Every later handler only reads. Rolling a second time would tell the player one story and hand them the outcome of another.

If you override this handler, you must make both rolls yourself. The outcome step reads them.

docs.title: set_mission_impact
docs.text:
Called when the flight is over and the outcome has been decided. Effects from the JSON outcome have already been applied, and missions_api.IsMissionSuccessful already gives the answer.

Use it for consequences the JSON cannot express, and to hand out follow-up missions:

@event_handler(MissionEvent.SET_MISSION_IMPACT)
def set_mission_impact(mission_entity_id):
    if missions_api.IsMissionSuccessful(mission_entity_id):
        missions_api.CreateMission("mymod_pursuit")

See Chains and campaigns.

docs.title: send_mission_result_text
docs.text: Called after the planes have come back from a mission that was flown to the end. The usual job is one closing line in the event log with event_log.Create. The Python constant is MissionEvent.SEND_MISSION_RESULT_EVENT.

docs.title: send_mission_cancelled_text
docs.text: Called instead of send_mission_result_text when the player called the mission off. The Python constant is MissionEvent.SEND_MISSION_CANCELLED_EVENT. A cancelled mission applies no outcome and counts as cancelled for chains, not as a failure.

docs.title: get_mission_result_text
docs.text:
Called when the player opens the result window of a mission that was flown to the end. Return the text key of the line the window should show. Only read the rolls here; never make them.

@event_handler(MissionEvent.GET_MISSION_RESULT_TEXT)
def get_mission_result_text(mission_entity_id):
    going_as_planned = missions_api.GetAsPlannedRoll(mission_entity_id)
    skill_passed = missions_api.GetSkillRoll(mission_entity_id)
    prefix = "ap" if going_as_planned else "gw"
    suffix = "success" if skill_passed else "failure"
    return "missions/{}/{}_{}_transmission".format(MISSION_ID, prefix, suffix)

A key of the form missions/<id>/<slot> also picks up the mission's _raw* text from the JSON (see Localization).

docs.title: get_mission_name
docs.text: Script-only missions. Returns the text key of the mission's name. Default when missing: the mission id.

docs.title: get_mission_description_text
docs.text: Script-only missions. Returns the text key of the description in the mission window. Default when missing: empty.

docs.title: get_time_to_start
docs.text: Script-only missions. Returns how many in-game minutes the mission waits on the war map before it expires. Default when missing: 60.

docs.title: get_completion_time
docs.text: Script-only missions. Returns the flight time in in-game minutes. Default when missing: 120.

docs.title: get_threat_level
docs.text: Script-only missions. Returns the text key of the threat line in the mission window. Default when missing: Low.

docs.title: get_enemy_count
docs.text: Script-only missions. Returns the number of enemy planes reported. Default when missing: 0. There is no API call to change it later, so on the second and later creation of a script-only mission the count is 0.

docs.title: get_mission_events_count
docs.text: Script-only missions. Returns how many times send_mission_event fires during the flight. Default when missing: 3.

docs.title: get_fuel_level
docs.text: Script-only missions. Returns the fuel the flight costs. Default when missing: 100. If the script calls SetMissionLocation, the fuel is recalculated from the distance to that location.

docs.title: get_mission_result
docs.text:
Returns True if the mission succeeded, False if not. The game only asks when it has no outcome data for the mission: a script-only mission that authored no outcomes, or one whose authored data was lost because the player loaded a save. If it is missing in that situation, the mission fails with an error when it ends.

@event_handler(MissionEvent.GET_MISSION_RESULT)
def get_mission_result(mission_entity_id):
    return missions_api.GetAsPlannedRoll(mission_entity_id) and missions_api.GetSkillRoll(mission_entity_id)

docs.title: get_mission_icon
docs.text: Never called. The icon comes from _missionIcon in the JSON. Old example scripts implement this handler at length; that code does nothing.

docs.title: calculate_mission_modifiers
docs.text: Never called. Do not implement it.

docs.title: calculate_airplane_modifiers
docs.text: Never called. Do not implement it.

docs.title: calculate_pilot_modifiers
docs.text:
Never called. Do not implement it.

get_mission_fatalities, found in very old documentation, no longer exists at all. Losses come from the Damage outcome effect.

docs.title: JSON schema
docs.text:
The mission file is read field by field. Field names start with an underscore and must be spelled exactly; an unknown or misspelled field is silently ignored. Every field is optional as far as loading goes, but a playable mission needs the ones marked required.

Field Type Meaning _maxPlaneSlots int How many planes the player may assign. _timeToStartRange {"x": min, "y": max} Minutes the mission waits on the war map before it expires, rolled between min and max. Ignored for historic missions. _timeToCompleteRange {"x": min, "y": max} Flight time in minutes, rolled between min and max. _missionRequirements list Gates that must all pass before the mission can appear. See Requirements. _missionOutcomes list Required, exactly 4, in the fixed order. See Outcomes. _asPlannedChance int Chance in percent (0–100) that the mission goes as planned. _missionStats list Required, at least 2. The first is rolled when the mission goes as planned, the second when it does not. See Mission stats. _enemyPlaneReport int Enemy planes shown in the mission window. Keep it at 18 or below; the validator warns above that. _missionIcon string The icon on the war map. See Icons. _potentialLocations list Candidate places on the war map; one is drawn per mission. Distance and fuel follow from it. With an empty list the game picks a random location. See Locations. _difficultyRating int Stars shown to the player, 1–3. Default 1. _tags list of strings Which maps the mission belongs to. See Map tags. _isHistoric bool Makes the mission a story beat. See Chains and campaigns. _historicDay date Earliest date a historic mission appears. A year below 1900 counts as "no date". _rawMissionName ... _rawGwFailureTransmission string Nine optional text fields. See Localization. _distanceLocationDependant {"x", "y"} Written by Blindflug's own mission tool. The game does not read it; leave it alone or leave it out.

Dates are written as an object:

"_historicDay": { "Year": 1940, "Month": 8, "Day": 13, "Hour": 0, "Minute": 0 }

Fields that older files and older documentation carry, and which the game no longer reads: _distanceRange, _hasMaximumDay, _maximumDay, _mapId, _mapIds, _mapTags, _missionTags. A mission that still relies on _mapTags loses its map restriction without any warning and appears everywhere. Use _tags.

The "Name" entries inside lists ("Name": "RunwayTier") are labels for humans. The game ignores them.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Each entry in _missionRequirements is one gate. All gates must pass.

"_missionRequirements": [
    { "Name": "RunwayTier",            "_requirementType": 0, "_value": "1" },
    { "Name": "EarliestAppearanceDay", "_requirementType": 1, "_value": "3" }
]

_value is always a string, even for numbers.

_requirementType Name _value Passes when 0 RunwayTier tier as a number, "2" the base has a runway of at least this tier 1 EarliestAppearanceDay days, "14" at least this many days have passed since the campaign started 2 LatestAppearanceDay days, "40" at most this many days have passed since the campaign started 3 CompletedMission "<missionId>" or "<missionId>,<outcome>" the player has finished that mission with that outcome at least once

For CompletedMission, the outcome is success, failure or cancelled. Without an outcome, any finish counts, including a cancelled one. The game remembers every finish, so after a failed and a later successful attempt both ,failure and ,success pass. See Chains and campaigns.

docs.title: Outcomes
docs.text:
Exactly four entries, in the order of the outcome index:

{
    "Name": "3 - as planned, skill passed",
    "_missionSuccess": true,
    "_outcomeEffect": [
        { "_outcomeEffectType": 7, "_effectValue": "5",     "_effectIcon": "ui_resource_victoryPoints" },
        { "_outcomeEffectType": 5, "_effectValue": "15",    "_effectIcon": "ui_confidence" },
        { "_outcomeEffectType": 3, "_effectValue": "10-40", "_effectIcon": "ui_health_poor_injured" }
    ]
}
Field Meaning _missionSuccess Whether this ending counts as a success, for chains, quests and the player's records. _outcomeEffect List of effects applied when the mission ends this way. May be empty. _outcomeEffectType Which effect, see the table below. _effectValue A string. A whole number for everything except Damage; a range "min-max" for Damage. _effectIcon Icon shown next to the effect in the result window. Copy it from an example; an empty string shows no icon. _outcomeEffectType Name _effectValue Effect 0 CrewMood number, "-20" mood of everyone who flew 1 CrewConfidence number confidence of everyone who flew 2 CrewEnergy number energy of everyone who flew 3 Damage range, "20-60" damage to each plane, rolled per plane; heavy damage also hurts the crew 4 BaseMood number mood of the whole base 5 BaseConfidence number confidence of the whole base 6 BaseEnergy number energy of the whole base 7 VictoryPoints number victory points, capped at the current limit 8 MaxVictoryPoints - do not use. The game uses it internally to show "victory point limit reached"; in a mission file it crashes the mission when it ends.

A number where a range is expected, or the other way round, is not a crash: the game logs an error in Player.log and skips that one effect.

docs.title: Mission stats
docs.text:
"_missionStats": [
    { "Name": "Recon",           "_missionSkillType": 2, "_statRange": { "x": 10.0, "y": 45.0 } },
    { "Name": "Maneuverability", "_missionSkillType": 4, "_statRange": { "x": 20.0, "y": 60.0 } }
]

_statRange is the range the target is rolled in. The squadron's combined skill must reach it. The shipped missions sit around 40–70 for an ordinary patrol; 85 and above is meant to be lost more often than won.

_missionSkillType Name 0 Fight 1 Bomb 2 Recon 3 Transport 4 Maneuverability 5 Stealthiness

docs.title: Icons
docs.text:
Values for _missionIcon:

Value Use Fight, Recon, Bomb, Transport, Maneuverability, Stealth, Luxury mission type icons Success, Failure result markers Cancel cancelled marker

Note the spelling: the icon is Stealth, the skill type is Stealthiness.

docs.title: Location flags
docs.text:
Every place on the war map carries flags that describe it. They are a bitmask: add the numbers together (10 = sea and enemy territory).

Value Flag 0 None 1 Land 2 Sea 4 OwnTerritory 8 EnemyTerritory

The list of places, with their coordinates, is on the Locations page. Copy the coordinates exactly: the game measures distance and fuel from the coordinates in your file, not from the name.

docs.title: Map tags
docs.text:
"_tags": ["campaign_debden"]

A map lists the tags it supports in its Metadata.json, and a mission lists the tags it is written for. The mission can appear on a map only when the two lists share at least one tag (upper and lower case do not matter). An empty or missing list on either side counts as ["default"], and every built-in map supports default, so an untagged mission appears everywhere.

A mission tagged only campaign_debden appears only on maps that list that tag. A mission that should appear on your campaign map and everywhere else lists both: ["campaign_debden", "default"].

Tags are checked by the weekly draw, by the historic spawn and by missions_api.CreateMission. The create_mission cheat ignores them. Quests have no tags; a map chooses its quests differently (see Quests).

docs.title: Known pitfalls
docs.text: Problem What you see Fix Not exactly 4 _missionOutcomes crash when the mission ends always 4, in index order Fewer than 2 _missionStats crash on the skill roll always at least 2 .py named differently from the .json the script is ignored, the default runs identical file names Id already used by a built-in or another mod one mission silently replaces the other prefix ids with your mod name A never-called handler implemented nothing happens delete it MaxVictoryPoints in an outcome crash when the mission ends use VictoryPoints _coordinates left at 0, 0 the mission is placed far away, with a huge fuel cost copy coordinates from Locations Old field _mapTags instead of _tags map restriction silently lost rename to _tags Script-only mission without gates appears anywhere once it has been created AddMissionRequirement in initialize_mission

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
A quest is a list of goals the player sees in the quest panel: build an airstrip, order an aircraft, fly five missions. Each goal (a step) is a counter that fills up as the player does the thing, and when every required step is full the quest is complete and the next one in the chain can start.

Quests are not missions. A mission is a flight with dice rolls and a script; a quest is a checklist that watches the game and ticks boxes. There is no Python in a quest and nothing to "run" - a quest is a single .json file, and everything it can watch for is built into the game.

No quest editor

Quests are written and changed in a text editor only. The Mission Editor does not open them, and the game does not check them before loading - the checklist near the end of this page is your check.

Page Contents Missions missions, and the events a quest can wait for when a mission returns Locations the location flags a mission step can filter on (sea, enemyterritory, ...) CSV tables the data tables that hold the ids you use in quests - buildings, aircraft, resources, plants Example quests complete quest files to copy

docs.title: Where quests come from
docs.text:
The game reads quests from two places, and the later one wins when both carry the same id:

  1. Shipped quests - inside the game, read-only. You can override one by re-using its file name, but you cannot edit it in place.
  2. Mods - Mods/<your mod>/Quests/, holding .json files. Only files directly inside Quests/ are read; subfolders are ignored. Only enabled mods are read - a mod switched off in the Mods window contributes no quests.

Unlike missions, there is no personal quests folder outside a mod. To try a quest, put it in a mod folder (How mods work explains where that folder is and how the Mods window works). The quests go into a Quests subfolder next to the other content types:

Mods/
  my_campaign/
    config.json                  optional
    Quests/
      mycampaign_first_steps.json
      mycampaign_first_patrol.json
    Missions/                    optional - mission files, and the .py that holds your quest text
    Maps/                        optional - the map that starts your quest line

Two rules follow from how the files are read:

  • The file name is the quest id. mycampaign_first_steps.json is the quest mycampaign_first_steps, whatever the _questId field inside says. Keep the two identical: the game checks whether a quest already exists in the save by its file name but stores the field in the save, so if they differ the quest is handed out again every time the game loads, and chains (requirement type 1) refer to the field.
  • Prefix your ids with your mod name. A file called quest3.json silently replaces the shipped quest3. Between two mods with the same file name, the one loaded later wins (see Which mod wins).

When changes show up

Quest files are re-read every time a level is loaded - return to the main menu and load again (loading a save is enough). A brand-new mod folder, or a Quests/ folder that was still empty when the game started, needs Refresh in the Mods window first, or a restart.

docs.title: A first quest
docs.text:
This is a complete, working quest. Save it as Mods/my_campaign/Quests/mycampaign_first_steps.json, start the game, and load or start any map: it appears in the quest panel right away.

{
    "_questId": "mycampaign_first_steps",
    "_questTitle": "mycampaign/first_steps/title",
    "_questDescription": "",
    "_subQuests": [
        {
            "_subQuestTitle": "mycampaign/first_steps/step0_title",
            "_subQuestDescription": "mycampaign/first_steps/step0_description",
            "_isOptional": false,
            "_subQuestRequirement": {
                "_type": 7,
                "_parameter": "building_finished,Sickbed",
                "_amount": 1
            },
            "_genericIconKey": "ui_health"
        },
        {
            "_subQuestTitle": "mycampaign/first_steps/step1_title",
            "_subQuestDescription": "",
            "_isOptional": true,
            "_subQuestRequirement": {
                "_type": 4,
                "_parameter": "Bed",
                "_amount": 4
            },
            "_genericIconKey": "ui_bed"
        }
    ],
    "_requirements": [],
    "_isHiddenInUI": false,
    "_questType": 0
}

Reading it top to bottom: the quest has two steps. The first waits until a sickbed has been finished building - once. The second counts beds standing on the base and is full at four, but it is optional, so the quest completes as soon as the sickbed is done. _requirements is empty, which means the quest starts on every map the moment the game loads.

The titles are localization keys, not text - until you register them, the player sees no title at all. The section Text explains how to give them words.

docs.title: The file, field by field
docs.text:
Field Meaning _questId The quest's id. Keep it equal to the file name. _questTitle Localization key of the title shown in the quest panel. _questDescription Localization key of a longer text under the title. Leave "" for none - shipped quests do. _subQuests The steps, in the order they are listed in the panel. At least one. _requirements When the quest is handed out - see How a quest starts. Not progress. _isHiddenInUI true hides the quest from the panel while it still runs. Used by the shipped skin-unlock quests. _questType 0 a normal quest, 1 an aircraft-skin quest, 2 a tutorial quest. Use 0 - see Quest types. _highlightedUIElements Tutorial quests only: buttons the tutorial points at. Ignored for type 0. _cheatsOnStart, _completionCheats Tutorial quests only, and ignored in every mod quest - see Quest types.

Fields you leave out take their default: false, 0, or empty. Extra fields (the shipped files carry a "Name" the game no longer reads) are ignored. There is no tags field: quests are tied to maps differently from missions, see Quests and maps.

Each entry of _subQuests is one step:

Field Meaning _subQuestTitle Localization key of the step's title. Also the name the game uses for the step (other quests can wait for it through sub_quest_completed). _subQuestDescription Localization key of the step's tooltip. "" for none. _isOptional true - the quest can complete without this step. _subQuestRequirement What is counted: a _type, a _parameter and an _amount. Exactly one per step. _genericIconKey Which icon the step shows. See Icons.

And the requirement inside it:

Field Meaning _type A number picking the kind of condition - the full table is under What a step can wait for. _parameter A comma-separated list whose meaning depends on the type. No spaces around the commas. _amount The count at which the step is complete. At least 1.

_amount must be at least 1

A step with _amount: 0 behaves inconsistently: depending on whether the quest was created while a save loaded or later in the running game, it either completes instantly or never completes - and in the second case, unless it is optional, it blocks its quest forever. If you want a step the map already satisfies (a "you are here" step), give it a real, already-true condition instead: _type: 1, _parameter: "0", _amount: 1 is complete as soon as the base has any parking spot.

docs.title: Text
docs.text:
Every text field of a quest is a localization key - a name the game looks up in its translation table when the panel is drawn. A key that is registered in no language is not shown at all: the quest card keeps the text it had before (a placeholder, or the text of the quest that last used that card) and the tooltip stays empty. Register every key.

Missions can carry their text directly in the JSON. Quests cannot - there are no raw-text fields, and a quest has no script of its own. You have two options:

Reuse a shipped key. The tutorial and main-line quests already have translated titles for things like "Build an airstrip" or "Order an aircraft". Open the matching shipped quest and copy its key. This costs nothing and is translated into every language the game ships, but you are limited to sentences that already exist.

Register your own keys from a script. A .py file in your mod's Missions/ folder runs when a level loads, for every enabled mod, and its top level can register terms:

TERMS = {
    "mycampaign/first_steps/title":             "First steps",
    "mycampaign/first_steps/step0_title":       "Build a sickbed",
    "mycampaign/first_steps/step0_description": "Injured crew recover faster in a bed of their own.",
    "mycampaign/first_steps/step1_title":       "Build four beds",
}

try:
    for term, text in TERMS.items():
        localization.SetTerm("en", term, text)
except Exception as error:
    print("MyCampaign: could not register quest terms: %s" % error)

The file needs no mission handlers; it exists only to run this block. Put it in Missions/, not in Quests/ - Quests/ is read for .json only, and Missions/ is the one folder the game loads scripts from. Call SetTerm once per language you want to support ("de", "fr", ...). A language you leave out shows the text of a language you did register, so always register en. The try/except matters: a syntax error skips only your script, but any other error at the top level of a script can stop the loading of every script after it - yours and other mods'.

Registering a key the game already ships - a building name, a shipped quest title - replaces the game's own text for that language. Prefix your keys with your mod name so this can never happen by accident. Shipped quests name their keys quest/<questId>/title, quest/<questId>/subQuest0_title and quest/<questId>/subQuest0_description; nothing enforces that shape for your quests. More on terms: Localization.

docs.title: Icons
docs.text:
_genericIconKey picks the step's icon from a fixed set built into the game. A key the game does not know simply shows no icon; nothing is logged. There is no way to add your own icons from a mod.

Kind Keys Base ui_path_runway, ui_runway, ui_path_cars, ui_functionarea_runway, ui_functionarea_parking, ui_functionarea_parking_1, ui_functionarea_parking_2, ui_functionarea_resources, ui_functionarea_safety, ui_functionarea_gardening, ui_hangar_roof, roof, wall, floor, door, house, ui_decoration_wall, ui_decoration_poster, ui_props_kitchen, ui_props_social Aircraft ui_plane, ui_plane_GlosterGladiator_MKI, ui_scramble, ui_aagun, ui_alarm, ui_radio Resources ui_resource_wood, ui_resource_planks, ui_resource_metal, ui_resource_bricks, ui_resource_cement, ui_resource_fuel, ui_resource_gunAmmo, ui_resource_repairParts, ui_resource_trash, ui_resource_rubble, ui_resource_victoryPoints, ui_seeds_beans, ui_harvesting, ui_tool_gathering, ui_fire Crew ui_crew_person_single, ui_crew_people_multiple, ui_crewjob_cook, ui_crewjob_medic, ui_health, ui_morale, ui_bed, ui_prop_bed, ui_prestige_full, Endurance Interface ui_camera, ui_move_tool, ui_pause, ui_speed_1, ui_speed_2, ui_speed_3, ui_timer_clock, ui_clock, ui_schedule, ui_eventlog, ui_notifications_all, ui_attention, ui_search_looking_glass, ui_lock_open, ui_headquarters, ui_stamp_headquarters_approved, ui_repairandcrafting, ui_cogwheel, ui_crown, ui_mark_exclamation, ui_assigned, ui_trash, plus Workbenches SawStation, FieldKitchen, IndoorKitchen, ElectronicsWorkbench, BrickStation, CementMixer Prop thumbnails PP0151_SickBed_thumbnail, PP1101_Bofors40mm_thumbnail, PP1002_SirenOnAPole_thumbnail, PP1006_LargeFuelTankWithConnector_thumbnail, PP1020_Flagpole5m_thumbnail, PP1030_Water_Pump_thumbnail, PP1000_RadioTower_thumbnail, PP0101_WoodenChair_thumbnail, PP0102_BarStool_thumbnail, PP0911_BarCounter_thumbnail, PP0956_DividerCurtains_thumbnail, BB0900_Sandbag1mStraightVarA_thumbnail, BB1300_Table1x2_thumbnail, Simple-Rack_thumbnail, GraveStoneWhite_thumbnail

"" is fine and means no icon. When in doubt, copy the key from a shipped step that shows the picture you want.

docs.title: What a step can wait for
docs.text:
Each step has one requirement, and its _type decides what the game counts. There are two kinds:

  • Counted state (polled) - every couple of seconds the game counts something on the base (airstrips, beds, storage zones) and writes the count into the step. The count can go down again if the player demolishes things, right up until the step completes.
  • Counted events - the step adds one each time something happens (a building is finished, an aircraft returns from a mission). These never go down.

Progress is capped at _amount, and a completed step stays complete.

docs.title: All types at a glance
docs.text:
_type Name Kind Section 0 Airstrip polled Building the base 1 Parking polled Building the base 2 Airplane polled Aircraft and missions 3 PropCategory - does nothing Types that do nothing 4 Prop polled Building the base 5 SimpleEvent event Events 6 Workbench polled Building the base 7 AnyAttributeEvent event Events 8 AllAttributesEvent event Events 9 FunctionArea (zone) polled Building the base 10 ShelteredStorage polled Building the base 11 TrashStorage polled Building the base 12 SuccessfulMission event Aircraft and missions 13 FlownMission event Aircraft and missions 15 UnluckyMission - does nothing Types that do nothing 16 TakePartInScramble event Aircraft and missions 17 FailedMission event Aircraft and missions 18 ScramblePlaneDestroyed event Aircraft and missions 19 ScrambleToSafety event Aircraft and missions 20 CoveredFunctionArea polled Building the base 21 PlannedAirstrip polled Building the base 22 CharacterJob polled Crew 23 QuestDismissed (button) event A button on the quest card 24 GardeningZone polled Building the base 25 StorageAllResourcesEnabled event Building the base

There is no type 14.

docs.title: Building the base
docs.text:
_type Counts _parameter 0 Finished, unobstructed airstrips of at least this tier The tier as a number: "1" ... "5". Required. 21 Airstrips at any stage - planned, under construction or finished - whose planned length, width and material all reach this tier The tier as a number. Required. 1 Usable parking spots of at least this size The size as a number; "0" is any parking spot. Required. 4 Finished props with one of these ids Prop ids, e.g. "Bed" or "Flagpole5,Flagpole10". Planned or unbuilt props do not count. 6 Usable workbenches with one of these ids Workbench ids, e.g. "SawStation", "FieldKitchen". 9 Zones of a type, optionally of a size "<Zone>", or "<Zone>,<min tiles>", or "<Zone>,<min>,<max>". Zones: Airstrip, Parking, SafetyZone, Storage, GardeningZone. Example "Storage,20" - a storage zone of at least 20 tiles. 20 Zones whose every tile is covered by a given building "<Zone>,<building id>", optionally ,<min>,<max> tiles. Example "Storage,roof_tent" - a storage zone entirely under tent roof. 10 1 if at least one storage zone has floor and roof over every tile, else 0 Leave empty. A size in here does not restrict which storage counts - it only decides whether the check runs at all. Use _amount: 1. 11 Storage zones that accept trash and rubble Empty - any storage that lets trash and rubble in. "true" - only storages set up for nothing but trash and rubble. 25 Completes when every listed resource is allowed in at least one storage zone Resource names, e.g. "GunAmmo,AntiAirAmmo,PlaneBombs". Re-checked whenever the player changes a storage's settings or places a zone. Use _amount: 1. 24 Gardening zones growing a plant for a purpose "<plant>,<Seeds or Food>", optionally ,<min tiles>,<max tiles>. Example "beans,Food,10". Plant ids are those of the gardening data table.

The one mistake that hurts other quests too

Types 0, 1 and 21 must have a number in _parameter, and types 20 and 24 must have their second part (the building id, the Seeds/Food purpose). Anything else - including an empty string - is an error inside the game every time the step is checked, and it stalls every other counted-state step that is checked in the same batch until the save is reloaded.

docs.title: Aircraft and missions
docs.text:
_type Counts _parameter 2 Aircraft the player owns One or more aircraft ids, comma-separated - "spitfire" or "spitfire,hurricane" - or empty for any aircraft. 12 Aircraft that returned from a successful mission See below. 13 Aircraft that returned from any mission, won or lost See below. 17 Aircraft that returned from a failed mission See below. 16 Aircraft that took part in a scramble Aircraft ids, or empty for any. 18 Enemy aircraft shot down during a scramble Aircraft ids of the defending aircraft that scored, or empty for any. 19 Aircraft that scrambled to safety Aircraft ids, or empty for any.

Types 12, 13, 16, 17, 18 and 19 add one per aircraft, not per mission. A three-aircraft mission that succeeds adds three to a type-12 step. For "fly one mission", keep _amount: 1 and accept that the step completes when the first aircraft is home.

Filters for 12, 13 and 17. An empty _parameter accepts every returning aircraft. Otherwise the list is read as a bag of words, and the aircraft must satisfy all of them:

Word Types Meaning an aircraft id - spitfire, blenheim, ... all three the returning aircraft must be one of the listed ids. Required whenever the list is not empty - a filter with no aircraft id in it matches nothing. a skill - fight, bomb, recon, transport, maneuverability, stealthiness - or any_skill_type 12, 17 the mission was rolled on that skill. One of these is required for types 12 and 17. gone_wrong 12, 17 only missions that did not go as planned location followed by land, sea, ownterritory or enemyterritory 12, 13 the mission's location must carry every listed flag (see Locations) low_hp 13 the aircraft came back with a quarter of its health or less high_success_rate 17 the mission failed although the forecast was above 90 %

Aircraft ids are the first column of the VehicleData table: gladiator, hurricane, spitfire, meteor, mustangmk1, vampire, beaufighter, typhoon, tempest, kittyhawk, blenheim, hampden, stirling, lancaster, b17raf, mosquito, defiant, flamingo, lysander.

Examples that work in a normal quest:

"spitfire,hurricane,any_skill_type"                  type 12 - a Spitfire or Hurricane won any mission
"blenheim,bomb,location,enemyterritory"              type 12 - a Blenheim won a bombing mission over enemy land
"lysander,any_skill_type,gone_wrong"                 type 12 - a Lysander pulled through a mission that went wrong
"spitfire,low_hp"                                    type 13 - a Spitfire limped home
""                                                   type 13 - any aircraft flew any mission

Note

The shipped skin-unlock quests write a role - fighter, bomber, multirole or special - where the aircraft id goes. That works only for _questType: 1, where the game makes one copy of the quest per matching aircraft and fills the real id in. In a _questType: 0 quest a role name matches nothing - list the aircraft ids.

Waiting for one particular mission. Types 12, 13 and 17 cannot name a mission. Use type 7 with the mission's return event instead - see Events:

{ "_type": 7, "_parameter": "airplane_on_mission_succeed,mycampaign_channel_sweep", "_amount": 1 }

This is how a quest follows a chain of your own missions, one step per mission.

docs.title: Crew
docs.text: _type Counts _parameter 22 Living, not heavily injured crew members with a job One job: RAFAircrew, AAFCook, FieldMechanic, FieldEngineer, RAFMedic, AAFLabour.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Three types watch the stream of things that happen on the base (the game's minor events, listed in full on Events). Each adds one per matching event - with one exception: resource_gained carries the number of units gained and adds that number, so "resource_gained,Metal" with _amount: 20 means twenty metal, not twenty deliveries.

_type Adds one when... _parameter 5 the named event fires, whatever its details "<event>" 7 the named event fires and any of its details is one of the listed values "<event>,<value>,<value>,...". With no values listed, every occurrence counts. 8 the named event fires and every listed value is among its details "<event>,<value>,<value>,..."

Type 7 is the workhorse - "a specific building was finished", "a specific resource arrived":

"building_finished,Sickbed"                          a sickbed finished building
"building_finished,Flagpole5,Flagpole10"             either flagpole finished
"building_type_finished,PropSocial"                  any social prop finished
"project_finished,SawStation.Planks"                 planks came off the saw station
"harvesting_finished,tree,tree_big"                  a tree was felled
"resource_gained,Metal"                              metal arrived by any route - harvest, workbench, delivery
"shipment_received,Bofors40mm"                       a shipment containing a Bofors gun arrived
"assigned_to_equipment,Bofors40mm"                   someone was posted to a Bofors gun
"airplane_on_mission_succeed,mycampaign_sweep"       your mission "mycampaign_sweep" came back a success

Type 8 narrows to combinations, and is rarely needed:

"project_finished,SawStation,SawStation.Planks"      planks finished, and at a saw station
"harvesting_finished,bs_owen_m,tree"                 one particular crew member felled a tree

Type 8 has two limits type 7 does not have. It compares the listed values against the event's details as text only: details that are names (crew ids, building ids, project ids, mission ids) match, but details the game carries as numbers or as types - the resource of harvesting_finished and resource_gained, the category of building_type_finished, the zone of function_area_placed - never do. Use type 7 for those. And a type-8 step with listed values on an event that carries no details at all (victory_points_added, quest_dismissed) is an error every time that event fires. When one value is enough, use type 7.

Events available in normal play, with the details each one carries:

Event Details building_started, building_finished, deconstruction_finished worker, building id (e.g. Sickbed, roof_concrete, wall_tent) building_type_finished worker, building category (e.g. PropSocial, PropPosters) project_started, project_finished worker, workbench id, project id (as SawStation.Planks) harvesting_started, harvesting_finished worker, harvested object (e.g. tree, tree_big, berry_bush), resource resource_gained resource name resource_picked_up, resouce_consumed crew member, resource name (the second is spelt that way in the game) shipment_received the ids in the delivery victory_points_added - assigned_to_equipment crew member, equipment id training_started, training_finished crew member, training object task_started, task_completed crew member, task name (e.g. Harvest, Build, Repair, RepairAirplane, Refuel, Recover) chat_started, chat_finished the two crew members mission_started, mission_success, mission_failed the mission's location name airplane_on_mission_succeed, airplane_on_mission_failed aircraft id, aircraft, mission id, skill, went-as-planned, location name, forecast airplane_took_part_in_scramble, airplane_scramble_fly_to_safety, airplane_scramble_airplane_destroyed aircraft id plane_takeoff, plane_landing the aircraft's internal number (not its id - you cannot filter for spitfire here), pilot storage_resource_enabled, function_area_placed resource name / zone type day_phase_change previous phase, current phase midnight, midday year, month, day sub_quest_completed the completed step's _subQuestTitle key - a quest can wait for a step of another quest quest_dismissed - dog_sleep, dog_walk_started, dog_walk_finished, dog_sniff_wait the dog

Tutorial-only events

A second group of events exists only while the tutorial is running: camera_moved, camera_zoomed, camera_rotated, character_selected, task_created, tooltip_shown, preview_created, building_placed, state_entered, time_scale_changed, window_opened, character_job_assigned, day_phase_ended, plane_ordered, plane_selected, plane_assigned_to_mission, shipment_item_added, scramble_started, attack_finished, storage_resource_disabled, button_clicked, plane_back_from_mission, hour_changed, workbench_selected, project_planned.

The shipped tutorial quests use them freely, which makes them tempting to copy. Outside the tutorial they are switched off and a step waiting for one never moves. Prefer building_finished over building_placed, and airplane_on_mission_succeed over plane_back_from_mission.

docs.title: A button on the quest card
docs.text:
_type Completes when... _parameter 23 the player clicks the button this step puts on the quest card The localization key of the button label, e.g. "basic_ui/ok" or "basic_ui/start".

The button is drawn on the quest card of the quest that owns the step. Note that any such button on any quest advances every type-23 step that is currently open, so keep to one at a time. With an empty _parameter no button is drawn, but the step still completes when a button on another quest is clicked.

docs.title: Types that do nothing
docs.text: _type: 3 and _type: 15 exist in old files but have no logic behind them; a step using either never progresses and nothing is logged. The same goes for any number outside the table. If a step sits at zero forever, check its _type first.

docs.title: How a quest starts
docs.text:
_requirements decides when the quest is handed to the player. It has nothing to do with progress. All entries must pass (they are combined with AND). The check runs when a game is loaded or started, and again every time any quest completes - at that point only quests with a type-1 entry are checked again.

_requirementType Name Meaning _value 0 None No condition. "" 1 CompletedQuestId Start once the named quest is complete. the other quest's id 2 MinimumDate Not implemented. The entry is skipped, so the quest starts as if it were not there. Do not use it. 3 MapDependent Start only when the loaded map names this quest in StartingQuestIds - see Quests and maps. ""

With an empty list, the quest starts on every map as soon as the game loads. That is right for a side quest or an achievement-like quest, and wrong for anything that belongs to a story or a map.

A chain is a series of quests, each requiring the one before it:

"_requirements": [
    { "_requirementType": 1, "_value": "mycampaign_first_steps" }
]

A quest is handed out at most once per playthrough - once it exists in the save, complete or not, it is not created again, and a completed quest stays completed. Requiring a quest that never starts on this map (because that quest carries requirement type 3 and the map does not list it) is a convenient way to keep a whole chain off a map: only the first link needs the map, the rest follow through requirement type 1.

docs.title: Quests and maps
docs.text:
Every map names the quests it starts, in the Metadata.json inside its .goamap file:

"StartingQuestIds": ["mycampaign_first_steps"]

Those quests are handed out when the map is loaded, whatever their _requirements say. A map that names none - an older map, or one whose field was left empty - starts the game's default quest line, quest0, so no map is ever without quests.

The shipped quest0 carries requirement type 3, and every later questN requires the one before it. So the moment a map lists your quest instead of quest0, the whole shipped main line stays away from that map - which is usually what a campaign wants. If you want both, list both: ["quest0", "mycampaign_first_steps"].

To make a quest belong to a map, and only to that map, do both halves:

  1. Put the quest id in the map's StartingQuestIds.
  2. Give the quest the requirement { "_requirementType": 3, "_value": "" } so no other path - not an empty requirement list, not another quest completing - can start it elsewhere.

A quest with an empty requirement list still starts everywhere, listed or not. A quest with only type 1 still starts wherever its predecessor completes. Type 3 is the only thing that says "here and nowhere else".

Missions use tags, quests do not

Missions are tied to maps through tags (the _tags field, see Missions). Quests are not: a quest has no tags field, and the map's StartingQuestIds list is the whole story. The two mechanisms are independent - a campaign map typically uses both, tags for its missions and StartingQuestIds for its quests.

Editing the map's list in the game. Open the map in the map editor and find the Starting quest field in the map settings, next to the tags. Type the quest ids separated by commas - quest0, mycampaign_first_steps - and save the map. Maps you save this way land in your Maps folder (next to the Mods folder); copy the .goamap into your mod's Maps/ folder to ship it. A map that already lives inside a mod folder cannot be saved over from the editor - edit the copy in Maps, then replace the one in the mod. More on maps: Maps.

Editing it in a text editor. A .goamap is an ordinary zip archive with a different file extension. Open it with any archive tool, edit Metadata.json, and put it back with the same name. Everything else in the archive stays as it is. StartingQuestIds sits at the end of the file, next to _tags; add the key if it is missing.

An id in the list that no quest file provides is skipped without a message in the released game; the map still loads.

docs.title: Changing a shipped quest
docs.text:
To change a quest the game ships with, drop a file with the same name into your mod's Quests/. Your copy replaces the shipped one entirely, so start from a full copy of the original and change what you need: an _amount, a _parameter, a step made optional, a step added or removed.

The shipped files are plain JSON inside the game's installation folder, under GroundOfAces_Data/StreamingAssets/Scripts/Quest/ (on macOS: GroundOfAces.app/Contents/Resources/Data/StreamingAssets/Scripts/Quest/) - quest0 to quest14, the tutorial_* quests and the *_skin_unlock quests. Copy from there; never edit them in place, because a game update overwrites that folder. The shipped maps sit nearby in StreamingAssets/Maps/, which is also the place to look at a real Metadata.json.

Changes reach existing saves too. When a save is loaded, every quest already in it is compared with the current file: step titles, step descriptions, requirement types, parameters and amounts are updated in place, steps you added are appended, steps you removed are deleted, and a step whose progress already meets the new amount completes right away. Steps are matched by position, so inserting a step in the middle re-labels everything after it in a running save - append new steps at the end when a quest is already out in the wild. Not updated in a running save: the quest's own _questTitle, _questDescription and _isHiddenInUI, and a step's _isOptional and _genericIconKey - those are fixed when the quest is first handed out.

docs.title: Quest types
docs.text:
_questType: 0 is a normal quest and the one you want. The other two exist for the game's own content, and both come with strings attached.

Tutorial quests (2) additionally point the tutorial highlight at the buttons listed in _highlightedUIElements, one after the other, and can run console commands from _cheatsOnStart and _completionCheats. In a mod:

  • The commands are removed. A mod quest with either list still loads, but the lists are ignored (with a warning in the log) and nothing runs.
  • The highlight ids are a fixed list inside the game - the ids in the shipped tutorial quests (SawStation, Sickbed, ParkingSmall, CrewRoleDropdown, ...) are the vocabulary. An unknown id does nothing.
  • The tutorial-only events (see Events) fire only while the tutorial itself is running, which only the player can switch on (the checkbox in the new-game window), not a mod.

Aircraft-skin quests (1) are created once per aircraft whose role or id appears in the first step's _parameter, and the aircraft's id is appended to every step's parameter. On completion they unlock a skin - but which skin is a table inside the game keyed by the shipped quest ids, so a new quest of this type unlocks nothing.

The same table is what makes completing quest2 unlock new buildings: rewards are not part of the quest file. A mod quest cannot unlock a building, an aircraft or a skin. What it can do is gate: requirement type 1 chains quests behind each other, and a quest step can wait for a mission chain. The reverse is not available - a mission can be gated by map tags, runway tier, a day window or a completed mission, but not by a quest (see Missions).

docs.title: Example quests
docs.text:
Three complete quest files to open, copy and change. They live in the modkit repository as a small mod: examples/quests (the files themselves are in its Quests/ folder). Each one goes into Mods/<your mod>/Quests/ under its file name; the titles are localization keys you give words to as described in Text.

File What it shows example_first_steps.json The quest from A first quest: one required step waiting for a finished sickbed, one optional step counting beds. Starts on every map. example_patrol_chain.json A follow-up quest. It starts once example_first_steps is complete, waits for a Spitfire to be owned, then for the shipped mission calm_supply_drop to come back a success, and optionally counts three winning sorties by Spitfires or Hurricanes. calm_supply_drop only appears from day 20 with a tier-3 runway, so the mission step cannot progress before that. example_map_campaign.json A quest that belongs to one map. Requirement type 3 keeps it off every other map; the map lists it in StartingQuestIds (see Quests and maps). Its steps use the counted-state types: an airstrip of tier 1, two parking spots, a storage zone of twenty tiles.

Install all three together and you have a two-quest chain plus a map-bound quest to compare against. Rename the ids before you build on them - example_ is only a placeholder prefix.

Here is the chained quest in full:

And the map-bound one:

The game's own quest files (quest0.json, quest1.json, the *_skin_unlock and tutorial_* quests) are worth reading too; find them in the installation folder as described in Changing a shipped quest.

docs.title: Testing a quest
docs.text:
Load a level again after every edit (a new folder needs Refresh in the Mods window first), then use the cheat console:

Command Effect quest <id> Hands out the quest right now, whatever its requirements or map say. The console suggests loaded quest ids as you type - if yours is never suggested, the file was not read. Running it twice creates a second copy of the quest. complete_current_quests Completes every open normal quest, so the next links in a chain start. go_to_quest <id> Completes every quest the named one requires (through requirement type 1, following the chain back), so the named quest is handed out. It does not complete the named quest itself, and it works for mod quests too. start_shipment <Resource> <amount> ... Puts resources on the base - start_shipment Wood 12. create_mission <mission id> Puts a mission on the map to test a mission-return step.

When a quest does not show up, or a step does not move, read the game's log file Player.log (where it is: How mods work).

  • A quest file with no JSON object in it at all is skipped, with an error in the log. A file that starts like JSON but is broken inside (a missing comma, an unclosed bracket) can break the loading of the level - check your JSON in an editor before you test.
  • A map that lists an unknown quest id, and a step that never progresses because of a wrong _type or a misspelt id, get no line in the log - check the tables above.

More testing tips: Testing and reloading.

docs.title: Checklist before you ship
docs.text:
• Valid JSON: every { and [ closed, a comma between entries and none after the last one.
  • File name equals _questId, and both carry your mod's prefix.
  • Every _amount is at least 1.
  • Types 0, 1 and 21 have a number in _parameter; types 20 and 24 have their second part.
  • Types 12 and 17 include a skill or any_skill_type; any of 12, 13, 17 that is not empty includes at least one aircraft id.
  • No tutorial-only event outside a tutorial.
  • No _requirementType: 2.
  • Story quests carry _requirementType: 3 and the map lists them; side quests that should start everywhere have an empty list on purpose.
  • Every localization key is either a shipped key or registered by your script - load the game and look at the panel.
  • No spaces inside _parameter.

docs.title: Saves and removing a mod
docs.text:
A quest that has been handed out lives in the savegame - name, progress and requirement - independently of your file. Saving and loading with the mod installed is uneventful. A quest you add in an update appears in existing saves the next time they are loaded, as long as its requirements pass.

Remove the mod and the quest stays in the save, still visible, frozen where it was. Nothing removes a quest because its file is gone, and the text your script registered goes away with the script, so the card shows the bare keys. Steps that wait for your missions can never move, because those missions no longer exist. Putting the mod back restores everything - text, progress, no duplicates.

For the player this means: a quest that can be finished leaves a tidy save behind; one that strands them halfway through a chain does not, and there is nothing they can do about it from inside the game. Prefer quests that reach an end, and treat removing a quest from a published mod as a breaking change for anyone in the middle of a playthrough.

docs.title: What a quest cannot do
docs.text:
• Invent a new condition. The types in the table are everything. If what you want to count is not there, it cannot be expressed - but a script can watch for it and hand out a mission, and a quest can wait for that mission's return.
  • Run logic. No Python, no branching, no reading of game state beyond the counters above.
  • Show text without a key. See Text.
  • Give a reward. See Quest types.
  • Reload inside a running level. Changes show after the next level load.

For anything that has to decide, use a mission or an event script (see Missions and Scripting) and let the quest report where the player has got to.

docs.title: Scripting
docs.text:
The game runs Python scripts for random events and mission logic, and your mod can add its own. A script can react to things that happen on the base - a day phase changing, a building being finished, a mission coming back - and change the game in return: lift the crew's mood, write an entry to the event log, put a mission on the map.

Scripts run on IronPython 3.4, a version of Python 3.4 that runs inside the game. Everyday Python works, including f-strings (the game's own scripts use them). Avoid syntax that came after Python 3.6 - no walrus operator :=, no match, no positional-only / parameters - and packages built for regular Python with compiled parts (numpy and the like) do not work. The standard library that ships with the game is in its Scripts/Lib folder; not every module is there, so stick to what the examples use.

Page Contents Events every event a script can subscribe to, with its arguments API the objects a script uses to talk to the game (characters_api, missions_api, ...) Localization adding and changing text with localization.SetTerm Missions mission scripts and their handlers Python mods and safety what scripts in a mod can do, and what to check before installing one

docs.title: Where scripts live
docs.text:
Your own scripts belong in a mod, in its Missions/ folder:

Mods/
  my_mod/
    Missions/
      morale_boost.py

The game's own scripts sit in the installation folder, under GroundOfAces_Data/StreamingAssets/Scripts (on macOS: GroundOfAces.app/Contents/Resources/Data/StreamingAssets/Scripts). That is read-only shipped content - read it for ideas, but do not change it, because a game update overwrites it. The shipped folders are:

Folder Contents Default the random events (random_events.py, random_health_events.py) Mission the mission scripts, including the shared default_mission.py Lib the Python standard library - not a script folder

docs.title: How scripts are loaded
docs.text:
Scripts are loaded every time a level is loaded, in this order:

  1. the game's Scripts/Default folder
  2. the Supporter Pack's event scripts, if you own it
  3. the game's Scripts/Mission folder
  4. the Supporter Pack's mission scripts
  5. the Missions/ folder of every enabled mod, in mod load order (see Which mod wins)
  6. your own Missions folder next to Mods (on Windows %USERPROFILE%\AppData\LocalLow\Blindflug Studios\Ground Of Aces\Missions\; the other platforms are on Missions)

Rules worth knowing:

  • Only .py files directly inside a folder are read - subfolders are ignored.
  • Each file becomes a Python module named after the file.
  • A file with a syntax error is skipped, with the error in the game's log, and the other files still load.
  • Any other error at the top level of a file (a failing import, an exception while the file runs) is not caught and can stop the folders after it from loading - including other mods' scripts. Wrap risky top-level code in try/except.

Every handler is identified by <module>.<function>, that is the file name plus the function name. If two files define a handler with the same module and function name, the one loaded later replaces the earlier one. This is how a mod can override one of the game's random events: copy random_events.py into your mod's Missions/ folder and change the functions you want changed.

docs.title: Seeing your changes
docs.text: Edit your script, return to the main menu and load a level again - loading a save is enough. If the mod folder itself is new, press Refresh in the Mods window first (see How mods work). More in Testing and reloading.

docs.title: Scripts in a mod
docs.text: Every .py file in a mod's Missions/ folder is a full event script, not only mission logic: it can subscribe to any event exactly like the game's own random_events.py. The scripts of every enabled mod are loaded. A player who does not want a mod's scripts to run disables the mod in the Mods window; the per-mod Scripting switch there does not change this at the moment. See Python mods and safety.

docs.title: Mission scripts
docs.text:
Mission scripts are a special kind of script that decides how a mission plays out. They are covered on Missions, together with the in-game Mission Editor and the JSON file behind every mission. Mission handlers use the same event_handler decorator as the scripts on this page, with the constants from MissionEvent:

from Blindflug.FlightMission import MissionEvent

@event_handler(MissionEvent.GET_MISSION_ID)
def get_mission_id(mission_entity_id):
    return "mymod_coastal_patrol"

The full list of mission handlers is on Reference.

docs.title: Your first event script
docs.text:
Let's write a script that runs every time a day phase changes and lifts the whole crew's mood by 10.

To do this, we subscribe to the DAY_PHASE_CHANGE event. This is just one of the events you can use - the full list is on Events.

Create a mod folder (see How mods work), give it a Missions/ subfolder and create a new file named morale_boost.py in it. Paste the following code into it:

# Import MinorEvent to have access to built-in event names
from Blindflug.MinorEvents import MinorEvent
# Import MoraleCategory to have access to morale type constants
from Blindflug.Game.Characters.Morale import MoraleCategory

# Define a localization term that can be displayed in the game.
# This term contains a single placeholder value named "MOOD".
# Since this is outside any function, it runs when the script is loaded.
localization.SetTerm("en", "mymod/morale_up", f"New day phase, [morale:{MoraleCategory.Mood}] improves by {{[MOOD]}}!")

# Use a decorator to mark the function `on_day_phase` as an event handler.
# The function is called when the event happens.
# The arguments are specific to the day phase change event:
# the previous and the current phase.
@event_handler(MinorEvent.DAY_PHASE_CHANGE)
def on_day_phase(previous_phase, current_phase):

    # The amount of mood to add
    mood_boost = 10

    # Change the mood of all characters
    characters_api.ModifyMorale(MoraleCategory.Mood, mood_boost)

    # Create an event log entry, using the localization term defined above.
    # The "MOOD" placeholder is replaced with the value of str(mood_boost).
    event_log.Create("mymod/morale_up", {"MOOD": str(mood_boost)})

Now launch the game (or press Refresh in the Mods window if the game was already running when you made the folder), load a level and wait until a day phase changes. You should see the message in the event log, and the mood of the whole crew should go up by 10. Congratulations - you have written your first script!

Note

DAY_PHASE_CHANGE is not fired for the very first phase of a game, nor while an air-raid alert is running.

What is @event_handler?

event_handler is a decorator, marked by the @ sign in front of it. A decorator changes the function written right after it - here, it registers the function so the game calls it when the event happens. You do not need to understand more than that to use it.

Why the doubled braces?

In an f-string, {MoraleCategory.Mood} is replaced by Python right away, while {{ and }} produce single braces. So the term ends up containing {[MOOD]}, which is the placeholder the game fills in later.

docs.title: Adding more logic
docs.text:
Everyone at the base likes their work, but they probably enjoy a well-deserved break more. Let's make the effect depend on which day phase has just started.

First, import DayPhase to have access to the day phase constants:

from Blindflug.DayPhases import DayPhase

Inside the on_day_phase function, change the value assigned to mood_boost:

    mood_boost = 10 if current_phase == DayPhase.Leisure else 5 if current_phase == DayPhase.Sleep else 0

If the day phase is neither leisure nor sleep, we do not want to do anything, so add an early return:

    if mood_boost == 0:
        return False

The returned value matters: False means this run does not count towards the maximum number of runs (see below). Returning nothing, or True, counts it normally.

docs.title: Chance and maximum number of runs
docs.text:
Without further settings, the handler runs every time the event happens, as often as it happens. That is great for testing, but for real use some randomness is a good idea. This gives the function a 10 % chance to run when the day phase changes, at most 4 times in one game:

@event_handler(MinorEvent.DAY_PHASE_CHANGE, chance=0.1, max_occurrences=4)
def on_day_phase(previous_phase, current_phase):
    ...

Only the decorator line changes; the body of the function (shown here as ...) stays as it is.

docs.title: Adding translations
docs.text:
If you want your script to support several languages, register the term for each of them. Here is the message in Polish:

localization.SetTerm("pl", "mymod/morale_up", f"Nowa faza dnia, [morale:{MoraleCategory.Mood}] wzrasta o {{[MOOD]}}!")

Switch the game language between English and Polish, and the message in the event log follows. The language code must be one the game offers in its options (pl is).

Note

A language you leave out shows the text of a language you did register, so always register en. A key registered in no language at all is shown as the raw key in the event log.

Warning

SetTerm on a key the game already ships - a building name, a menu label - replaces the game's own text for that language. That is a useful way to retext the game, and an easy way to break it by accident. Prefix your own keys with your mod's name, as in mymod/morale_up. More on Localization.

docs.title: The finished script
docs.text:
After all the changes above, the script looks like this:

from Blindflug.MinorEvents import MinorEvent
from Blindflug.Game.Characters.Morale import MoraleCategory
from Blindflug.DayPhases import DayPhase

localization.SetTerm("en", "mymod/morale_up", f"New day phase, [morale:{MoraleCategory.Mood}] improves by {{[MOOD]}}!")
localization.SetTerm("pl", "mymod/morale_up", f"Nowa faza dnia, [morale:{MoraleCategory.Mood}] wzrasta o {{[MOOD]}}!")

@event_handler(MinorEvent.DAY_PHASE_CHANGE, chance=0.1, max_occurrences=4)
def on_day_phase(previous_phase, current_phase):

    mood_boost = 10 if current_phase == DayPhase.Leisure else 5 if current_phase == DayPhase.Sleep else 0

    if mood_boost == 0:
        return False

    characters_api.ModifyMorale(MoraleCategory.Mood, mood_boost)

    event_log.Create("mymod/morale_up", {"MOOD": str(mood_boost)})

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: A good way to get a feeling for what is possible is to read the game's own scripts: random_events.py and random_health_events.py in Scripts/Default (the second one shows event log types, icons and the health API), and default_mission.py in Scripts/Mission. The Examples page has complete mods to copy, including an event script.

docs.title: Global variables
docs.text:
Every script can use a few ready-made objects, without importing anything, to talk to the game:

Name What it is for logger the game's logger; logger.Log("text") writes a line to the game's log file event_log create event log entries localization add or change localization terms resources_api spawn a resource pile next to an object, or spoil a pile characters_api read and change crew state: health, morale, carried resources, fire, breaking-point effects missions_api manage missions airplanes_api manage airplanes game_api get general game data

Every function of these objects is described on API.

These names are available everywhere, so they also work inside any helper module your script imports. The game's own types are available to Python as well, so any public enum or type can be imported by its full name, for example:

from Blindflug.GameResources import ResourceType
from Blindflug.Tasks import Task
from Blindflug.Game.Characters.Morale import MoraleCategory

eval is removed and cannot be used.

docs.title: Event log entries
docs.text:
event_log.Create(term, parameters=None, event_log_type=EventLogType.Default) takes an optional third argument that colours the entry: from Blindflug.MinorEvents import EventLogType gives Default, Warning, Error and Success. The parameter key "icon" is reserved: its value names a picture from the game's generic icon set (for example "ui_health") shown next to the entry. random_health_events.py uses both:

from Blindflug.MinorEvents import EventLogType

event_log.Create("random_events/" + id, {"CHARACTER": character, "icon": "ui_health"}, EventLogType.Warning)

docs.title: Events
docs.text: The events a script can subscribe to, and the arguments each one passes to your function, are listed on Events. Character arguments are character ids (text), resource arguments are ResourceType values, and task arguments are Task values (from Blindflug.Tasks import Task). Some events are fired without arguments; a few exist only for the game's interface and tutorial.

docs.title: Event handler functions
docs.text:
Event handlers are normal Python functions, marked with the event_handler decorator:

@event_handler(event_name, chance=1.0, max_occurrences=-1)
def handler_function(arg1, arg2):
    pass
  • event_name - the name of the event to handle. This can be any text that matches an existing event, but the easier way is from Blindflug.MinorEvents import MinorEvent and the constants defined there, such as MinorEvent.DAY_PHASE_CHANGE.
  • chance - the chance, from 0.0 to 1.0, that the handler is called when the event happens. 0.5 gives it a 50 % chance. The default is 1.0 (always).
  • max_occurrences - the maximum number of times the handler can run in one save game. The count is stored in the save, keyed by the handler's <module>.<function> name, so renaming the file or the function resets it. A negative value means "no limit" and is the default (-1); 0 means the handler never runs. The chance roll and the limit check both happen before the handler is called.

The name of the function can be any valid Python name. Together with the file name, it identifies the handler when the game counts how often it ran.

The function's arguments depend on the event (see Events). The function can return False so that this run does not count towards max_occurrences. That is useful when a handler should run a limited number of times, but only under certain conditions. Returning nothing, or True, counts the run normally.

docs.title: String formatting
docs.text:
Text in the event log (and other terms you register) understands a few tags that turn a name into a coloured link or icon:

Tag What it shows Where the names come from [character:<id>] a clickable link to the crew member with that id character ids, as passed to your handler [resource:<name>] the resource's icon and colour from Blindflug.GameResources import ResourceType [morale:<name>] the morale category's icon and colour from Blindflug.Game.Characters.Morale import MoraleCategory [CharacterStat:<name>] a crew skill's icon and colour (Flying, Shooting, Bombing, Endurance, Engineering, Navigating) from BlindGame.CharacterStats.Data import CharacterStatType
