CharacterStat is written with a capital C and S - this tag is case-sensitive.

The name inside a tag must be the exact name of the enum member; a name the game does not know is left in the text as it is. Writing the enum value into an f-string, as the examples above do, produces exactly that name.

Tags are resolved after the term's placeholders are filled in, so a tag can wrap a placeholder:

localization.SetTerm("en", "mymod/found", "Found some [resource:{[RESOURCE]}]!")
event_log.Create("mymod/found", {"RESOURCE": str(resource)})

Here resource is a ResourceType value your handler received, for example from the resource_gained event.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Everything a mod script can call. Eight objects are available in every script without an import, plus the decorator event_handler:

Name Purpose event_handler the decorator that registers a handler, see Events and Missions event_log write lines to the in-game event log localization define or override text missions_api mission state, dice rolls, authoring missions from a script characters_api crew morale, health, state airplanes_api plane health, integrity, fuel, pilot resources_api spawn and spoil resources game_api save-game identity and a folder for your own files logger write debug lines to Player.log

Names of game values come from imports:

Import Used for from Blindflug.FlightMission import MissionEvent mission handler names, MissionEvent.SEND_MISSION_EVENT from Blindflug.MinorEvents import MinorEvent event names, MinorEvent.MIDNIGHT from Blindflug.MinorEvents import EventLogType the look of an event log line from Blindflug.GameResources import ResourceType resource types, ResourceType.FoodRations from Blindflug.Game.Characters.Morale import MoraleCategory MoraleCategory.Mood, .Confidence, .Energy from Blindflug.Game.Characters.Morale import CharacterMoraleStateFlag temporary morale states from Blindflug.DayPhases import DayPhase DayPhase.Work, .Leisure, .Sleep

Mod scripts run on IronPython 3.4. Avoid syntax newer than Python 3.6 (:=, match), and stick to the standard library modules the examples use (json, os). Mod scripts can import each other by file name when they sit in the same Missions/ folder.

docs.title: event_log
docs.text:
event_log.Create(loc_key, parameters=None, event_log_type=EventLogType.Default)

Writes one line to the event log. loc_key is a text key (see Localization). parameters is a dictionary that fills {[NAME]} placeholders in that text; all values must be strings.

event_log.Create("mymod/pilot_returned", {"PILOT": str(character_id)})

Characters written as [character:<id>] in the text become clickable names, and are linked to the log line.

event_log_type changes how the line looks: EventLogType.Default, EventLogType.Warning, EventLogType.Error or EventLogType.Success.

docs.title: localization
docs.text:
localization.SetTerm(language_code, key, text)

Defines a text for one language, or replaces it. Call it at the top level of your script so the text exists as soon as the script loads. The Localization page explains keys, languages, placeholders and what happens when your mod is removed.

docs.title: missions_api
docs.text:
Mission state and dice rolls. Every call takes the mission_entity_id your handler received.

Call Returns GetMissionId(id) the mission's id (its file name), or None if the mission no longer exists GetMissionAirplaneFormation(id) the numbers of the planes assigned to the mission GetEnemyCount(id) reported enemy planes IsMissionSuccessful(id) whether the mission succeeded; meaningful from set_mission_impact on GetNumberOfEventsSent(id) how many in-flight steps have fired, counting the current one MakeAsPlannedRoll(id) rolls whether the mission goes as planned, stores and returns it GetAsPlannedRoll(id) reads that roll back MakeSkillRoll(id) rolls the squadron's skill check, stores and returns it; the crew gains experience on a pass GetSkillRoll(id) reads that roll back CreateMission(mission_id) puts another mission on the war map now, see below

Roll once, read afterwards. Make... performs a roll; Get... reads it. Make the as-planned roll before the skill roll: the skill roll uses it to pick which of the two mission stats to roll against. Rolling twice gives the player one story and a different outcome.

GetMissionId exists because many missions share one script: a handler cannot tell from the file name which mission it is running for, so it asks. The shared default mission script uses it to build its text keys.

docs.title: Creating a mission
docs.text:
missions_api.CreateMission("mymod_airfield_pursuit")

Puts a mission on the war map immediately, skipping the weekly draw. Returns True if a mission was created.

It still checks the target mission's own requirements and its map tags. If either fails, nothing is created, it returns False, and a warning naming the mission is written to Player.log. It also returns False for an unknown id. A script-only mission that has never been created has nothing to check yet and is always allowed.

Call it from set_mission_impact, where the outcome is known. From initialize_mission it is refused and logged, because that handler runs in the middle of creating a mission.

@event_handler(MissionEvent.SET_MISSION_IMPACT)
def set_mission_impact(mission_entity_id):
    if missions_api.IsMissionSuccessful(mission_entity_id):
        missions_api.CreateMission("mymod_pursuit")
    else:
        missions_api.CreateMission("mymod_regroup")

When the condition is simply "the previous mission succeeded", a JSON requirement is better: "_requirementType": 3 with "<id>,success", no script at all. See Chains and campaigns.

docs.title: Authoring a mission from a script
docs.text:
These calls write what a mission's JSON would otherwise declare. A script-only mission needs them, because nothing else sets its stats, location or outcomes. Call them from initialize_mission.

Call Sets SetMissionStat(id, skill, min, max) one skill's target range. skill is "Fight", "Bomb", "Recon", "Transport", "Maneuverability" or "Stealthiness". The first skill you set is rolled when the mission goes as planned, the second when it does not. Setting the same skill again replaces its range. SetAsPlannedChance(id, chance) 0–100. Default for a script-only mission: 50. SetMissionLocation(id, name) places the mission on the war map and works out distance and fuel. name is a location from Locations. SetMaxAirplaneSlots(id, slots) how many planes may be assigned, at least 1. Default: 1. SetDifficulty(id, rating) the star rating, 1–3. Default: 1. SetOutcome(id, index, is_success) whether outcome index (0–3, in the mandatory order) counts as a success AddOutcomeEffect(id, index, type, value) adds an effect to outcome index. type is "CrewMood", "CrewConfidence", "CrewEnergy", "Damage", "BaseMood", "BaseConfidence", "BaseEnergy" or "VictoryPoints". value is a whole number like "-40", or a range like "70-140" for Damage. AddMissionRequirement(id, type, value) one appearance gate. type is "RunwayTier", "EarliestAppearanceDay", "LatestAppearanceDay" or "CompletedMission". Gates combine with AND. SetTags(id, tag, ...) which maps the mission belongs to, like _tags in JSON. Replaces what was set before.

All of them return True on success and False when the mission, the index or a name is unknown. None of them raises an error, so check the return value while developing.

Do not use "MaxVictoryPoints" with AddOutcomeEffect. It is accepted, but crashes the mission when it ends.

A script-only mission starts each creation with its effects and requirements cleared, so initialize_mission can add them every time without piling up duplicates. On a mission that has a JSON file, the calls change the loaded file data for the rest of the session instead: effects and requirements you add accumulate with every copy of the mission. Adjust stats and chances there if you like; add effects and gates only in script-only missions.

docs.title: Gating a script-only mission
docs.text:
Without gates, a script-only mission appears anywhere once it has been created the first time: the weekly draw now knows its data, and with no requirements it passes every check. Set them in initialize_mission alongside the rest:

@event_handler(MissionEvent.INITIALIZE_MISSION)
def initialize_mission(mission_entity_id):
    missions_api.AddMissionRequirement(mission_entity_id, "RunwayTier", "2")
    missions_api.AddMissionRequirement(mission_entity_id, "EarliestAppearanceDay", "14")
    missions_api.AddMissionRequirement(mission_entity_id, "LatestAppearanceDay", "40")
    missions_api.AddMissionRequirement(mission_entity_id, "CompletedMission", "mymod_convoy_spotted,success")
    missions_api.SetTags(mission_entity_id, "campaign_debden")

CompletedMission takes "<missionId>", or "<missionId>,success", ",failure" or ",cancelled" to require a particular outcome. Day numbers count from the start of the campaign.

Tags work like _tags in JSON: the mission can appear only on maps that share one of its tags. Leaving tags unset means "default", which every built-in map supports. That is right for a mission meant to appear anywhere, and wrong for one that belongs to a single campaign. See Map tags.

docs.title: characters_api
docs.text:
Character ids are strings, as they arrive in event arguments or from airplanes_api.GetPilot. Several calls come in two forms: one for every character, one for a single character.

Call Effect GetMorale(character_id, category) read one morale value SetMorale(category, value) set for everyone SetMorale(character_id, category, value) set for one character ModifyMorale(category, delta) change for everyone ModifyMorale(character_id, category, delta) change for one character TriggerEffect(character_id, category) trigger that character's breaking-point reaction for that category, as if the morale had bottomed out; returns whether the character was found SetTemporaryMoraleState(character_id, state, duration) put a character into a temporary state, see below ModifyHealth(character_id, delta, notify=True) change health; with notify=True the player gets the usual health notification HealthEventsBlocked() True while the game protects a young base from health events, see below SetFire(character_id, fires) set a character on fire, with fires fires around them GetPilotMissionCount(character_id) missions flown GetPilotSuccessfulMissionCount(character_id) missions won DestroyCarriedResource(character_id) destroy what they carry; returns whether there was something DropCarriedResource(character_id) drop what they carry; returns whether there was something GetVoxelObjectId(character_id) the number of the character's object in the world, for resources_api.SpawnNextTo; 0 if not found

Morale runs from -100 to 100. category is MoraleCategory.Mood, MoraleCategory.Confidence or MoraleCategory.Energy.

SetTemporaryMoraleState takes a CharacterMoraleStateFlag: Happy, Sad, Injured, Sick, Exhausted, Fearful, Angry, Panic, Collapse, Rage or HeavilyInjured, and a duration.

HealthEventsBlocked() returns True during the first days of a campaign while a member of the ground crew is already hurt, so a young base is not hit twice. A script that hurts someone should check it first and return False if it is set:

@event_handler(MinorEvent.TASK_COMPLETED, chance=0.01, max_occurrences=1)
def twisted_ankle(character_id, task_type):
    if characters_api.HealthEventsBlocked():
        return False

    characters_api.ModifyHealth(character_id, -10)
    event_log.Create("mymod/twisted_ankle", {"CHARACTER": str(character_id)})

docs.title: airplanes_api
docs.text:
Planes are identified by number: the values missions_api.GetMissionAirplaneFormation returns, and the airplaneEntityId arguments of events.

Call Returns or does GetPilot(airplane_id) the character id of the first crew member GetAirplaneHealth(airplane_id) health as a fraction, 0.0–1.0 SetAirplaneHealth(airplane_id, value) set health in points (whole number), limited to the plane's maximum AddAirplaneHealth(airplane_id, value) change health by that many points; negative values damage GetAirplaneIntegrity(airplane_id) structural integrity as a fraction, 0.0–1.0 GetAirplaneParkingLot(airplane_id) the number of the plane's parking spot; raises an error if it has none ReduceAirplaneFuel(airplane_id, fuel) burn fuel; a plane that runs dry is missing in action

For damage caused by a mission, prefer the Damage outcome effect in the JSON. It also handles injuries to the crew.

@event_handler(MissionEvent.SET_MISSION_IMPACT)
def set_mission_impact(mission_entity_id):
    for airplane_id in missions_api.GetMissionAirplaneFormation(mission_entity_id):
        pilot = airplanes_api.GetPilot(airplane_id)
        characters_api.ModifyMorale(pilot, MoraleCategory.Energy, -10)

docs.title: resources_api
docs.text:
Call Effect SpawnNextTo(voxel_object_id, resource_type, amount) drop a pile of resources on the nearest free spot beside an object SpoilPile(resource_type) spoil one pile of that resource

Both return True or False. SpoilPile fails when there is nothing to spoil, which is a natural moment for return False in an event handler. Get a voxel_object_id for a character with characters_api.GetVoxelObjectId; dog events deliver one directly.

from Blindflug.GameResources import ResourceType

resources_api.SpawnNextTo(characters_api.GetVoxelObjectId(character_id), ResourceType.FoodRations, 2)

docs.title: game_api
logger
docs.text:
Writes to Player.log (where to find it: Testing and reloading).

logger.Log("mymod: campaign state loaded")

Use event_log for anything the player should see; logger is for you, while debugging. Prefix your lines with your mod name so you can search for them.

docs.title: What is not available
docs.text:
• eval is removed from the scripts' built-in functions.
  • The handlers get_mission_icon and calculate_*_modifiers are never called, so there is no way to add success modifiers from a script. Change stats and chances with the authoring calls above instead.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Events (the game calls them minor events) are the second way a script can hook into the game. They have nothing to do with owning a mission: they fire from life on the base (construction, crew, time of day, resources, planes coming and going), and any script can listen to them.

That makes them the tool for small stories: someone's patrol comes back shot up, a crew member has a bad night, mice get into the rations at midnight. The event_script example reacts to missions it did not write; see Examples.

docs.title: A complete event script
docs.text:
Save this as Mods/my_first_mod/Missions/mymod_quiet_night.py. No JSON, no mission id, nothing else needed:

from Blindflug.MinorEvents import MinorEvent

localization.SetTerm("en", "mymod/quiet_night",
                     "A quiet night. The duty officer reports nothing but owls.")


@event_handler(MinorEvent.MIDNIGHT, chance=0.02, max_occurrences=2)
def quiet_night(year, month, day):
    event_log.Create("mymod/quiet_night")

Event scripts live in the mod's Missions/ folder, like mission scripts. It is a mod's only script folder; a script in any other folder never runs.

docs.title: The decorator
docs.text:
@event_handler(event_name, chance=1.0, max_occurrences=-1)
def handler(argument1, argument2):
    ...
  • event_name: which event, usually written as MinorEvent.SOME_NAME (import it with from Blindflug.MinorEvents import MinorEvent). The plain string, like "midnight", works too.
  • chance: the probability that the handler runs when the event fires, from 0.0 to 1.0. Default 1.0 (always).
  • max_occurrences: how often the handler may run in one playthrough. -1 means unlimited, which is the default.

Returning False does not count against max_occurrences. Use it to check a condition and bail out without using up the budget. Returning nothing, True or any other value counts.

@event_handler(MinorEvent.MIDNIGHT, chance=0.05, max_occurrences=2)
def midnight_mice(year, month, day):
    if resources_api.SpoilPile(ResourceType.FoodRations):
        event_log.Create("mymod/midnight_mice")
    else:
        return False    # nothing to spoil: try again another night

The count is stored per handler under the name <file name>.<function name>. Renaming either the file or the function starts the count again. Two handlers with the same function name in the same file share one count.

Several scripts may listen to the same event. Each handler is rolled and counted on its own.

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
The game passes arguments by position, in the order listed below. The names are only descriptions: call your parameters whatever you like, but take the right number of them, or the call fails.

  • Ids of characters, buildings, workbenches and so on arrive as strings.
  • Ids of planes and dogs (...EntityId, voxelObjectId) arrive as numbers. These are the numbers airplanes_api and resources_api expect.
  • Values like a resource type or a day phase arrive as game values you can compare directly: if resource == ResourceType.MilitaryConstruction:. Turn them into text with str(value).

Useful imports for comparing:

from Blindflug.GameResources import ResourceType
from Blindflug.Game.Characters.Morale import MoraleCategory
from Blindflug.DayPhases import DayPhase

docs.title: Missions and flights
docs.text:
Event Arguments mission_started locationName mission_success locationName mission_failed locationName airplane_on_mission_succeed airplaneId, airplaneEntityId, missionId, skillType, isGoingAsPlanned, locationName, successEstimate airplane_on_mission_failed same seven plane_takeoff airplaneEntityId, characterId plane_landing airplaneEntityId, characterId airplane_took_part_in_scramble airplaneId, airplaneEntityId airplane_scramble_fly_to_safety airplaneId, airplaneEntityId airplane_scramble_airplane_destroyed airplaneId victory_points_added none

The seven-argument pair is the most useful hook in the whole system: it fires once for every plane that comes back from any mission, including ones you did not write. airplaneId is the plane's type name, airplaneEntityId the number to pass to airplanes_api, skillType the rolled skill as text ("Fight"), isGoingAsPlanned True or False, and successEstimate the success chance in percent the player was shown (0 if none).

plane_takeoff and plane_landing fire once per crew member aboard, each time with that person's id.

mission_success and mission_failed fire for missions whose outcome comes from outcome data (every mission with a JSON file). A script-only mission that decides its result with get_mission_result does not fire them.

docs.title: Time
docs.text: Event Arguments midnight year, month, day midday year, month, day day_phase_change previousPhase, newPhase (day phases: DayPhase.Work, DayPhase.Leisure, DayPhase.Sleep)

docs.title: Crew
docs.text: Event Arguments chat_started characterId, targetCharacterId chat_finished characterId, targetCharacterId training_started characterId, trainingObjectId training_finished characterId, trainingObjectId assigned_to_equipment characterId, propId task_started characterId, taskType task_completed characterId, taskType

docs.title: Construction and economy
docs.text:
Event Arguments building_started characterId, buildingId building_finished characterId, buildingId building_type_finished characterId, buildType deconstruction_finished characterId, buildingId (or the id of the terrain object that was cleared) project_started characterId, workbenchId, projectId project_finished characterId, workbenchId, projectId resource_picked_up characterId, resourceType resource_gained resourceType resouce_consumed characterId, resourceType harvesting_started characterId, harvestableId, resourceType harvesting_finished characterId, harvestableId, resourceType shipment_received a variable number of shipment ids, one argument each function_area_placed functionAreaType storage_resource_enabled resourceType

Notes:

  • resouce_consumed is spelled with the missing r. That is the real event name; MinorEvent.RESOURCE_CONSUMED gives you the right string.
  • resource_gained carries an amount that quests read, but a script only receives the resource type.
  • harvesting_started and harvesting_finished fire only for resource containers, not for crates.
  • building_type_finished does not fire for buildings without a type.
  • For shipment_received, write the handler as def on_shipment(*shipment_ids): so it accepts any number of arguments.

docs.title: Quests
docs.text: Event Arguments sub_quest_completed subQuestName (the text key of the sub-quest's title) quest_dismissed none

docs.title: Dogs
docs.text: Event Arguments dog_walk_started voxelObjectId dog_walk_finished voxelObjectId dog_sleep voxelObjectId dog_sniff_wait voxelObjectId

docs.title: Tutorial-only events
docs.text:
25 events fire only while the tutorial is switched on. In a normal game they never reach a script, so they are no use for content mods. They are listed here so you do not wonder why your handler stays silent:

Event Arguments camera_moved none camera_zoomed none camera_rotated none character_selected characterId task_created taskType (as text), targetId tooltip_shown id preview_created buildingId building_placed buildingId state_entered stateName, argument time_scale_changed timeScale (as text) window_opened windowId character_job_assigned jobName day_phase_ended endedPhase plane_ordered airplaneId plane_selected airplaneId plane_assigned_to_mission airplaneId shipment_item_added shipmentId scramble_started none attack_finished none storage_resource_disabled resourceType button_clicked id plane_back_from_mission airplaneEntityId hour_changed hour (0–23) workbench_selected workbenchId project_planned projectId, repetitionCount (as text)

docs.title: Writing to the event log
docs.text:
event_log.Create("mymod/pilot_tired", {"PILOT": str(character_id)})

The first argument is a text key, the second fills {[NAME]} placeholders in that text. A character written as [character:{[PILOT]}] in the text becomes a clickable name. How to define the text, and the other inline tags, is on the Localization page. All of event_log is on the API page.

docs.title: Localization
docs.text: Every piece of text the player sees is looked up by a key, a short name like missions/coastal_patrol/mission_name. The game finds the text for that key in the player's language. This page shows how a mod gives its keys their text, in one language or many, without touching any of the game's own files.

docs.title: The simplest way: text in the mission JSON
docs.text:
A mission can carry its text directly in its JSON file. No script, no keys:

{
    "_rawMissionName": "The Lost Bombers",
    "_rawMissionDescription": "A flight of our own bombers is limping home from France."
}

This is one language only, and it covers exactly nine slots per mission. See Text in the JSON instead of a term below. For anything else you register text from a script.

docs.title: Defining text from a script
docs.text:
localization.SetTerm("en", "mymod/greeting", "Good morning, gentlemen.")

SetTerm(language_code, key, text) gives a key its text in one language. A key with its texts is called a term.

Call it at the top level of a script, not inside a handler. The top level runs once, when the game loads the script, so the text exists before anything needs it.

A script that only defines text is perfectly valid. It needs no handler, no JSON and no mission id. Put it in the mod's Missions/ folder like any other script; the game runs every script it finds there.

docs.title: Why this is safe
docs.text:
Text you register does not go into the game's translation files. The game keeps a separate store for text from scripts, adds keys to it as scripts register them, and looks there as well. Nothing you do with SetTerm changes a file on disk, and there is no translation step to run.

If the key already exists in the game's own texts, SetTerm replaces that text for as long as your mod is loaded. That is how a mod can reword a built-in line. It is also why you should prefix every key of your own with your mod name: an accidental match silently overwrites the game's text.

docs.title: Mission texts
docs.text:
A mission uses nine keys, all shaped missions/<missionId>/<slot>.

Three are read by the game itself and cannot be renamed:

Key Shown in missions/<id>/mission_name the mission list and the result window missions/<id>/mission_description the mission window missions/<id>/intel_threat_report the threat line in the mission window

If one is missing, the raw key appears in the game.

Six are used by the mission script. The shared default mission script uses exactly these names, so a mission without a script of its own needs them too:

Key When missions/<id>/ap_transmission in flight, going to plan missions/<id>/gw_transmission in flight, gone wrong missions/<id>/ap_success_transmission as planned, skill passed missions/<id>/ap_failure_transmission as planned, skill failed missions/<id>/gw_success_transmission gone wrong, skill passed missions/<id>/gw_failure_transmission gone wrong, skill failed

ap means "as planned", gw means "gone wrong". The four *_success and *_failure keys match the four outcome slots of the mission JSON one to one.

A small helper keeps a mission script readable:

MISSION_ID = "mymod_coastal_patrol"


def _term(slot, text):
    localization.SetTerm("en", "missions/{}/{}".format(MISSION_ID, slot), text)


_term("mission_name", "Coastal Patrol")
_term("mission_description", "Fly the shoreline. Report anything that moves.")

A mission script may register as many extra keys as it likes (missions/<id>/veteran_departure, say) and use them with event_log.Create.

docs.title: Text in the JSON instead of a term
docs.text:
The nine _raw* fields of a mission JSON answer the nine slots above directly. When a raw field is filled, the game uses it before it looks up the key, so a mission with raw text needs no SetTerm call and no script at all.

JSON field Slot it answers _rawMissionName mission_name _rawMissionDescription mission_description _rawIntelThreatReport intel_threat_report _rawApTransmission ap_transmission _rawGwTransmission gw_transmission _rawApSuccessTransmission ap_success_transmission _rawApFailureTransmission ap_failure_transmission _rawGwSuccessTransmission gw_success_transmission _rawGwFailureTransmission gw_failure_transmission

An empty field counts as not filled, and the game falls back to the key.

Only these nine slots work this way. There is no tenth _raw* field: event_log.Create("missions/mymod_patrol/my_own_line") with no term behind it prints the raw key.

docs.title: Which to use
docs.text:
_raw* in JSON SetTerm in a script Needs a script no yes Number of texts exactly nine unlimited Languages one any, including ones the game does not ship Good for a mission whose text is fixed text that varies with what happened in flight

The two combine: raw text covers the nine standard slots, and a script adds its own terms for anything beyond them. The raf_collection example does exactly that: three missions ship raw text alone, and greenhorn_watch adds terms of its own so it can tell a different story depending on how experienced the crew is.

docs.title: Quest texts
docs.text:
Quest files carry keys, not text: _questTitle, _subQuestTitle and _subQuestDescription hold keys, and the game looks them up. The game's own quests use this pattern:

quest/<questId>/title
quest/<questId>/subQuest<N>_title
quest/<questId>/subQuest<N>_description

To give a mod quest its text, ship a small script in the mod's Missions/ folder that registers those keys:

QUEST_ID = "mymod_first_steps"

localization.SetTerm("en", "quest/{}/title".format(QUEST_ID), "First Steps")
localization.SetTerm("en", "quest/{}/subQuest0_title".format(QUEST_ID), "Clear the field")
localization.SetTerm("en", "quest/{}/subQuest0_description".format(QUEST_ID), "Fell five trees.")

The keys only have to match what the quest file says. See Quests.

docs.title: Placeholders
docs.text:
event_log.Create takes a dictionary that fills {[NAME]} placeholders:

localization.SetTerm("en", "mymod/pilot_tired",
                     "{[PILOT]} came back exhausted after {[HOURS]} hours in the air.")

event_log.Create("mymod/pilot_tired", {"PILOT": str(pilot_id), "HOURS": "6"})

Placeholder names are case-sensitive and must match exactly. Values must be strings, so wrap numbers and ids in str(...).

docs.title: Inline formatting
docs.text:
Three tags work inside any text:

Tag Effect [character:<id>] a clickable link to that character, shown as their name [resource:<name>] the resource's icon and color [morale:<name>] the morale category's icon and color

Combine them with placeholders to name a character from an event:

localization.SetTerm("en", "mymod/chat",
                     "[character:{[FIRST]}] talked to [character:{[SECOND]}] until dawn.")

event_log.Create("mymod/chat", {"FIRST": str(first_id), "SECOND": str(second_id)})

For resources and morale, put the game's own value into the text when the script loads:

from Blindflug.GameResources import ResourceType
from Blindflug.Game.Characters.Morale import MoraleCategory

localization.SetTerm("en", "mymod/mice",
                     "Mice got into the [resource:{}] again.".format(ResourceType.FoodRations))
localization.SetTerm("en", "mymod/good_chat",
                     "Their [morale:{}] improved.".format(MoraleCategory.Mood))

f-strings work as well, and the game's own scripts use them. Remember to double the braces of a placeholder inside an f-string: f"[character:{{[FIRST]}}] shared the [resource:{ResourceType.FoodRations}]".

docs.title: Languages
docs.text:
Always define English ("en"). When a term has no text in the player's language, the game falls back to a language that has it, which is English if you defined it, rather than showing the raw key.

To translate, call SetTerm once per language:

localization.SetTerm("en", "mymod/greeting", "Good morning, gentlemen.")
localization.SetTerm("de", "mymod/greeting", "Guten Morgen, meine Herren.")
localization.SetTerm("fr", "mymod/greeting", "Bonjour, messieurs.")

The game ships these language codes:

en, en-GB, de-DE, de, ar, bg, ca, zh-CN, zh-TW, cs, da, nl, fi, fr, el, hu, id, it, ja, ko, ms, nb, fa, pl, pt, pt-BR, ro, ru, es, es-419, sv, gsw-CH, th, tr, uk, vi

German is de - that is the language players pick in the options (de-DE in the list is a test language, you can ignore it). An unknown code is added automatically, so text for a language the game does not ship needs no preparation (the player still needs a way to select that language).

A handy pattern for several languages:

TEXTS = {
    "mymod/greeting": {
        "en": "Good morning, gentlemen.",
        "de": "Guten Morgen, meine Herren.",
    },
}

for key, translations in TEXTS.items():
    for language, text in translations.items():
        localization.SetTerm(language, key, text)

docs.title: When the mod is removed
docs.text:
Text registered with SetTerm exists only while the script that registered it is loaded. It is never written into the save game or into the game's files.

If a player removes or switches off your mod and loads a save:

  • Your terms are gone. Anything in the save that still points at one of your keys shows the raw key instead of the text. That applies to old event log lines your scripts wrote and to missions from your mod that were still waiting on the war map.
  • A key of the game's own that your mod had reworded shows the game's original text again.
  • Nothing is damaged; reinstalling the mod brings the text back.

Mission text from _raw* fields is copied into the mission when it is created, so a mission that was already on the war map keeps its name even after the mod is gone.

docs.title: Naming your keys
docs.text: Prefix every key with your mod name (mymod/...) so it cannot collide with the game or another mod: an existing key is silently overwritten. Mission keys are the exception, because they must follow missions/<missionId>/.... Make the mission id itself distinctive instead, which you should anyway.

docs.title: Steam Workshop
docs.text:
The Steam Workshop is how a finished mod reaches other players. You upload from inside the game, players subscribe on the Workshop page, and Steam delivers the mod to them. Players who do not use the Workshop can still install a mod by copying its folder by hand.

Workshop page for Ground of Aces: https://steamcommunity.com/app/2308690/workshop/

Steam version only

The Workshop needs the Steam version of the game, started through Steam. DRM-free builds (for example from a store without a Workshop) have no Workshop at all: they list no Workshop mods, and the Upload button only reports that Steam is not available. Mods in your own Mods folder work the same in every version, so players of a DRM-free build install by hand.

docs.title: Uploading your mod
docs.text:
1. Make the folder exactly what you want to ship. The whole mod folder is uploaded as it is - config.json, preview.png and every content subfolder. Remove test files, backups and notes you do not want to publish first.
  2. Give it a name and a picture. The Name in config.json becomes the Workshop title on a first upload (without a config.json the folder name is used). preview.png at the root of the mod folder becomes the Workshop picture. It must be a PNG of at most 1 MB; a larger file makes the upload fail with an error.
  3. Open Main menu → Mods and press Upload on the mod. Only your own mods (from your Mods folder) have this button; Workshop items you are subscribed to do not.
  4. Pick the target. A window lists Create new Workshop item... followed by every Workshop item you have published before. Pick Create new Workshop item... for a first upload, or one of your existing items to replace its contents with this version.
  5. Confirm. The game asks once more - "Do you want to create a new Workshop item for ...?" or, for an update, whether to use the existing item - and you answer Yes.
  6. Wait for the upload. The window shows the progress as a percentage. When it is done, a button opens the new item's Workshop page in the Steam overlay.

What the game sends with the upload:

Part New item Update of an existing item Files the whole mod folder the whole mod folder, replacing the old files Title the mod's Name left as it is Description none left as it is Picture preview.png, if there is one preview.png, if there is one Visibility public public Workshop tag Mod Mod

The description is always written on the item's Steam page; the game never sends one. To change the title of an item you already published, edit it on the Steam page too.

Tip

Steam may ask you to accept the Workshop legal agreement the first time you publish. Until you do, the item stays hidden. Open the item's Steam page and accept the agreement there, and the item becomes visible.

docs.title: Keep working after you publish
docs.text:
Your own copy in Mods always wins over the Workshop copy of the same mod (see Which mod wins). So you can stay subscribed to your published mod, keep editing the local folder, test, and upload again when you are happy. Pick your existing item in step 4 so players get the update instead of a second item.

Before you upload an update, think about players who are in the middle of a playthrough with your mod. Removing a quest, renaming a mission id or changing the order of quest steps can strand them. The Quests page explains what happens to quests in a running save.

docs.title: When the upload fails
docs.text: What you see What to do Steam not available Start the game through Steam. In a DRM-free build there is no Workshop. An error while fetching your items Check that Steam is online, then press Upload again. An upload error naming the preview image Make preview.png smaller than 1 MB (a smaller resolution, or fewer colours). Any other upload error The message includes Steam's error code. Try again later; if it keeps happening, ask in the Discord modding channel.

docs.title: Installing a mod from the Workshop
docs.text:
Subscribe to the item on the Steam Workshop. Steam downloads it into its own Workshop folder - nothing lands in your Mods folder - and the game lists it in the Mods window the next time it starts, or after you press Refresh. It is switched on by default and marked as a Workshop item. An item that Steam is still downloading does not appear until the download has finished.

The Workshop button in the Mods window opens the game's Workshop page in the Steam overlay, so you can browse and subscribe without leaving the game. Press Refresh afterwards.

Unsubscribing removes the mod again. Saves that used the mod keep loading. What happens to the content the mod added depends on the kind of content; for quests, see Quests.

docs.title: Installing a mod by hand
docs.text:
Copy the mod's folder into your Mods folder so that its config.json or its content subfolders sit directly inside it:

Mods/some_mod/CSV/...            correct
Mods/some_mod/some_mod/CSV/...   wrong - one folder too deep

A mod you downloaded as a .zip usually needs to be unpacked first; check that unpacking did not add that extra folder level. Then press Refresh in the Mods window or restart the game.

Where the Mods folder is on each platform is listed on How mods work. The quickest way there is Main menu → Mods → Open folder.

Warning

A mod can contain Python scripts, and scripts run whenever the mod is enabled. Only install mods from people you trust, and read Python mods and safety first.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text: Welcome to the flight line. This section takes you from "I own Ground of Aces on Steam" to "my own mission shows up in my game". No programming experience needed.

docs.title: Pick your door
docs.text: You are... Start here Never programmed. You have never opened a terminal and that is fine. Install on Windows or Install on Mac, then Your first mod in 10 minutes. Keep the Glossary open in a second tab. Want to dive in. You know your way around files and a text editor. Without an AI agent: copy an example, edit the JSON, validate, load it. Then How mods work. Using Claude or Codex. You already have an AI coding agent. Clone the kit (step 3 of the install pages), start your agent in the folder, and go to Your first mod in 10 minutes.

docs.title: Get access first
docs.text: During the developer preview the modkit is private. Before you install anything, email your GitHub username to nuria@blindflugstudios.com or moritz@blindflugstudios.com (no GitHub account yet? The install pages show how to make one - it is free). You will get an invitation email from GitHub; accept it, and the download step on the install pages works. Without the invitation, GitHub answers "Could not resolve to a Repository".

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Ground of Aces on Steam, on Windows or Mac.
  • A computer where you can install programs (admin rights).
  • About 20-30 minutes for the one-time setup below.
  • A free GitHub account. GitHub is the website where the modkit lives.

The install pages set up these tools for you, one command at a time:

Tool What it does for you Needed? Git Downloads the modkit and keeps it up to date Yes GitHub CLI (gh) Logs you in to GitHub from the terminal Yes Claude Code The AI agent that builds your mod Yes, for the AI route Python Runs the mod checker (validator) directly Optional, recommended

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text:
Honest up front

The modkit, the game's modding and the Steam Workshop are free. The AI agents are not.

  • Claude Code needs a paid Claude subscription (Pro or higher). The free Claude plan does not include it.
  • Codex needs a paid ChatGPT plan.

Don't want to pay for an AI? Everything also works by hand: see Without an AI agent. The in-game Mission Editor needs no tools at all.

docs.title: The whole journey in 5 steps
docs.text:
1. Install the tools once: Windows or Mac.
  2. Get the modkit: gh repo clone blindflugstudios/goa-modkit. You do this once. Later, git pull fetches updates. Your own mods live in the mods/ folder and are never touched by updates.
  3. Describe your mod to the agent in plain English, for example "Make me a mission where two Spitfires escort a damaged bomber home over the Channel."
  4. The agent builds it, checks it and copies it into the game's Mods folder.
  5. Load it in the game: open the Mods window, load your save, and fly. Your first mod in 10 minutes shows every click.

The 10 minutes count from step 2, once the tools are installed.

Stuck at any point? See When nothing happens or ask in the modding channel on Discord.

docs.title: Your first mod in 10 minutes
docs.text: You will describe a mission in plain English, let the agent build it, and fly it in your own game. The clock starts now, with the tools already installed (Windows / Mac).

docs.title: 1. Open the modkit and start the agent
docs.text:
Open the terminal and type:

WindowsMac 
cd ~\goa-modkit
git pull
claude

cd ~/goa-modkit
git pull
claude

git pull fetches the newest version of the kit. claude starts the agent. Always start it inside the goa-modkit folder: that is where it finds the rules, examples and skills that teach it how Ground of Aces mods work.

docs.title: 2. Describe your mission
docs.text:
Type this into Claude Code and press Enter:

Make me a mission where two Spitfires escort a damaged bomber home over the Channel.

Change anything you like: the planes, the place, the mood. Plain English is fine. The agent may ask a question or two, for example about difficulty. Answer them the same way.

docs.title: 3. Watch the agent work
docs.text:
The agent now does three jobs. It tells you what it is doing and asks before it changes files outside the kit. Answer Yes when it asks to create files or run the checker.

Job What happens Build (skill new-mission) Creates your mod in mods/, for example mods/channel_escort/Missions/channel_escort.json (numbers: stats, location, outcomes) and channel_escort.py (texts and radio messages). Check (skill validate) Runs the validator, which catches the mistakes that would crash the game or hide your mission. It fixes what it finds and runs the check again until it is clean. Install (skill install-mod) Copies the finished mod into the game's Mods folder.

The game's Mods folder is here:

WindowsMac 
%USERPROFILE%\AppData\LocalLow\Blindflug Studios\Ground Of Aces\Mods\

~/Library/Application Support/Blindflug Studios/Ground Of Aces/Mods/

When the agent says the mod is installed, note the mission id it tells you (for example channel_escort). You need it in a moment.

The agent cannot press buttons in your game

It builds, checks and copies. Loading the mod in the game is your job, and it takes a minute.

docs.title: 4. Load the mod in the game
docs.text:
The game reads mods when a game is loaded. So:

  1. Start Ground of Aces. If it is already running with a save open, go to Options → Quit to main menu first.
  2. In the main menu, open Mods. The list refreshes when the window opens. Your mod should be listed and switched on.
  3. Your mod has a Python file (the .py), so it also shows a Scripting switch. Switch it on and confirm - you wrote the scripts. (The current version of the game runs a mod's scripts either way, so this does no harm; see Python mods and safety.)
  4. Close the Mods window and load your save (or start a new game).

Restarting the whole game also works and is the safest option if anything looks off.

docs.title: 5. Find your mission
docs.text:
Your mission now joins the pool the game draws missions from, so it turns up on the war map when its conditions are met (for example a certain day or runway). To see it right now, use the cheat console:

  1. Open Options and switch on Cheats.
  2. A cheat button appears on the game screen. Click it to open the console.
  3. Type your mission id and press Enter:
create_mission channel_escort

You should see Mission created! in the console. Close the console and open the war map. There it is.

Assign crews and planes, send them off, and wait for the radio messages you asked for. That is your first mod.

More about the console: Cheat console.

docs.title: 6. Change something
docs.text:
Go back to the terminal and ask for a change, for example:

Make the mission harder and let the bomber crew radio in when they spot the English coast.

The agent edits, checks and copies the mod again. Then in the game: Options → Quit to main menu, load your save, and check the mission again. (If the change added a new folder to the mod, for example a first Quests/, open Mods once before loading.)

docs.title: If something goes wrong
docs.text:
• The mission does not show up, the texts look like missions/..., or the game complains: see When nothing happens.
  • Or just tell the agent: read my Player.log and tell me what went wrong. It knows where the game writes its log on your computer.

docs.title: Using Codex instead
docs.text:
Codex works the same way. It reads the kit's AGENTS.md, which holds the same rules the skills follow.

  1. Install and log in to Codex (needs a paid ChatGPT plan). See Codex.
  2. In the terminal: cd into goa-modkit, then type codex.
  3. Paste the same prompt. Codex builds, validates and copies the mod. Steps 4 and 5 in the game are the same.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Every technical word used in this handbook, in plain language.

docs.title: Computer basics
docs.text:
Terminal - A window where you type commands instead of clicking. On Windows it is called Terminal or PowerShell, on Mac it is called Terminal.

Command - One line you type into the terminal and confirm with Enter, for example git pull. The first word is the program, the rest tells it what to do.

Prompt - The text at the start of the terminal line (ending in > on Windows or % on Mac). It means the terminal is ready for the next command.

Folder / path - A folder is a directory on your disk. A path is its address, written as folder names joined by \ (Windows) or / (Mac), for example ~/goa-modkit/mods. The ~ is short for your personal home folder.

cd - "Change directory". Moves the terminal into a folder, so the next commands work there. cd ~/goa-modkit goes into the modkit.

PATH - The list of places where the terminal looks for programs. That is why you sometimes need to reopen the terminal after installing something.

Package manager - A program that installs other programs with one command. On Windows this handbook uses winget, on Mac Homebrew (brew).

Admin rights - Permission to install programs on a computer. Your own PC or Mac usually has them. A work or school computer may not.

docs.title: File types
docs.text:
JSON - A plain-text format for data, with "name": value pairs in curly braces. Mission numbers (stats, outcomes, timings) are JSON files ending in .json.

Python - A programming language. Mods use it for texts and for logic that reacts to what happens in the game. Script files end in .py. The game runs them with IronPython 3.4, an older Python built for .NET, so very new Python syntax does not work.

CSV - A table saved as plain text, one row per line, values separated by commas. Mods use CSV files to change game data such as building or plane stats.

Text editor - A program for editing plain-text files like JSON and Python. This handbook recommends Visual Studio Code. Word processors like Word are not text editors.

docs.title: Git and GitHub
docs.text:
Git - A program that downloads a project and keeps track of every change to it.

GitHub - The website where the modkit is published. You need a free account to use the GitHub CLI.

Repository (repo) - A project folder that Git tracks, with its full history. The modkit is a repository.

Clone - Downloading a repository to your computer for the first time: gh repo clone blindflugstudios/goa-modkit.

Pull - Fetching the latest changes of a repository you already cloned: git pull. Your own mods in mods/ are never touched.

CLI - "Command-line interface". A program you use by typing commands in the terminal instead of clicking.

GitHub CLI (gh) - GitHub's own terminal program. You use it to log in (gh auth login) and to clone the modkit.

Release - A published, numbered version of a project on GitHub, with ready-made files to download. The ready-made validator comes from the modkit's releases.

docs.title: AI agents
docs.text:
Agent - An AI program that can read files, write files and run commands on your computer to finish a task you describe. Claude Code and Codex are agents.

Claude Code - Anthropic's agent that runs in the terminal. Needs a paid Claude subscription (Pro or higher).

Codex - OpenAI's agent that runs in the terminal. Needs a paid ChatGPT plan.

Prompt (for an agent) - What you type to the agent: a request in plain English, like "make me a mission where...".

Skill - A written set of instructions in the modkit that teaches the agent one job, for example new-mission, validate or install-mod. The agent picks the right skill by itself.

AGENTS.md - The rulebook for agents in the modkit: folders, pitfalls, and the build, check, copy routine.

docs.title: Modding
docs.text:
Mod - A folder of files that adds to or changes the game: missions, quests, scripts, maps, objects or data tables.

Mods folder - Where the game looks for installed mods. Open it from the main menu: Mods → Open folder.

mods/ folder (in the modkit) - Where you and your agent build your own mods before they are copied to the game's Mods folder. Git ignores it, so updates never change it.

Content folder - A folder inside a mod whose name tells the game what is in it: Missions, Quests, Maps, Objects, CSV, TerrainObjects, Biomes.

Id - The unique name of a thing in the game, for example the mission id coastal_patrol. Ids must not contain spaces and must be unique: two missions with the same id replace each other.

Localization key - The name of a text, like missions/coastal_patrol/mission_name. The game looks up the key to find the text in the player's language. If the text is missing, you see the key itself.

Validator - The modkit's checker (goa_validate). It reads your mod and reports what would break in the game, without starting the game and without running your scripts.

Outcome - One of the four possible results of a mission (as planned or gone wrong, skill passed or failed). Every mission has exactly four.

Handler - A function in a mission or event script that the game calls at a certain moment, for example when a mission sends a radio message.

Mission Editor - The in-game tool, in the main menu, for creating missions without any files or tools.

Console / cheat console - A small window in the game where you type commands such as create_mission. Switch it on in Options → Cheats. See Cheat console.

Player.log - The text file where the game writes what it does and every error. The first place to look when a mod misbehaves. See When nothing happens.

Steam Workshop - Steam's page for sharing mods. Players subscribe to a mod there and Steam installs it for them.

Subscribe - Clicking Subscribe on a Workshop mod. Steam downloads it, and the game loads it next time.

docs.title: Install on Mac
docs.text:
This page sets up everything once. Take it one step at a time: type (or paste) the command, press Return, and compare what you see with "You should see". It takes about 20-30 minutes, mostly waiting for downloads.

You need macOS 13 (Ventura) or newer and your Mac's login password (an administrator account).

docs.title: 1. Open the terminal
docs.text:
The terminal is a window where you type commands instead of clicking. It looks old-fashioned, but you only need a handful of commands.

  1. Press Cmd+Space to open Spotlight.
  2. Type terminal.
  3. Press Return.

You should see a window with a line ending in %, for example:

yourname@MacBook ~ %

That line is the prompt. It means "ready, type a command".

Pasting

Copy a command from this page with the copy button in the corner of each box. In the terminal, paste with Cmd+V, then press Return.

docs.title: 2. Install Homebrew
docs.text:
Homebrew is an app installer for the terminal. Everything else on this page is installed with it.

Go to brew.sh, copy the install command shown at the top of the page (it starts with /bin/bash -c) and paste it into the terminal. At the time of writing it is:

/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"

What happens next:

  1. It asks for your Mac password. Type it and press Return. You will not see any characters while typing. That is normal.
  2. It tells you what it will install and asks you to press Return.
  3. It installs Apple's Xcode Command Line Tools if they are missing. This can take 5-15 minutes. A window may pop up asking to install them: click Install.

You should see Installation successful! near the end.

docs.title: The "Next steps" lines (Apple Silicon Macs)
docs.text:
On Macs with an Apple chip (M1, M2, M3, M4 ...) Homebrew ends with a section called ==> Next steps that shows two or three commands. They look like this:

echo >> /Users/yourname/.zprofile
echo 'eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"' >> /Users/yourname/.zprofile
eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"

Copy the lines from your own terminal (they contain your user name), paste them, and press Return. They tell the terminal where Homebrew lives. On older Intel Macs there are no such lines and you can skip this.

Check it:

brew --version

You should see something like Homebrew 4.4.10.

If it fails with "command not found: brew": you skipped the Next steps lines. Scroll up in the terminal, find them, run them. Or close the terminal, open it again and retry.

docs.title: 3. Install Git and the GitHub CLI
docs.text:
Git downloads the modkit and keeps it up to date. The GitHub CLI (gh) connects your terminal to GitHub, the website where the modkit lives.

brew install git gh

Check both:

git --version
gh --version

You should see something like git version 2.47.1 and gh version 2.63.0.

docs.title: 4. Install Claude Code
docs.text:
Claude Code is the AI agent that writes and checks your mods. Remember: it needs a paid Claude subscription (Pro or higher). No subscription? Skip to step 6 and use Without an AI agent later.

brew install --cask claude-code

Check it:

claude --version

You should see a version number followed by (Claude Code).

If it fails: close and reopen the terminal and try again. If it still fails, run claude doctor and paste its output into the Discord modding channel.

docs.title: 5. Optional: install Python (recommended)
docs.text:
Python lets the agent run the mod checker (the validator) directly. Without it the agent downloads a ready-made version of the checker instead, so this step is optional, but recommended.

brew install python

Check it:

python3 --version

You should see Python 3.x.x (3.9 or newer). On a Mac the command is python3, not python.

docs.title: 6. Create a GitHub account and log in
docs.text:
1. Go to github.com/signup and create a free account. Confirm your email.
  2. In the terminal, type:
gh auth login

It asks a few questions. Use the arrow keys and Return:

Question Choose Where do you use GitHub? GitHub.com What is your preferred protocol for Git operations? HTTPS Authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials? Yes How would you like to authenticate GitHub CLI? Login with a web browser

It then shows a one-time code like ABCD-1234. Press Return, your browser opens, paste the code, and click Authorize.

You should see ✓ Logged in as YourName in the terminal.

docs.title: 7. Get the modkit
docs.text:
Invitation needed

During the developer preview the modkit is private. This step only works once you have accepted the GitHub invitation - see Get access first.

This downloads the modkit into a folder called goa-modkit in your home folder. You do this once.

cd ~
gh repo clone blindflugstudios/goa-modkit
cd goa-modkit

You should see a few lines ending in done, and your prompt now shows goa-modkit.

Later, to get updates (new docs, examples, checker fixes), open the terminal and type:

cd ~/goa-modkit
git pull

Your own mods live in goa-modkit/mods/. Updates never touch that folder.

docs.title: 8. Start Claude Code and log in
docs.text:
Still inside the goa-modkit folder, type:

claude

The first time:

  1. Pick a color theme with the arrow keys and Return.
  2. Choose to log in with your Claude account (your subscription). Your browser opens. Log in and click Authorize.
  3. Claude Code asks whether you trust the files in this folder. Choose Yes.

You should see a box with a cursor where you can type. That is where you talk to the agent. Type /exit (or press Ctrl+C twice) to leave.

docs.title: Done
docs.text: You are ready for Your first mod in 10 minutes.

docs.title: Keeping tools up to date
docs.text:
Homebrew does not update Claude Code on its own. Every few weeks, run:

brew update
brew upgrade claude-code git gh

Close Claude Code before upgrading it.

docs.title: Install on Windows
docs.text:
This page sets up everything once. Take it one step at a time: type (or paste) the command, press Enter, and compare what you see with "You should see". It takes about 20-30 minutes, mostly waiting for downloads.

You need Windows 10 or 11 and permission to install programs on this PC.

docs.title: 1. Open the terminal
docs.text:
The terminal is a window where you type commands instead of clicking. It looks old-fashioned, but you only need a handful of commands.

  1. Press the Windows key.
  2. Type terminal.
  3. Click Terminal (on Windows 10 it may be called Windows PowerShell).

You should see a dark window with a line like:

PS C:\Users\YourName>

That line is the prompt. It means "ready, type a command". The PS tells you it is PowerShell, which is what this guide uses.

Pasting

Copy a command from this page with the copy button in the corner of each box. In the terminal, paste with right-click or Ctrl+V, then press Enter.

docs.title: 2. Check winget
docs.text:
winget is Windows' own app installer. It is built into Windows 10 and 11. Type:

winget --version

You should see a version number, for example v1.9.25200.

If it fails with "winget is not recognized": open the Microsoft Store, search for App Installer, click Update (or Get), then close and reopen the terminal and try again.

The first time you use winget it may ask you to accept the store terms. Type Y and press Enter.

docs.title: 3. Install Git
docs.text:
Git downloads the modkit and keeps it up to date. Claude Code also uses it on Windows.

winget install --id Git.Git -e

Windows may ask "Do you want to allow this app to make changes to your device?". Click Yes.

You should see a download bar and then Successfully installed.

Close and reopen the terminal now

Windows only learns about new programs in a fresh terminal window. Close the terminal and open it again (step 1). Do this after every install on this page.

Check it:

git --version

You should see something like git version 2.47.1.windows.1.

If it fails with "git is not recognized": you probably did not reopen the terminal. Close it, open it again, try once more.

docs.title: 4. Install the GitHub CLI
docs.text:
The GitHub CLI (gh) connects your terminal to GitHub, the website where the modkit lives.

winget install --id GitHub.cli -e

Close and reopen the terminal, then check:

gh --version

You should see something like gh version 2.63.0.

docs.title: 5. Install Claude Code
docs.text:
Claude Code is the AI agent that writes and checks your mods. Remember: it needs a paid Claude subscription (Pro or higher). No subscription? Skip to step 7 and use Without an AI agent later.

winget install Anthropic.ClaudeCode

Close and reopen the terminal, then check:

claude --version

You should see a version number followed by (Claude Code).

If it fails: reopen the terminal once more. If it still fails, run claude doctor and paste its output into the Discord modding channel.

docs.title: 6. Optional: install Python (recommended)
docs.text:
Python lets the agent run the mod checker (the validator) directly. Without it the agent downloads a ready-made version of the checker instead, so this step is optional, but recommended.

winget install --id Python.Python.3.12 -e

Close and reopen the terminal, then check:

python --version

You should see Python 3.12.x.

If the Microsoft Store opens instead: close it, reopen the terminal and try again. If it keeps happening, open Settings → Apps → Advanced app settings → App execution aliases and switch off the two python entries.

docs.title: 7. Create a GitHub account and log in
docs.text:
1. Go to github.com/signup and create a free account. Confirm your email.
  2. In the terminal, type:
gh auth login

It asks a few questions. Use the arrow keys and Enter:

Question Choose Where do you use GitHub? GitHub.com What is your preferred protocol for Git operations? HTTPS Authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials? Yes How would you like to authenticate GitHub CLI? Login with a web browser

It then shows a one-time code like ABCD-1234. Press Enter, your browser opens, paste the code, and click Authorize.

You should see ✓ Logged in as YourName in the terminal.

docs.title: 8. Get the modkit
docs.text:
Invitation needed

During the developer preview the modkit is private. This step only works once you have accepted the GitHub invitation - see Get access first.

This downloads the modkit into a folder called goa-modkit inside your user folder. You do this once.

cd ~
gh repo clone blindflugstudios/goa-modkit
cd goa-modkit

You should see a few lines ending in done, and your prompt now ends in goa-modkit>.

Later, to get updates (new docs, examples, checker fixes), open the terminal and type:

cd ~\goa-modkit
git pull

Your own mods live in goa-modkit\mods\. Updates never touch that folder.

docs.title: 9. Start Claude Code and log in
docs.text:
Still inside the goa-modkit folder, type:

claude

The first time:

  1. Pick a color theme with the arrow keys and Enter.
  2. Choose to log in with your Claude account (your subscription). Your browser opens. Log in and click Authorize.
  3. Claude Code asks whether you trust the files in this folder. Choose Yes.

You should see a box with a cursor where you can type. That is where you talk to the agent. Type /exit (or press Ctrl+C twice) to leave.

docs.title: Done
docs.text: You are ready for Your first mod in 10 minutes.

docs.title: Keeping tools up to date
docs.text:
winget does not update these tools on its own. Every few weeks, run:

winget upgrade Anthropic.ClaudeCode
winget upgrade --id Git.Git -e
winget upgrade --id GitHub.cli -e

Close Claude Code before upgrading it.

docs.title: When nothing happens
docs.text: Most mod problems come from a handful of causes. Find your symptom, then try the fix. If you use an agent, the fastest fix is often one sentence: read my Player.log and tell me what went wrong.

docs.title: First, always
docs.text:
1. Run the validator on your mod. It catches most of the problems below before the game ever sees them. Ask the agent to validate my mod, or see Without an AI agent.
  2. Reload properly: Options → Quit to main menu, open Mods, then load your save. If in doubt, restart the game.

docs.title: Symptom, cause, fix
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Fix My mod is not in the Mods window The mod is not where the game looks, or its content is not in a content folder. The game only sees Mods/<your mod>/Missions/... (or Quests/, Maps/, CSV/ ...). A Missions folder with nothing in it counts as empty. Open Mods → Open folder and check the structure. The mod folder must sit directly in Mods, and the files inside a folder named exactly Missions. My mod is listed but switched off It was switched off in the Mods window. Switch it on, then load your save again. My mod folder is there but ignored It is a shortcut, alias or linked folder. The game skips those on purpose. Copy the real folder into Mods. The agent's install-mod skill always copies. The mission never appears Its appearance rules are not met yet: _missionRequirements such as a minimum day (EarliestAppearanceDay) or runway tier (RunwayTier), or the mission's _tags do not match the map you play. Or the game has simply not drawn it yet. Test with the console: create_mission <your_mission_id> creates it right away. If that says Unknown mission ID, the mission did not load: check the Player.log. The game breaks when my mission ends (error in the log, no result) _missionOutcomes does not have exactly 4 entries. The game only notices when it picks the result. Give it exactly 4 outcomes in the fixed order. The validator reports this as an error. The mission breaks when the crew's skill is rolled _missionStats has fewer than 2 entries. Add a second stat. The first is rolled when the mission goes as planned, the second when it goes wrong. My changes to the mission are ignored A mission with the same id is saved in the Missions folder (next to Mods), for example from the in-game Mission Editor. That folder is loaded last and wins over every mod. Delete or rename that copy in the Missions folder, or give your mod mission a different id. One of two missions is missing, or the wrong one shows Two missions share an id. One silently replaces the other, and which one wins can differ between computers. Give every mission a unique id. The validator reports duplicates. I changed a function in my script, nothing changed When a mission has a JSON file, the JSON supplies the numbers, and some script functions (for example the one for the icon) are never called. Change the value in the JSON instead. The validator warns about functions the game never calls. Texts show things like missions/my_mission/mission_name, or null The text for that key was never set: a typo in the key, a missing localization.SetTerm line, or the script did not load at all. Compare the key in the text with the key in SetTerm. If all texts are missing, the script failed to load: check the Player.log. The whole script seems to be skipped It uses Python syntax newer than the game's Python (IronPython 3.4) understands: the walrus :=, a match statement, or positional-only / parameters. The game skips the entire file. Rewrite those lines in older syntax. f-strings are fine. The validator reports these as errors. My new or changed quest does not show up Quests are read each time a save loads, but a brand-new Quests/ folder is only noticed after the Mods window rescans. Options → Quit to main menu, open Mods (or press Refresh), then load your save. My CSV changes do not apply Table changes are merged when a game is loaded. Quit to main menu and load your save again. The console says Unknown cheat A typo, or a command that does not exist in your version. Type help to list all commands. Press Tab to complete a command name.

docs.title: Find the Player.log
docs.text:
The game writes everything it does, including every error, into a text file called Player.log. It is rewritten each time the game starts, and the previous run is kept as Player-prev.log. Look at it right after the problem, before restarting the game.

System Where Windows %USERPROFILE%\AppData\LocalLow\Blindflug Studios\Ground Of Aces\Player.log Mac ~/Library/Logs/Blindflug Studios/Ground Of Aces/Player.log Linux ~/.config/unity3d/Blindflug Studios/Ground Of Aces/Player.log WindowsMac

Press Windows+R, paste %USERPROFILE%\AppData\LocalLow\Blindflug Studios\Ground Of Aces, press Enter, and open Player.log with Notepad or VS Code.

In Finder, press Cmd+Shift+G, paste ~/Library/Logs/Blindflug Studios/Ground Of Aces/, press Return, and open Player.log with TextEdit or VS Code.

Search it (Ctrl+F / Cmd+F) for your mod's name, your mission id, Error or Exception.

docs.title: Hand it to the agent
docs.text:
You do not need to read the log yourself. In Claude Code (or Codex), inside the goa-modkit folder, type:

read my Player.log and tell me what went wrong with my mod

The agent knows where the log lives on your system, finds the lines about your mod and suggests a fix.

docs.title: Still stuck?
docs.text: Ask in the modding channel on Discord. Attach your Player.log, the validator output, and your mod folder as a zip.

docs.title: Without an AI agent
docs.text: Everything an agent does, you can do by hand. There are two routes.

docs.title: The easiest route: the in-game Mission Editor
docs.text:
No tools, no terminal. In the main menu, open the Mission Editor, create a mission, fill in the fields and save. The editor checks your mission when you save and refuses to save one that would break. Missions you save there land in the Missions folder next to the game's Mods folder and are loaded with your next game.

See Write your first mission for a guided tour.

docs.title: The hand-made route: copy an example and edit it
docs.text: This gives you a real mod folder you can share on the Steam Workshop later. You need a text editor and, for the check in step 4, Python (see the install pages for Windows or Mac). You also need the modkit on your computer, either with gh repo clone blindflugstudios/goa-modkit or by downloading it from the GitHub page (green Code button → Download ZIP, then unzip).

docs.title: 1. Get a proper text editor
docs.text: Use Visual Studio Code (free, Windows and Mac). It colors JSON and Python, shows mistakes like a missing comma, and lets you open the whole modkit folder with File → Open Folder. Notepad and TextEdit work in a pinch, but TextEdit must be in plain text mode (Format → Make Plain Text).

docs.title: 2. Copy the example
docs.text:
Inside the modkit, make this folder structure and copy the two files from examples/coastal_patrol/ into it:

goa-modkit/
  mods/
    my_first_mod/
      Missions/
        coastal_patrol.json
        coastal_patrol.py

The folder name Missions matters: the game looks for content by folder name. The mod folder name (my_first_mod) is up to you.

docs.title: 3. Edit it
docs.text:
Open coastal_patrol.json. Try small changes first, save, and check each one:

"_maxPlaneSlots": 2,
"_asPlannedChance": 80,

Raise _maxPlaneSlots to 3 to allow three planes, or lower _asPlannedChance to make things go wrong more often.

Open coastal_patrol.py and change the texts inside the quotes, for example the mission name:

_term("mission_name", "Coastal Patrol")

Three things not to break

  • _missionOutcomes must have exactly 4 entries, in their order.
  • _missionStats must have at least 2 entries.
  • The file names and the id returned by get_mission_id in the .py must match. If you rename the mission, rename both files and the MISSION_ID line together.

Missions reference explains every field.

docs.title: 4. Check it with the validator
docs.text:
The validator reads your mod and tells you what would go wrong in the game, without starting the game. Open the terminal in the modkit folder and run:

WindowsMac 
cd ~\goa-modkit
python tools\validator\goa_validate.py mods\my_first_mod

cd ~/goa-modkit
python3 tools/validator/goa_validate.py mods/my_first_mod

You should see a summary line like 2 file(s) checked - 0 error(s), 0 warning(s), 0 note(s).

Each problem is printed as file:line: error: ... with a hint underneath. Fix the line it names, save, run again. Errors must go. Warnings are worth reading.

docs.title: 5. Copy it into the game
docs.text:
Copy the whole my_first_mod folder into the game's Mods folder. The quickest way to open that folder: in the game's main menu, Mods → Open folder. Or paste the path into Explorer or Finder:

WindowsMac

Paste into the Explorer address bar:

%USERPROFILE%\AppData\LocalLow\Blindflug Studios\Ground Of Aces\Mods\

In Finder, press Cmd+Shift+G and paste:

~/Library/Application Support/Blindflug Studios/Ground Of Aces/Mods/

Copy the folder, do not create a shortcut or alias: the game skips linked folders.

docs.title: 6. Load it and fly
docs.text:
1. If a save is open, Options → Quit to main menu.
  2. Open Mods. Your mod is listed. It has a .py file, so it also shows a Scripting switch: switch it on and confirm (the current game runs the scripts either way).
  3. Load your save.
  4. Turn on Options → Cheats, open the console with the cheat button and type create_mission coastal_patrol. The mission appears on the war map.

After each later change: validate, copy again (replace the old files), Quit to main menu, load your save (open Mods first if you added a new folder such as Quests/).

Nothing happening? See When nothing happens.

docs.title: Ground of Aces Modkit
docs.text:
Developer Preview - Nutzung auf eigene Gefahr

Dieses Modkit ist eine Developer Preview. Alles hier - die Doku, die Werkzeuge, die Regeln und die Modding-Funktionen des Spiels selbst - kann sich jederzeit ohne Ankündigung ändern. Lesen darf jeder, das Kit selbst gibt es zurzeit nur auf Einladung - siehe "Zugang bekommen" unten. Du nutzt es auf eigene Gefahr: Sichere deine Spielstände, bevor du eine Mod ausprobierst, und verlass dich nicht darauf, dass etwas so bleibt, wie es ist.

Bau deine eigenen Missionen, Quests, Ereignisse, Karten und vieles mehr für Ground of Aces. Kein Unity, kein Compiler - ein Mod ist ein Ordner voller Textdateien. Und wenn du magst, schreibt ein KI-Agent sie für dich.

Ich habe noch nie programmiert Fang hier an. Wir installieren alles gemeinsam, Schritt für Schritt, und zehn Minuten später ist dein erster Mod im Spiel.

Ich will direkt loslegen Du kennst dich mit Dateien und Ordnern aus. Beispiel kopieren, ändern, neu laden - fertig.

Ich nutze Claude Code oder Codex Klone dieses Repository, starte deinen Agenten darin und beschreib den Mod, den du willst. Der Agent kennt die Regeln.

docs.title: Zugang bekommen
docs.text: Die Doku ist für alle offen. Das Modkit selbst - das Repository mit Beispielen, Vorlagen, Validator und KI-Regeln - ist während der Preview privat. Für einen Zugang schick eine kurze Mail mit deinem GitHub-Benutzernamen an nuria@blindflugstudios.com oder moritz@blindflugstudios.com. Erzähl uns gern, was du bauen möchtest - wir freuen uns darauf.

docs.title: Was du bauen kannst
docs.text: Was es ist Einstieg Missionen Flüge, auf die der Spieler Flugzeuge schickt, mit vier möglichen Ausgängen Missionen Ketten und Kampagnen Missionen, die sich gegenseitig freischalten, historische Operationen an ihrem echten Datum Ketten und Kampagnen Ereignis-Skripte Python, das auf das reagiert, was auf dem Stützpunkt und in der Luft passiert Scripting Quests Checklisten, die den Spieler anleiten Quests Spieldaten Flugzeuge, Gebäude, Angriffe, Kosten - dreh an den Zahlen CSV-Tabellen Karten und Grafik Eigene Karten, Modelle, Geländeobjekte und Biome Karten Workshop Teil deinen Mod mit allen Spielern Steam Workshop

docs.title: So funktioniert es in einer Minute
docs.text:
1. Öffne das Spiel und geh auf Hauptmenü (Main menu) → Mods → Open folder.
  2. Leg dort einen Mod-Ordner ab - zum Beispiel eine Kopie eines der Beispiele.
  3. Zurück im Spiel: Geh ins Hauptmenü, öffne einmal Mods (dabei wird der Ordner neu eingelesen) und lade deinen Spielstand.

Das ist schon die ganze Runde - die Details stehen unter Testen und neu laden. Alles andere auf dieser Seite dreht sich darum, was du in diesen Ordner legst.

docs.title: Komm zur Staffel
docs.text:
• Fragen, Ideen, Angeben: der Modding-Kanal auf Discord
  • Einen Fehler auf dieser Seite gefunden? Öffne ein Issue oder verbessere die Seite selbst mit dem Stift-Symbol oben.
  • Mod fertig? Stell ihn in den Steam Workshop.

docs.title: Beispiele
docs.text:
Vollständige, funktionierende Mods zum Lesen, Kopieren und Verändern. Jeder Ordner in examples/ hat eine eigene README, die erklärt, worauf du achten solltest.

Der schnellste Weg zu deiner eigenen Mission: Kopier coastal_patrol, benenne die Dateien und die Id um und ändere die Zahlen und den Text.

docs.title: Die Beispiele, grob nach Anspruch sortiert
docs.text: Ordner Was es ist coastal_patrol Eine Mission: eine JSON-Datei und ein kleines Skript. Fang hier an. Es ist das fertige Ergebnis von Deine erste Mission. raf_collection Fünf eigenständige Missionen, jede zeigt eine andere Mechanik. Drei tragen ihren Text im JSON und brauchen kein Skript. night_interception ist das lange ausgearbeitete Beispiel, in dem das Handler-Modell Zeile für Zeile erklärt wird. event_script Python, das auf die Basis und auf Missionen reagiert, die du nicht geschrieben hast. Keine eigene Mission. Siehe Events. chain_convoy Eine Gabelung: Eine Mission führt zu einer von zwei anderen, je nachdem, wie sie ausgegangen ist. chain_airfield Eine Kette mit vier Stufen, komplett in JSON. campaign_kanalkampf Eine Kampagne mit Gedächtnis: Bedingungen, die JSON nicht ausdrücken kann, weil dabei gezählt wird. script_only_scramble Eine Mission ganz ohne JSON, die sich selbst aus Python heraus sperrt und skaliert. quests Drei Quest-Dateien: eine einfache Einstiegsquest, eine Folgequest und eine Quest, die zu einer bestimmten Karte gehört. Siehe Quests.

docs.title: Kette oder Kampagne?
docs.text:
Die zwei Missionssets unten in der Liste lohnen einen Vergleich.

Kette (chain_convoy, chain_airfield) Kampagne (campaign_kanalkampf) Fragt "War Mission X erfolgreich?" "Wie oft?", "Wer war an Bord?", "Was hat der Spieler gewählt?" Gebaut mit JSON-Voraussetzungen (CompletedMission) einem Skript, das entscheidet, plus einer Zustandsdatei Gedächtnis keins: spielt sich jedes Mal gleich merkt sich Dinge über Flüge, Tage und Sitzungen hinweg Übersteht Speichern und Laden ja, von selbst ja, weil das Skript seinen Zustand in eine Datei schreibt Braucht Python nein (die Skripte in den Ketten-Beispielen tragen nur Text) ja

Eine Kette stellt eine Ja-oder-Nein-Frage über die Mission davor, und das kann JSON allein. Eine Kampagne fragt nach dem ganzen Spieldurchlauf, und dafür braucht es ein Skript und einen Ort, an dem der Zustand gespeichert wird. Ketten und Kampagnen erklärt beides.

docs.title: Ein Beispiel verwenden
docs.text:
1. Kopier die Dateien des Beispielordners in den Missions/-Ordner einer Mod: Mods/my_mod/Missions/. (Das quests-Beispiel ist als ganze Mod aufgebaut; kopier den Ordner selbst nach Mods/.)
  2. Benenne die Ids um. Die Beispiele verwenden kurze Ids wie coastal_patrol, weil sie Dokumentation sind. Eine echte Mod setzt ihren Namen vor jede Id (mymod_coastal_patrol) und ändert sie überall, wo sie vorkommt: in den Dateinamen, bei MISSION_ID im Skript, in CompletedMission-Werten und in CreateMission-Aufrufen.
  3. Lass den Validator über deinen Mod-Ordner laufen (siehe Ohne KI-Agent).
  4. Lade einen Spielstand und prüfe das Ergebnis, siehe Testen und neu laden.

Eine Beispiel-Id, die mit einer eingebauten Mission übereinstimmt, würde diese ersetzen. Keines der Beispiele tut das, aber deine umbenannte Kopie sollte es auch nicht.

docs.title: Wie weit jedes Beispiel getestet ist
docs.text:
Jedes Beispiel wurde vom Spiel geladen. Wie weit es jeweils getestet wurde, ist unterschiedlich:

Beispiel Getestet coastal_patrol im Spiel geladen und erstellt; noch nicht bis zum Ende geflogen raf_collection alle fünf im Spiel erstellt; night_interception bis zum Ende geflogen event_script bestätigt, dass die Handler aus dem Missions/-Ordner einer Mod feuern chain_convoy im Spiel geladen und erstellt; die Verzweigung noch nicht geflogen chain_airfield das Freischalten im Spiel bestätigt; die Flüge noch nicht der Reihe nach durchgespielt campaign_kanalkampf im Spiel geflogen; die Schwierigkeitsanpassung über mehrere Angriffe gemessen script_only_scramble noch nicht im Spiel getestet

"Geladen" heißt, das Spiel hat die Dateien gelesen und create_mission hat die Mission mit den geschriebenen Werten erzeugt; "geflogen" heißt, eine Staffel ist gestartet und der Ausgang wurde beobachtet.

docs.title: KI-Agenten
docs.text:
